en: May that Lord of the Gaṇas protect you all—he whose neck, adorned by the flowing ichor of his temples, shines like a garland of rudrākṣa beads encircled by a swarm of bees. || 1 ||
Where are the utterances of Kālidāsa, and where are we, his commentators?
This is like entering a theater with a dim lamp.
Although the greatness of this exalted source would be [sufficient] for those eager for their own renown, nevertheless, we compose this *pañjikā* on the birth of Skanda. (3)

For here, considering that for great poets who act with circumspection, at the commencement of a poetic work, just as the praise of one's chosen deity is the cause of prosperity, so too is the proclamation of an exalted subject; the poet Śrī Kālidāsa says:
"There exists in the northern quarter a king of mountains named Himālaya, whose very nature is divine.
Stretching across the eastern and western oceans, he stands like a measuring rod of the earth. (1)
In the northern direction, there is the king of mountains, the lord of the earth named Himālaya;
he exists even today.
Since mountains are commonly regarded as being of a stationary nature, the author speaks of him as "the divine self" (devatātmā) in order to dispel that misconception.
The meaning is that his self is of divine form, belonging to him who possesses a mobile (human) form;
and that he stands having plunged into and crossed over both the eastern and western oceans—this is an expression of his supreme greatness.
And from this, he is figuratively conceived as being like a measuring rod for the earth.

For by its pervasion of the two oceans, the earth becomes as if measured; "measurement" (*mā*) means the act of measuring, and for that purpose there is the staff (*daṇḍa*). Regarding this, those who consider themselves wise have exerted their efforts in vain by attempting to forbid the displacement of the word *iva*; whether that [word] is displaced or not, no harm whatsoever is done to the actual fact by such a thing.
For great poets are seen employing words such as *iva* and others in similes and similar constructions by means of any word whatsoever;
for example:
"like the wind from the eastern ocean."
For here, in some places the word *iva* is used with a nominative case ending, in some places with a genitive case ending,
and in some places as in "as one desiring the festival of the twilight dance" (*sandhyānṛttotsavecchor iva*).

Thus, by means of this qualifying word, there is no alteration of the meaning whatsoever. If the word *eva* (indeed/only) were connected with "earth" (*pṛthivyā*), then the distinction between this as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and that as *upamā* (simile) based on the "measuring rod" would be entirely groundless;
therefore, in every respect, this ornament is simply *utprekṣā*.

Furthermore, the displacement of the word *eva* does not contradict the definition [of the particle], because when it is compounded with *iva*, the elision of the case-ending is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*) and not for the sake of making the compound obligatory (*nityasamāsa*).

For such usage is observed in a great many instances, as in: "The two elephants, their temples smeared with ichor, were as if facing all directions" (*kacācitau viṣvagivāgajau gajau*), and "She whose beautiful sprouts were bound together was like a garland made of green leaves by the hosts of Maruts" (*haritapatramayīva marudgaṇaiḥ sragiva naddhamanoramapallavā*).
And so forth. Enough of this digression. One who rules over (*adhirājate*) is an *adhirāja*, a sovereign lord (*prabhu*).
[The suffix] *ac* is applied after *padya* in the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Alternatively, he is both superior (*adhika*) and a king (*rājā*).

*Adhirājaḥ*: [formed] by *ṭac* according to the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaḥ ṭac*. The word *nāma* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) that indicates recognition; it does not have the sense of a proper name (*saṃjñā*), because that would result in its failing to be expressive.
In this composition, the meter is *upajāti*:
in some places it is *indravajrā*, in some *upendravajrā*, in some *ākhyānikā*, and in some *viparītā*.
This is because, throughout, with the exception of the first syllable, there is a similarity in the arrangement of heavy and light syllables across all four other quarters.
In that regard, when the first syllable is heavy in all four feet, it is Indravajrā,
as in "āmekhalam" and so forth;
when it is light, it is Upendravajrā, as in "vanecarāṇām" and so forth.
When these two are combined, fourteen varieties of *upajātis* arise.
Among them, when the first syllable of the first and third quarters is heavy (*guru*) and that of the second and fourth is light (*laghu*), it is called *ākhyānikā*;
for example, this very same verse. When this is reversed, however, it is *viparītākhyānikā*; for example, [the verse beginning with] "padaṃ..."
"Tuṣārasruti," and so forth.
Elsewhere, the remaining twelve varieties are *upajātis*,
such as "Yaṃ sarvaśailāḥ," and so forth.
Thus, by others who have conducted such a subtle investigation, it was stated that everything [stated] subsequently in the Upajāti meters is indeed entirely correct. || 1 ||
When Meru stood as the skilled milker and all the mountains conceived him as the calf,
they milked from the earth— as directed by Pṛthu— the radiant jewels and great medicinal herbs.
Having conceived the Himavat as the calf, all the mountains beginning with Mandara milked the earth of jewels and great medicinal herbs;
the verb *duh* (to milk) takes two objects.
By the word "yat" (which), the king of mountains is referred to in every instance. When did they milk it?
While I stand as the milker, since he is skilled in milking and expert in the act of extraction—
what kind of earth?
One that was instructed in the art of milking by Pṛthu, the first king, the son of Vena.
For first he milked all the crops;
then, by his direction, the sages, gods, asuras, ancestors, serpents, rākṣasas, gandharvas, mountains, and trees [milked them].
And there, for each of these, there were distinct calves, milkers, and milks according to their respective divisions.
And when she was milked by the mountains, then Himavat was the calf, Meru the milker, and the jewels and medicinal herbs were the milk; such is the traditional account.
As it has been said:
"O King, it is heard that the Earth was milked again by the mountains."
The herbs in their embodied forms and various kinds of jewels were the milk;
the Himavat was the calf, and the great mountain Meru was the milker.
One whose primary concern is her calf is "milk-yielding" (kṣīrasrāvikā). And it is said: "Behold my calf, so that I, out of maternal affection, may flow with milk. (2)
For Him, from whom an endless stream of jewels originates, even snow has not become a destroyer of His splendor;
for a single defect is submerged in a multitude of virtues, like the spot on the moon amidst its rays.

Of that Himavat, the snow—the frost which destroys good fortune and cuts short beauty—was never born, nor did it ever come into being. For he is the source (*prabhava*) of endless jewels; "source" means that from which things arise, for he is the ancestral home of a multitude of excellent objects. One might ask: if he is the source of abundant jewels, why does the carrying of this wicked snow not constitute a fault? To this he replies: because when there is a gathering or collection of many virtues, a single defect sinks away, is submerged, and perishes; it does not cause defilement.
Just as there is a mark called a hare produced upon the moon's nectar-shedding rays—the suffix *kta* being used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). (3)
And he who, with his peaks, bears a richness of minerals that produces the playful ornaments of the celestial nymphs,
appearing like an untimely twilight with its colors distributed by fragments of clouds.
And that Lord of Mountains (Aga-īśa), who by his peaks possesses the state of being rich in minerals—that is, the quality of having minerals—carries that mineral-richness with his summits.

Here, "minerals" (dhātavaḥ) refers to red substances such as vermilion; he is "rich in minerals" (dhātumān) because those [red substances] exist in him. The meaning is that he supports minerals. Of what kind [is that mineral-richness]?
She who brings about—that is, prepares—the playful charms, amorous gestures, and ornaments such as forehead-marks for the sake of the celestial nymphs' dalliance;

likewise, she by whom a redness or glow is distributed and bestowed upon the fragments of clouds, that is, upon the masses of rain-clouds. And thus she is metaphorically described as being like an untimely twilight.
It is said that at the time of twilight, there are red clouds;
even at midday and other times, such an inference arises from observing crimson clouds.
By the mention of "unseasonable," it is understood that the clouds are always imbued with color.
And this is poetic fancy (utprekṣā), not simile (upamā). For that which is possible is indeed offered as the object of comparison;
an "unseasonable twilight" does not exist anywhere.
In poetic fancy, however, the cause is simply its appearing as such through direct perception.
Just as—
having left its temples for a moment in the sky with outspread wings,

a blue-colored swarm of bees shone upon the elephant, appearing as if it had become separate from them, even though color is a quality that resides in a substance, while the elephant was submerged within the flood of water. (4)
Having sought refuge beneath the shade of clouds moving as far as their mountain-waists,
the Siddhas, distressed by the rains, take shelter on its sun-drenched peaks.
Whose sunlit peaks and summits the Siddhas resort to and frequent;
for "the Siddhas are declared by the wise to be those who have attained the eightfold sovereign powers.
Having done what?

Having resorted to the shade cast beneath the dense clouds as they wander down to the very edge of the mountain slopes—shade falling upon the foothills (upatyakā)—and thus being distressed by the rains, they ascend the peaks radiant with the sun's glow to dispel the cold; this is said to emphasize their great height. "Mekhala" refers to the middle region of the mountain. Ā... [text fragment]
In the expression *āmekhalam* from *mekhalā*, the prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*) or inclusion (*abhividhi*), according to the rule: *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ*.

In that place, even without seeing the tracks of the elephants they have slain, the Kirātas discern the path of the lions by means of the pearls released from the hollows of their claws, which have been washed clean of blood by the flow of melting snow.

Where the Kirātas and Pulindas know the path—the route of lions that have torn out elephants—[the poet says this] because they might sometimes see a track marked by blood due to having slain an elephant: "even without seeing a footprint," since [the ground] has its blood washed away by the flow of frost, that is, cleansed of blood by melting snow. How then?
He says they are "knowing" [the pearls]—by means of pearls released from the hollows of their claws, which have emerged from the cavities of their paws.

As the lions are engaged in tearing apart the temples of elephants, the pearls enter the openings of their claws; then, as those lions move about, those pearls which have fallen and remain there are what he refers to.
The description of prosperity:
There, pearls served as indicators of the path to lions for the Kirātas who were seeking the supreme Victor;
yet, no one else had any claim over them. (6)
Where birch-bark, reddened by the spots of elephants and inscribed with letters using mineral pigments,
serves as the medium for love-letters written by the beautiful Vidyādhara maidens.

There, the barks of the *bhūrja* trees attain utility and reach fulfillment by conveying the amorous messages of the beautiful Vidyadhara maidens, but not through the operation of income and expenditure. Of what sort are these barks?
They have characters inscribed upon them—letters written with mineral pigments such as vermilion and other substances.

Therefore, because the syllables are red like the spots on an elephant, they are "lohitāḥ" (red). For those who know [the matter] state that in the fifth stage, drops of blood issue forth from the lords of elephants;
and because of the similarity in color and configuration with the letters of the Dhātu script, even though [these names] are not well-known [in common usage], [they are appropriate].

"Kuñjarabindava" is the point of comparison. This word "dhātu," being used in a general sense, applies to both red and white [substances]. As it is said: "Red with the streams of liquid mineral-ore from the slopes of the Sunrise Mountain, as if with masses of clinging blood."
And as in: "Behold the twilight glow, as it were, distributed among the peaks of the mountain;
the richness of minerals, as it were, an untimely twilight."
And so it is; as in the expression "garments dyed with lac.

These and others who, through lack of understanding, claim that the redness in the veins of birch bark is natural—that is indeed worthy of neglect, for it is devoid of both the weight of evidence and the reality of the matter.
Filling the hollows of the kīcaka reeds with the wind rising from the mouths of its caves,
it seems as if it wishes to assume the role of providing a stage for the kinnaras who are about to sing aloud.

That mountain, as if desiring to assume the role of a provider of resting places for the *kiṃnaras* who wished to sing and were about to sing, seemed as if it intended to grant them a place; that is, it was as if it desired to attain the state of being a "provider of places"—one whose nature is to bestow the granting of space through its resonance.
For this reason, it pervaded the hollows of the *kīcaka* bamboos with the wind arising from the mouth of its caves.
For when one wishes to play, the flute-player provides the space for the bamboo;
the bamboos, possessing their own resonance, are called *kīcakas*. (8)

There, the wind, made fragrant by the scents of the Sarala trees whose trunks were rubbed against by elephants to relieve the itching of their temples, perfumes the mountain plateaus with the flowing resin.
Where the wind, by means of the fragrances and scents belonging to the devadāru trees whose sap has flowed out and whose essence has dissolved, makes the ridges fragrant—that is, sweet-smelling.
To explain the cause of this flow of sap, he asks: "Of what kind [of trees]? and answers: "By rubbing."
The elephants have split [the mountain] in order to dispel—that is, to remove—the itching of their temples;
so say those who proclaim [this]. The word *sānu* may optionally be masculine.
There, for the forest-dwellers accompanied by their wives, the medicinal herbs—whose luster is cast upon the interior of cave-dwellings—serve as oil-less lamps for lovemaking during the night. (10)
Where, at night, for the Pulindas dwelling in the forest who are joined with young women, medicinal herbs serve as lamps for the sake of amorous play.

He states the distinction from other lamps due to the pervasion of their brilliance: "filled with oil" means *tailapūrāḥ*; "not filled with oil" (*atailapūrāḥ*) means they are not artificial because they are natural. The caves themselves are the houses; those whose radiance is fixed or attached within the interior of those [caves] are so described.
"Friends of women" (*vanitāsakhāḥ*) means "companions of women. [The suffix] *ṭac* is applied according to the rule: *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac*.
Even on a path where the snow has turned to solid ice,
the horse-faced goddesses do not break their slow gait, though they suffer from the heavy burden of their hips and breasts which press against their toes and heels.

There, even on a path where the snow has become as hard as stone due to the force of the harsh wind, the Kinnara women—led by their horse-faced chief—do not break nor do they abandon their slow and languid gait.
Of what sort is that path?
Because it is covered in snow, it causes the heels and the regions of the toes to throb and split apart.

How is it, then, that they do not move with haste? He says: "Afflicted" (*ārtāḥ*), meaning oppressed, by their heavy and full hips and breasts—that is, their buttocks and bosoms; or alternatively, "prosperous" (*ṛtāḥ*). In the case of *ṛta*, the single substitute *vṛddhi* occurs according to the rule "after a prefix, before a root beginning with *ṛ*. (Pāṇini 6.1.90).
And because the bodies of those horse-faced women possess the form of females, there is the presence of breasts, hips, fingers, and heels.
For the Kinnaras have two forms: some are horse-faced with human bodies, and others are human-faced with horse bodies.
"Pārṣṇi" refers to the heel. 11.
This cave protects the darkness hidden within it from the sun, as if it were afraid of the day;
for surely, even toward a lowly being who has sought refuge, those of lofty character possess a sense of "mine" that is like true virtue.

The elephant who protects the darkness hidden in the caves as if it were afraid even during the day—surely he himself is protected from another with fear; for what benefit is there in protecting that which is already seen? To this he says: [it is for the sake of] those with lofty heads, the exalted, when they have found refuge even in a wicked person.

It is certain that, just as a virtuous wife feels "mamatva"—that is, a sense of ownership—as toward her husband, so too do the great protect those who have come for refuge without discriminating between the meritorious and the unmeritorious.
*Mamatva* and *mama* are indeclinables (*nipāta*) that function like words ending in the genitive case. || 12 ||
The camari deer, with their tails white as moonbeams and beautiful as they spread out in waving motions here and there,
make the name "King of Mountains" meaningful for him by using those tails as fly-whisks.
Even though he is a lord of mountains in the form of an immobile being,
the yak-tails (*camaryaḥ*)— acting as fly-whisks (*vālavyajana*) or ceremonial fans (*prakīrṇaka*)— make this title "King of Mountains" meaningful and significant;
for it is said that a king ought to be fanned with yak-tails, and his tail consists of the upper portion [of the animal].

By those whose splendor spreads and extends here and there through flickering movement; likewise, by those as bright and white as the rays of the moon. Here, the form [of the rays] itself should be understood as the object of comparison; otherwise, what would be the purpose of mentioning the "rays" (marīci) in this context?

It would be so formed. The word *vyajana* is derived from the root *aja* (meaning "to go" or "to throw") preceded by the prefix *vi*, used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). The word *vījana*, however, is derived from the root *īja* (meaning "to go"). [As in: "by means of fans of the southern breeze."
Thus, as [stated] above. 13.
There, for the Kimpuruṣa women who are embarrassed when their garments are snatched away,
the clouds— whose forms hang over the openings of the cave-dwellings— spontaneously become their privacy screens.
Where,
when the kinnarīs are embarrassed by the theft of their garments by their beloveds, the clouds serve as curtains— acting as veils at will— so that their bodies may remain unseen.
Because their forms hang down at the door of the cave-dwelling, their circles of light come to rest there;

it is called *tiraskariṇī* because it "obscures" (*tiraskaroti*) or "covers" (*sthagayati*). The suffix *ini* is applied here by virtue of the rule for diversity (*bāhulaka*), and the *s* in *tiras* is substituted according to the rule *tiro 'nyatarasyām*. The word *yadṛcchā* has the sense of "will" or "desire" and belongs to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*.

The breeze there, which carries the spray from the cascades of the Bhāgīrathī, repeatedly shakes the deodar trees, and which has torn at the plumage of the peacocks, is enjoyed by the Kirātas who are tracking deer. (15)
Or rather, it is the wind belonging to which is resorted to by the exhausted Śabara chiefs who have been searching for game; what kind of wind is it?
It is the bearer of the spray from the cascades of the Bhāgīrathī—the droplets of water falling from the Ganges.

"Scattering" (kṣeptṛ) is a statement regarding its coolness and merit; "having branches shaken repeatedly" (muhurasakṛccālitasurata-viṭapa) is a statement regarding its fragrance; "tearing apart the plumage of peacocks and breaking the wings of pigeons" (bhinna-śikhaṇḍi-barha-struṭita-kalāpi-pakṣa) is a description of its restlessness;
"it flows constantly" (niyataṃ jharati sravati) thus it is a "waterfall" (nirjhara); "it carries" (vahati) thus it is a "bearer" (voḍhṛ).
The sun, revolving below, awakens with his upward-pointing rays the lotuses that remain after being gathered by the hands of the Seven Sages—the lotuses which grew from the lakes at its summit. 16.
The sun causes her lotuses to bloom with its upward-pointing rays, but not with those directed downward;
for they are the foremost lotuses of that lake,
while he wanders, moving about at the very bottom of the waters.
Therefore, its capacity for blooming belongs solely to those five hundred rays that spread upwards.
Of what sort are they? They are the remnants left after being gathered by the hands of the thirty gods and the sages;
for at dawn, they daily take them away for the purpose of worship.
They are called "remnants" (avaśeṣa) because they remain over. || 16 ||
Observing that he was the source of the sacrificial components and that his essence was capable of supporting the earth,
Prajāpati himself established him in the lordship of the mountains, assigning him a share in the sacrifice.
What need is there for much? He to whom Brahmā himself personally bestowed the sovereignty over the earth—this means he was consecrated by him in person.
For he understood that this [child] was the source and origin of the sacrificial implements, such as the *soma* plant and the *palāśa* leaf.

Having seen that he possessed a core strength capable of bearing the earth, did he grant him merely the lordship over the mountains? No; the author says: "He assigned a portion for the sacrifice. This means he accepted even a share in the sacrificial rites. For this very reason, he possesses the nature of a deity.
It is called *sāra* because it flows (*sarati*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied according to the rule "in the senses of disease, fish, and strength. 17.
Knowing the principles of stability, that friend of Meru, for the sake of the continuity of his lineage, duly married Menā— the daughter of the Pitṛs,
worthy of honor even by sages, and a fitting match for himself.

That lord of mountains, being such as he was, duly married—that is, took as his wife—a daughter of the Pitṛs named Menā, created by their minds, for the sake of the stability and non-interruption of his lineage. For he was one who knew the established order and understood proper conduct; indeed, worldly custom must not be abandoned.
There is a destruction of the sense of shame due to the equality of lineage and origin, or even because of the marriage of his father’s daughter;

for it is recorded in tradition that his father created three daughters by his mind— one was given to Himavat, another to Meru, and the third to another— and for this very reason, she [was considered] even by the sages...

"One worthy of worship," meaning one who is suitable to oneself in terms of family, character, and so forth; "according to the rite" means by the procedure prescribed in the scriptures; "we shall marry" (*upayema*)—the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is applied because of the rule "*upādyamaḥ svakaraṇe*" (Pāṇini 1.3.56), and reduplication occurs.

Therefore, by the rule "in the case of a single consonant between vowels, not when there is a substitute, in the periphrastic perfect (liṭ), [the reduplication is elided]," there is both the singleness [of the root] and the elision of the reduplication. The same applies elsewhere. 18.

She gave birth to Maināka, who was destined for the enjoyment of Naga maidens and who formed a bond of friendship with the ocean; he remained unaware of the wounds from the thunderbolt even when the enemy of Vṛtra, the cutter of wings, was enraged.
She, Menā, gave birth to a son named Maināka, who had made an alliance with the ocean;
and because of that cohabitation, he became the object of enjoyment and service as a husband for the daughters of the Nāgas,
even though Indra was enraged at him for clipping the wings of the mountains.

He knows no pain from wounds inflicted by the thunderbolt; he does not experience suffering because Indra cannot enter into the midst of the ocean. For in former times, the mountains possessed wings; then, as they were causing distress to the world, the slayer of Vṛtra [struck] them with his thunderbolt.
"He cut off the wings"—this is the traditional teaching (āgama). "One who has cut the wings" (pakṣacchit) means one who has cut the wings.
"He brought forth" (asūta)—this is the aorist (laṅ) of the root *sū*. 19.
Then Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa and former wife of Bhava, being urged by her father’s contempt,
cast off her body through yoga and entered the daughter of the mountain for the sake of rebirth.
Then once, that daughter of Dakṣa Prajāpati, who was formerly the wife of Śiva known as Satī, attained Menā, the wife of Himālaya, for the sake of rebirth; that is to say,
she cast herself into the womb of Menā for the purpose of being born again,
having been impelled by the insult offered by her father.

And for this reason, having cast off her body through yoga and dhāraṇā—that virtuous and chaste woman (satī) who could not endure the humiliation of her husband—it is recorded in tradition that when Dakṣa invited all his sons-in-law along with their wives to a sacrifice but did not invite Gaurī together with the Lord, she said, "What use have I for such a father of mine, who is devoid of good conduct and lacks affection? and then performed the abandonment of her body. || 20 ||
By that lord of the mountains, she—being endowed with composure—was brought forth as a worthy bride;
just as prosperity, through the quality of diligence, arises from the application of right means in a state that is unimpaired, like a well-guided city.
That goddess was born—that is, produced—by the King of Mountains in that Menā;

the locative case is used here to express the substratum (*ādhāra*). "In her" refers to her being endowed with *samādhi*, which is a disciplined observance for the sake of obtaining a worthy offspring; she, moreover, was auspicious and praiseworthy.

He explains by what means, where, how, and what is produced: "Just as policy (*nīti*) is brought about through the quality known as energy (*utsāha*), [so too is prosperity]. Policy refers to the sixfold set of measures (*ṣāḍguṇya*). Of what kind? It is that which remains unimpaired—that is, undestroyed—due to its application and practice in accordance with the scriptures. For a seeker of victory who relies upon energy while employing the sixfold measures according to rule necessarily attains prosperity through the conquest of his enemies.
In this context, by the term "policy" (nīti), the power of counsel (mantra-śakti) is implied;
by "energy" (utsāha-guṇa), the power of energy (utsāha-śakti); and by "prosperity" (sampad), the power of lordship (prabhu-śakti). And the roots of this [power of lordship] are counsel and energy.
The word *udapādi* is derived from the causative (*ṇyanta*) root; it occurs in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*), while *bhavyāḥ* means "suitable" or "fitting. || 21 ||

That day of his birth became for the welfare of all embodied beings, both stationary and moving; the quarters were serene, the winds were free from dust, and a rain of flowers fell immediately following the sound of conch shells.
The stationary beings are trees and the like;
the moving beings consist of fourteen kinds of animals, categorized as domestic and wild, such as lions, humans, and so forth.
For both these classes of embodied beings, that day of the goddess’s birth was a day of auspiciousness.
Where the quarters of the sky were serene and the horizons stainless; where the wind was free from dust and the air devoid of impurity;
and where, following the sound of divine conchs, there were showers of flowers.
With that daughter, whose halo of radiance was shimmering, the mother shone all the more,
like a floor of lapis lazuli with a sprout of jewels bursting forth at the sound of a fresh cloud.
By that daughter Gaurī, the mother, her progenitress, shone forth brilliantly;
she gleamed with a shimmering halo and a radiant mass of luster.
For the radiance of the great is indeed an indicator of their rising prosperity.
Just as the earth—the ground of the mountain named Viḍūra, also known by the other name Vālavāya—shines with a radiant jeweled needle, a gem-pin produced by the thundering of dense clouds;
for it is the report that there, during the rainy season, gems are born from the sound of the clouds. 23.
Growing day by day and having attained her rise like the crescent of the moon,
she nurtured special qualities consisting of loveliness, just as the various digits of the moon nourish the different phases of its light.

That queen, having attained her rise and achieved her birth, nourished and increased daily—like the digit of the moon as it waxes—particular excellences consisting of loveliness and beauty. The phrase "jyotsnāntarāṇi" (interior spaces of the moonlight) is an adjective qualifying the various digits; the meaning of the sentence is that just as the crescent of the moon, having risen and increasing day by day, nourishes the digits containing moonlight, so too did the queen nourish loveliness.
Due to the distinction between the two actions, there is a comparison between both the agent and the object; thus, even the word *iva* is employed twice.
For, by the action of increasing (*vṛddhi*), the cow is compared to the crescent moon, while by the action of nourishing (*puṣaṇa*), the other digits are the object being qualified.
It is also proper to employ multiple instances of a word that expresses a common property (*sāmānya*). As for example:
Then Raghu set out toward the northern quarter like the sun,
intending to extract the riches of the northerners with his arrows as the sun draws up moisture with its rays.
Then, as if emerging from the mouth of the great seer like the splendor of the sun from its orb at the lovely break of day, that knowledge issued forth and entered the face of Pārtha,
which was as bright as a spark of fire, like radiance entering a blossoming lotus.
Oh, how infinite is the variety of speech, though it is composed of only a few phonemes, like musical notes; it is as diverse as a song!

O dear friend, the wicked Creator, having cast our minds into a succession of falls at the edge of the staff of calamity, whirls them about like a potter forcibly kneading clay; we know not what he will fashion here.
Ah! Having suddenly forgotten the splendor of the Lord of Siṃhala, I have been seized by my girth-straps with a great curiosity, like a rustic man by a doorkeeper.
"Attainment" (udaya) is that by which what has been obtained and what is yet to be obtained is reached;
the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of "expectation" (*āśaṃsā*) according to the rule "as if it were already past" (*bhūtavacca*).
Some maintain that other arts reach other arts, just as one moonlight reaches other instances of moonlight. 24.

Her kinsmen called that beloved of her relatives by her family name, Pārvatī; but when she was forbidden from asceticism by her mother with the words "Um! Ma!", the fair-faced girl subsequently took the name Umā.

Because she was beloved by her own kin, her relatives first called that goddess by the name Pārvatī, derived from her noble lineage as the daughter of the Mountain (Parvata). Subsequently, after some time, she herself acquired the name Umā, signifying her excellence.

She was forbidden from her asceticism by her mother with the two words "Um-mā" (Do not). Here, "um" expresses a protest of affection, and the word "mā" signifies prohibition; thus, by the rules of etymology (*nirukta*), she is called Umā. As it has been said:
"O fickle daughter, 'Um-mā'—your body is not yet fit for this."
O lady of lovely appearance, it is possible for you to endure such austerity, which consists of the very nature of affliction.
"Juhāva" is a form of the root *hveñ*. || 25 ||
Although the king had sons, his gaze never reached satiety upon that particular offspring;
for the swarm of bees has a special attachment to the mango tree amidst the springtime of infinite flowers.
Although the Lord of Mountains had many offspring, his gaze found no satisfaction in Umā as a child;
for this is observed in nature:
in spring, though it is laden with many flowers, the swarm of bees is especially attached to and delights in the mango blossom.
The genitive case in "madhoḥ" is used in relation to the garland (*mālā*), expressing a connection. || 26 ||
Like a lamp with its flame of great radiance, like the path to heaven with its threefold course,
or like a wise man with refined speech— he was both purified and adorned by her.
By that goddess, that king of mountains was both purified and adorned;
for he whose daughter is the Goddess herself is surely pure, and parents are adorned by their offspring. Who [is he], and by what [is he adorned]? By her who possesses great splendor.
Just as a lamp becomes purified and adorned by a great, blazing flame,
whereas with an extinguished flame the vessel becomes unsightly and devoid of splendor.
By the word "lamp" (*dīpa*), the entire aggregate consisting of the flame, the wick, and the oil-vessel is implied here.
Just as the path to heaven is purified and adorned by the triple-pathed Gaṅgā,
and just as a scholar is purified and embellished by speech refined through prosody, grammar, and other sciences.

"Prabhāmahatī" is a third-case (instrumental) compound meaning "one who possesses great splendor. "Manīṣā" means intellect. This is primarily the correct view: that the words in a conjunction are equal in status to what they conjoin; hence, there is the employment of two *ca* particles here, just as in the copulative compound (*dvandva*) "dhava-khadira-palāśāḥ" [the dhava, khadira, and palāśa trees]. || 27 ||
Amidst her friends, she took delight repeatedly upon sandalwood altars on the banks of the Mandākinī with balls and artificial dolls, as if experiencing the very essence of childhood play.

That young girl played in the midst of her companions. With what? On the sandy bank of the Mandākinī—the Gaṅgā—with altars (vedikābhiḥ), which are mounds (sthalībhiḥ), with balls, and with artificial dolls made of wood and other materials, as well as with toys.
And because she played again and again, it is thus figuratively described.
"Krīḍārasam" means that in which there is the flavor (rasa) or passion (rāga) for play;
"nirviśatīva" means as if entering or as if drinking; [the suffix] "nuṃ" is optionally applied;
"kareṇa nirvṛttam" means produced by the hand or artificial; [the suffix] "ktri" is added after a root ending in "ḍu".
In the sense of "one who constantly recites the *Trerma*," the suffix *kan* is applied [to form *putraka*].

At the time of instruction, the sciences acquired in previous births approached her— just as rows of swans approach the Ganges in autumn, or as natural radiance approaches great medicinal herbs at night— who possessed firm teachings.

At the time of her instruction, the sciences belonging to her previous births returned to that goddess; for, being divine, they possessed stable teachings and imperishable knowledge. This is an ornamented expression [of the poet], like saying that a row of swans approaches the Ganges in autumn.
And just as it is said that great medicinal herbs attain their own radiance at night, this is an expression of their brilliance.
"Prāgbhavam" means belonging to the past. || 29 ||
Then she attained that age which follows childhood— a natural adornment for her slender frame, a cause of intoxication known as no wine, and a weapon of Love other than his flowery arrows.
Then that goddess, immediately after childhood, attained the stage of life known as youth.
Of what kind was it?

It was an uncreated—meaning not brought about by external means or acquired through effort—ornament for her slender body, which is like a creeper; this serves to distinguish it from bracelets, earrings, and other such [artificial] decorations.
Likewise, that which is called "intoxicant" (*anāsava*) is the producer of intoxication—a mental transformation—distinct from the act of drinking;
for it is well known that wine and the like cause intoxication.
Similarly, the "weapon" of the flower-armed god (Kāma) is a power of subjugation distinct from flowers, differing in nature from flowers.
This is the poetic figure known as *vibhāvanā*. || 30 ||
Her body, graced by the symmetry of her form, became radiant with fresh youth, like a painting brought to life by a brush, or like a lotus opened by the rays of the sun.

The body of that goddess, divided and partitioned by her fresh youth, became beautiful in its symmetry and auspicious on all sides. With what, one might ask, is it like? It is said: just as a painting, once brought forth and made manifest in its details by a fine needle (*tūlikā*), shines with symmetrical beauty;
for previously, it was merely sketched with its limbs undivided.

And just as a lotus, split open and blossomed by the rays of the sun, becomes entirely beautiful, so too it is "beautiful on all sides" (caturaśraśobhi), meaning it shines with symmetry in every direction. 31.

He describes that very same thing by way of the description of his form: "His two feet, as if vomiting redness from the luster of their upraised big-toe nails due to their being set down, brought to the earth the shifting splendor of land-lotuses. (32)
It is the convention of poets to describe the form of goddesses starting from the big toes, whereas for human women it begins from the hair; thus he says accordingly:

"By the placing of her feet—the very act of setting them down—she brought about, and thereby removed, the unstable and shifting beauty of the land-lotuses upon the earth. This is because she produced a splendor equal to that [of the lotuses].
What are those two like?
They are the raised and slightly sunken nails of the two [toes], which, by their luster, seem to emit passion—that is, they appear to vomit redness;
for a lotus is indeed red, and feet and nails that are red are considered auspicious.
Words such as "vomiting" and so forth are used figuratively when applied to anything other than the mouth.
As she moved with graceful and playful charms, her body bent like that of a royal swan,
she was followed by those eager for instruction, who sought to learn the tinkling of her anklets.

The goddess Saṃnatāṅgī, whose body was bent by the fullness of her breasts, was—as it were—instructed in her gaits by royal swans, because her movement was exactly like theirs. To the question of why they would instruct her in that gait, he says: "By those greedy for further instruction, desiring to acquire other branches of knowledge from her presence."

Thus he says: "By those desiring to seize—meaning wishing to capture—the tinkling of her anklets (*nūpura-śiñjitāni*) and the jingling of her bracelets (*mañjīra-raṇitāni*); and for this reason, she was led away by them like swans, according to the principle that 'knowledge [is acquired] through knowledge. The meaning is that her gait and the tinkling of her bracelets were like those of royal swans."
In what kind of gaits? Those in which there is a charming grace (*vibhrama*) characterized by playfulness and ease;

that is to say, those possessing unartificial coquetry. [The form *añcita* is derived from the root *añc* with the augment *iṭ*, according to the rule] "the augment *iṭ* is added to *añc* when honor is expressed" [Pāṇini 7.2.53], and [the negative particle *naÑ* is applied] "not after *añc* when honor is expressed" [Pāṇini 6.4.37].

Thus, there is no elision of the *n* [in *gateṣu*]. In the word *gateṣu*, the locative case is used in the sense of a locus (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa*). In *vyanīyata*, the suffix is used in the passive voice (*karman*). || 33 ||
When the Creator fashioned her beautiful legs— round, tapering, and not too long—
it was as if he exerted all his remaining effort toward the production of beauty for the creation of the rest of her limbs.

When the Creator fashioned the two extended thighs of the goddess, which were overflowing with loveliness, it was as if an unavoidable effort toward beauty had been exerted in the creation of her other limbs, beginning with the hips;
for he deposited all his loveliness into those two in a state of undivided concentration. Of what sort were they?
"Round," "circular," "previously followed," and "gradual"—this is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
"Not too long, but rather of medium length. "Auspicious" means praised. The form *āsa* is a usage by poets arising from negligence; [the rule] is "for the root *as*, [substitute] *bhū*."
Thus, because of the context of becoming (*bhū-bhāva*).

As for what others say—that it is a particle (*nipāta*) that resembles a verbal form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix—that is correct, because such a thing arises precisely as a verbal form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix. || 34 ||
The trunks of the lord of serpents, because of their roughness to the touch, and the various species of plantain trees, because of their extreme coldness—
even though they possess a rotund form in this world, they fall short of being a comparison for her thighs.

The trunks of the lord of serpents (*nāgendra*), the trunks of elephants, and even the finest varieties of plantain trees—these distinct types of trees became unsuitable and unequal as comparisons for her thighs. One might wonder: "Could it be that they were not round? To this he says: "Even though they possess a girthly form—that is, a circular configuration—how then did they fall outside the range of comparison? He answers: "Because of the roughness of their bark and because of their absolute coolness."

The trunks of elephants are rough to the touch, whereas those two are soft. Plantain trees are also exclusively and invariably cool, yet the thighs are not cool even in the winter. Thus, because of such differences, how can there be a comparison?
"Exclusively cool" means absolute coolness; the compound is formed according to the rule of *bāhulaka* (generalization). "Pariṇāhi" refers to that which possesses circumference (*pariṇāha*). || 35 ||
Indeed, by this much alone, the region of the waist of the blameless lady, whose beauty was worthy of inference, had its loveliness established;
for it was subsequently placed upon the lap of Giriśa, which is unattainable by any other woman.
The place where the girdle-string—the cord of the waist-band—rests is the region of the hips; because it is not directly visible, its beauty is to be inferred by this much alone.
That which was later placed upon the lap—that is, taken onto the bosom—by Śiva.
He says that it might at some time become the object of enjoyment for many other women: "unlovely" (akamanīyam), meaning undesirable, to other women.
Because the Lord is one whose vital energy is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*);
for if that [state] were not superior, how would the Blessed One hold it in such high regard?
It is "blameless," meaning praiseworthy.
Even at the time of describing the maiden’s beauty, the fact that she was placed upon his lap is not contradictory, though it may seem improper for the poet;
for by the time of the poem's composition, the marriage had already taken place. It is for this very reason that she is mentioned later on. The same applies to what follows.

The word *giriśa* is fit for usage in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*) like [the words] *caitya*, *bhuvana*, and so forth. Alternatively, he is *giriśa* because Kailāsa, the mountain (*giri*), exists in him; the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule beginning with *loman*.
Others say that he is *giriśa* because he lies upon the mountain (*giriṃ śayati*). 36.
Having entered the cavity of her deep navel,
that slender line of fresh hair shone like the radiance of the central gem of a dark sapphire, having passed beyond the knot of her garment.
The slender line of hair on that goddess shone as it entered the deep, curved hollow of her navel, appearing there as if it had been severed;
and because of its blackness, it was imagined to be so.

The radiance of the central gem of the girdle—the sapphire that serves as the leader of the waist-belt—is as if it has entered upward, having crossed over the knot (*nīvī*) and transcended the gathered mass of cloth;
for the *nīvī* is indeed placed above the girdle. Alternatively, by the word *nīvī*, that which is tied by the *nīvī*—namely the lower garment—is indicated.
Therefore, having split the garment, she has entered within like a flame;
for the girdle is placed upon the garment.
The word *arcis* (flame) is feminine as well. [In the compound] *sitetara*, "other than white," the fifth case [is used].
Thus, by means of a grammatical split (yogavibhāga), there is a compound.
Because white and black are well-known as opposites, the color black alone is understood by terms such as "not-dark" (asiteta) and the like.
The temporal priority expressed by "having transgressed" (atikramya) is in relation to the action of entering. 37.
With her waist slender as the middle of a sacrificial altar, she bore three beautiful folds of skin;
they appeared like a staircase constructed by fresh youth for the ascent of the God of Love.

The young goddess bore three beautiful folds on her waist— a middle that was slender and sunken like the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) of those who maintain the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*), which is similarly recessed.
It is poetically imagined that these were fashioned like a staircase for the God of Love (*Kāma*) to ascend by means of her fresh youth.
For indeed, the manifestation of passion occurs in youth. || 38 ||
The two pale breasts of the lotus-eyed woman, pressing against each other and so greatly developed,
were such that not even the space of a lotus fiber could be found between them, which had become dark at their base.
The pair of breasts of that lotus-eyed woman grew so large in that manner that even the space for a lotus fiber between them became difficult to find;
for they pressed against one another.
This describes her physical form as having a dark face—that is, blue nipples. (39)
It is my conjecture that his two arms are more delicate than a garland of śirīṣa flowers—
those very arms which, though defeated by Śiva, were made into the noose for his neck by the god of love.
It is my conjecture—that is, my inference—that the two arms of the Goddess are even more delicate than a garland of *śirīṣa* flowers.

Why is this? He says: because even by the scorched Makaradhvaja (the God of Love), they were made into nooses for Śiva’s necks as means of subjugation. For Kāma is indeed one whose weapons are delicate;
the world was to be brought under his control by means of that soft weapon.
And if even compared to flowers that pair of arms were not soft, then how could he—having previously failed to subdue Hara despite possessing flowers such as the *śirīṣa* and others—conquer him now?
Or rather, the sense is: if one who is of such delicate nature [as Śiva] cannot even with his bodiless form (the *pāśa*) bind a hard object, how much less so this [Hara]?
In this context, instead of the word *yāvat*, the causal particle *yat* would be more appropriate.
As in the example: "That which was placed upon [the head] by Giriśa. (40)
Between her neck, which was made beautiful by her breasts, and her smooth string of pearls,
there arose a mutual relationship of ornament and the object to be adorned, as each produced beauty in the other.

Because the neck of the goddess and her pearl necklace produced mutual beauty for one another, they shared the state of being both the ornament and the object of adornment; this describes their natural splendor. For the throat was "bandhura," meaning charming, due to its proximity to the two breasts; and it was also "nistala," meaning rounded, because it lacked a flat surface (tala).
Because the word *bhūṣaṇa* (ornament) is primary due to its intended meaning being the ornamentation of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), it is placed first;
and this has already been stated by the word "cause" (*hetu*) itself. || 41 ||
Having gone to the moon, Lakṣmī does not enjoy the qualities of the lotus; having taken refuge in the lotus, she does not possess the splendor of the moon.
But having reached Umā’s face, the fickle goddess attained a joy that partakes of both.

Regarding the statement, "The face of Gaurī resembles the splendor of the moon," he expresses this very same matter through a different turn of phrase: The Goddess of Fortune (Śrī), though residing in the moon, does not enjoy the beauty of the lotus, because the lotus closes at night. The lotus, too, having attained the lunar splendor, does not experience it, because the moon is lusterless during the day.
But the Goddess, having reached his face, obtained the happiness of presiding over both simultaneously.
Because her face possesses a resemblance to both; for she is fickle, seeking the qualities of both the lecher and the libertine.
If there were a flower set upon a fresh sprout, or a pearl resting on bright coral,
then it might imitate her smile, which spreads its luster over her copper-hued lips.
If such a flower and pearl were to exist, they would then imitate the pure smile residing upon the bimba-like lips of the Goddess.
Of what sort is the flower? It is one set upon a *pravāla*, situated amidst young shoots. The pearl likewise—

[The face] resting upon a stainless coral; for in this way, through the blending of whiteness and redness, the imitation becomes complete—thus it is a "produced simile" (utpādyopamā) intended to generate an inference.
[It refers to] one whose luster and splendor have fallen and spread over his copper-colored lips.

The genitive case in "of the smile" (*smitasya*) is used to express a relationship of connection, as in the expression "one should not eat black gram" (*na māṣāṇām aśnīyāt*). Here, the word *puṣpa* refers to the white [color]. || 43 ||
When she of noble speech spoke with a voice that seemed to distill nectar, even the cuckoo—
though usually pleasing to the ear— seemed discordant, like a lute being played out of tune.
When that Pārvatī speaks with a voice of tender words and gentle speech,
even the *anyapuṣṭā* cuckoo becomes a source of agitation for the listener due to its discordant notes, like a stringed instrument out of tune.

The meaning is that even the cuckoo's voice causes no pleasure to the ears of one who hears her soft speech, just like a lute-string that has gone out of tune; for a string that has shifted from its proper place produces extreme distress. With what kind of voice?

"Amṛtasrut" means "flowing with nectar"; it flows with nectar by way of that very sweetness. Here, "svara" (sound) refers to sound in general; it is mentioned for the purpose of providing a qualifying attribute.
[The term] "anyapuṣṭā" (nourished by another) refers to cuckoos because they are reared by crows.
Since it is a name based on its meaning (*yathārthanāman*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur due to the absence of a pure feminine gender (*śuddhajāti*).

Regarding the word *tantrī*: by the rule "the suffix *ī* is added after the roots *avi*, *tṛ*, *stṛ*, and *tantri*," we have *tantrī*. She who has a discordant string (*visvara*) is a *vitantrī*. || 44 ||
Was that unsteady glance of the large-eyed woman, indistinguishable from a blue lotus in a strong breeze, taken from the female deer by her, or was it taken from her by the female deer? 45.
As for that restless and timid glance she cast— whether it was taken by Pārvatī from the deer, or whether it was taken by the deer from her— we do not know;
due to their resemblance, there is no certainty.
For it is not distinct from—that is, not different from—the blue lotus that exists when there is a strong wind; "nu" is used here in the sense of deliberation (vitarka). 45.

Beholding that beauty of her two curved eyebrows, which was as if fashioned from collyrium-sticks, the bodiless god of love abandoned his pride in the loveliness of his own bow, seeing it surpassed by the playful grace of her locks.

Beholding that beauty—the splendor—of the curved eyebrows of that goddess, Kāma perceived his own pride born from the loveliness of his bow to be utterly surpassed; this is a description of the deficiency of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and an expression of the superior excellence of the beauty of the object compared (*upameya*). [The phrase] "as if painted with the collyrium produced from the *añjana* (lampblack) of a brush (*tūlikā*)" expresses the thinness and blackness of her skin.
Of what sort was she? She was beautiful (*cikurāṃ*) with playful grace (*līlayā*).
The reading "cikurām" is an archaic (ārṣa) one because it is not commonly known. || 46 ||

If shame were present in the minds of animals, there is no doubt that the female yak would, upon seeing that mass of hair belonging to the daughter of the Mountain King, find her own fondness for her tail-lost. (47)

If animals possessed shame and modesty in their minds, then surely, upon beholding the beauty of Pārvatī’s mass of hair with its dark luster, the female yaks would have loosened their state of having beautiful tails. For they—
The female yaks, terrified by the severing of their tails caught in thickets of creepers, accept even the hunter’s arrow— which is capable of destroying them—
rather than the breaking of their hair, for their hair is dear to them.
Here, by means of the *kriyātipatti* (the conditional mood expressing non-occurrence), the sense of the past is conveyed.
Thus, the occurrence of the conditional suffix (*lṛṅ*) is to be considered. By the pronoun "that" (*tam*), he expresses the well-known beauty of the tress of hair;
the word *keśapāśa* (tress of hair) is used in a sense of praise. 47.

Having described the parts individually, he now speaks of them as a whole: "By the Creator of the Universe, she was fashioned with great effort through the collection of all comparable substances, arranged according to their respective places, as if out of a desire to behold beauty concentrated in one place. (48)

In short—by the collection and combination of all the substances used for comparison, such as the moon, the lotus, the water-lily, the plantain tree, and so forth, that goddess was fashioned by the skillful Creator;
and she was placed by him in their respective locations according to their suitability. For the beauty of the moon and the lotus resides in her face alone.
"The loveliness of the blue water-lily has been fashioned for her eyes; the exquisite grace of the plantain tree for her thighs," and so forth—thus it is imagined.

As if out of a desire to behold beauty gathered in one place, she was created through a collection of objects of comparison. Indeed, I now see the collection of substances that were previously scattered brought together in one place.
"What is this like?"—this means that it has been produced by the intellect itself according to a rule (*vidhi*).

That by which something is compared is an *upamā* (simile); those substances are called by that name, and their collection is [the compound] *tadākhyadravyasamuccaya*. "In whatever place" means according to each respective location (*yathāpradeśam*). || 48 ||
Once, it is said, Nārada, who wanders at will, beheld that maiden in the presence of her father and,
out of affection, ordained that she would become the sole wife of Hara, sharing half of his body.

Then, on one occasion, having observed that maiden of such a form in the presence of her parents, the sage Nārada, who acts according to his own will, prophesied—that is, declared—that she would become the future wife of Hara, his sole consort and one without a rival.

[The word] "kila" is used for the purpose of indicating traditional scripture. [He saw her] standing, out of love and under the influence of affection, occupying half of his body, which reaches down to the lower part of the torso.
For it has been said thus: "This beloved wife shall become the one who takes half the body of her husband Śaṅkara; of this there is no doubt.
[The term] *kāmacara* means "she who moves according to her own will" (*kāmena svecchayā carati*). [The form] *bhaviṣyatī* becomes *bhavitrī*.
In the compound *śarīrārdha*, when the intention is to express an equal division, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). (49)
Although she had reached a marriageable age, her father remained steadfast, having turned away from any desire for other suitors;
for no fires other than the sacrificial fire (Kṛśānu) are worthy of receiving the oblation purified by mantras.

Because Nārada had thus commanded him, for that reason his father, the guru, remained steadfast even in his youth with his desire for any other bridegroom turned away. He was one whose longing for another bridegroom—another husband—had ceased; the meaning is that he did not entertain the thought of any bridegroom other than Hara (Śiva) even in his mind.
For, without Kṛśānu—that is, without fire—other luminous bodies are not capable of, nor are they entitled to, consuming the oblation (havya), which is purified by mantra.
The word "havya" means that which is offered. In the phrase "kṛśānoḥ ṛte," the ablative case is used due to the employment of the word "ṛte. || 50 ||
Then [the poet] says why the father himself did not give her to Hara:
"The Mountain was indeed unable to make the God of Gods accept his daughter when he did not ask for her;
for a virtuous man, out of fear of rejecting a request, maintains neutrality even regarding a desired object. (51)

The meaning is that Himavat was unable to make his daughter accept Maheśvara, the God of gods, while he remained unpetitioned; as long as she had not been requested by the Blessed One, the mountain did not give her to him. Here, the word *ki* (for) has the sense of a reason based on what follows.
For one adopts and relies upon neutrality or indifference even toward an object desired by the mind;
by what means? By the fear of the frustration of one's request, thinking that at some point one might not even accept it. This is according to the rule: "And likewise for roots meaning 'to go'."
By the inclusion of the word "iti" (and so on), the status of having two objects (*dvikarmakatā*) applies even in connection with roots such as *grah* (to seize) and others; for example:
"Janaka made him take up that bow," and "The ocean was churned by the gods and demons for the sake of nectar."
"By the turn of fate, he has been made to abandon a pearl necklace long familiar to him;
it will surely release you as well from this new cloud of water.
"Let a hundred gargās be fined!"
Thus [ends the section]. 51.
Now, wishing to describe the activity of Īśvara, he says:

"From the very moment she herself cast off her body in a previous birth out of anger toward Dakṣa, from that time forth the Lord of creatures (Paśupati) became free from attachment and without possessions. (52)

From the very moment in his previous birth when the Goddess herself abandoned her body out of anger toward her father, the Lord of Beings (Bhūtanātha) remained without a companion because he had renounced sense objects; thus, he remained unmarried.

The meaning is that he practiced celibacy (*brahmacarya*) under the influence of love. The word *tadā* is a particle functioning in the sense of the ablative case. "Attachments" (*saṅga*) are objects (*viṣaya*), so called because they are attached to; it is that which is grasped (*parigṛhyate*).
The wife is the possession. || 52 ||

Clad in animal skins and restrained in soul for the sake of asceticism, he dwelt upon a certain plateau of the Himalayas— sprinkled by the falling waters of the Gaṅgā, fragrant with musk, and where the kinnaras sang faintly amidst the deodar trees.

The Blessed One, whose garment was an elephant hide and whose clothing was the bark of trees, having restrained his senses, dwelt upon a ridge of the Himalayan mountain for the sake of asceticism. Of what sort was it?
There, the deodar trees were sprinkled by the falling waters of the Ganges' cascades;
there, the scent of the musk found in the navels of deer—specifically the kastūrikā antelopes—is present. Not even the slightest [other scent]... [is found].
The description of its habitability is given by the phrase "where the Kinnaras sing with loud, resonant voices.
The word *prastha* may be used as both masculine and neuter. 53.
With clusters of *nameru* blossoms as their ornaments, wearing the soft bark of birch trees, and smeared with red arsenic,
the Gaṇas sat down upon the surfaces of rocks covered with bitumen.
The Gaṇas, the Pramathas, sat down—that is, they took their seats—upon the surfaces of the rocks and stone slabs; for wherever the Blessed One is, there they must be. Of what kind were they?
[They were adorned] with the blossoms of the trees or creepers known as *nami*.
Those who have flower and fruit as their ear-ornaments and crest-garlands;
likewise, those wearing soft, touchable birch-bark garments;
and those smeared and anointed with red arsenic, a particular mineral—among them...
"In *naddheṣu* (covered) by *śaileyaiḥ* (rock-creepers), which are *śilākusumaiḥ* (stone-flowers). *Śaileyam* is like *śilā*.
When the suffix *ḍhañ* is applicable after *vasti*, [the rule] "after *śilā*, the suffix *ḍha*" [applies].
Thus, by means of the division of the rule (yogavibhāga), the suffix ḍhañ is applied.
The humped bull, intoxicated with pride, scraping the masses of ice-stones with the tips of his hooves, let out a loud roar;
he was barely seen by the agitated gavayas, who could not endure the sound of a lion.
The humped bull of Hara roared and bellowed. Of what sort was he?
Scraping and tearing through masses of snow with the tips of his hooves; intoxicated with pride and sweet with rut;
and thus unable to endure the sound of lions, not even tolerating the roar of maned beasts. For this very reason—
He was somehow beheld from afar by the creatures called gavayas, who were agitated and distressed.

"Kakudmān" is one who possesses a hump (*kakud*); there is no substitution of *v* for *d* here because it belongs to the *yava*-class. This word ends in *d*, not in *t*. The form "vivigna" is derived from the root *ovij*. (55)

Having established the sacred fire there, the Eight-formed Lord (Aṣṭamūrti), who is himself the ordainer of the fruits of asceticism, performed austerities with some particular desire, kindling the fire with fuel as if it were another form of his own.
There, on a ridge of the Himalayas, having established his sacred fires, the Blessed One practiced austerities for some purpose with an unknown intention. He states the reason for this ignorance:
because he himself possesses the lordship to be the creator of the fruits of austerity, namely heaven and liberation.

What kind of fire? Kindled—that is, made to blaze—by fuel-sticks and offerings; likewise, his own very other form, his own particular body, since he is the one who possesses eight forms (Aṣṭamūrti). For earth, water, wind, fire, the sacrificer, ether, the moon, and the sun are indeed the forms of Śambhu.
"One form is another form"—this is a *sup-supā* compound (a compound of two nouns in the nominative case). || 56 ||
Having honored with priceless offerings that lord of mountains— who was himself worthy of honor and worshipped by the dwellers of heaven—
the mountain king commanded his daughter, who was accompanied by her friends and purified herself, to attend upon him.

Then, knowing that the Lord was performing penance on his own peak and recollecting the words of Nārada, the Lord of Mountains honored him with an *arghya* offering and, following the prescribed rites, commanded his daughter—who was accompanied by her companions and observed religious vows—to serve him.

Of what sort was he? He was "priceless" (*anarghya*), because he was beyond measure; and he was "worshipped by the dwellers of heaven," that is, by the gods. [This is according to the rule: *ktasya ca vartamāne*.

Thus ends the sixth [section]. *Arghya* refers to water and other substances for the purpose of the *argha* offering; the suffix *yat* is applied here by the rule "after *pāda* and *argha*" (*pādārghābhyāṃ ca*). *Oka* means a house. The word *tanu* also ends in the vowel *ū*. 57.
Even though she was an adversary to his meditative concentration, Śiva permitted her to continue listening;
for those whose minds do not waver even when a cause for change is present—they alone are the steadfast.
The Blessed One consented to— that is, accepted— that virtuous lady who was serving and attending upon him;
for non-consent would have been appropriate,
since she, by virtue of her womanhood, was an adversary and an obstacle to his meditative concentration and self-restraint.
"Pratyarthibhūtām" means having become an adversary, that is, having become an opponent.
Alternatively, the word "bhūta" may be used in the sense of a comparison; thus, the meaning is "resembling an adversary.
To the question, "How then is it inferred? he says:
For those whose minds are not perturbed—that is, are not led into transformation—even when a cause for transformation is present, they alone are the wise and the truly steadfast.
*Śuśrūṣā* means service. The expression "desiring to hear" (*śuśrūṣā*) is merely a derivative form; or rather, hearing is contained within service, meaning that comprehension is attained.

For a servant listens and does not disregard [the command]. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here according to the rule *jñā-śru-smṛ-dṛśāṃ sanaḥ*. The form *vikriyante* is used in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*). However, in the case of a reflexive object (*karmakartari*), the rule *veḥ śabdakarmaṇaḥ* applies.
Because of the rule "akarmakācca," which prescribes the ātmanepada for roots that are intransitive, there would be a prohibition of the *yaṅ* suffix by the rule "ṇi-śranthi-granthi. || 58 ||

Gathering flowers for the offerings, skilled in sweeping the altar, and bringing water and sacrificial grass according to the rules of her vow, that woman of beautiful hair, her fatigue restrained by the rays of the moon upon his head, attended upon Giriśa every day. (59)

That woman of beautiful hair, having been permitted by the Goddess, attended upon and served Giriśa day after day. He describes that very service: she was one who had gathered flowers for the sake of offerings and worship, and she was skillful and clever in sweeping the altar and tending the sacred fire.
She is the one who brings forth the waters for the ritual injunctions and the sacrificial grass, the *barhis* or *darbha*.

Because of this, whatever exhaustion or fatigue she might have been subject to has been restrained and dispelled by the rays of the moon upon the head of Hara; such is the fruit of beholding the grace of the Blessed One.
*Saṃmārjana* means sweeping or cleansing; it is formed with the suffix *ghañ*.
There is *vṛddhi* [substitution] for the root *mṛj*;
by the rule "cajoḥ ku," there is the substitution of *k* [for the palatals]. She who leads near (*upanayati*) is an *upanetrī*. Day after day means daily.

The *avyayībhāva* compound is used in the sense of "according to the object" (*yathārthe*). By the rules "*anaśca*" and "*napuṃsakādanyatarasyām*," the suffix *ṭac* is applied and the *ṭi*-portion is elided. In the case of *sukeśī*, [the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] by the rule "*svāṅgāccopasarjanāt*."
Thus ends the feminine suffix *ṅīḥ*. The meter is *Mālinī*. || 59 ||
Thus ends the first canto in the commentary on the Kumārasambhava composed by Vallabhadeva, the son of Ānandadeva.
The Second Chapter. At that time, the inhabitants of heaven, having been oppressed by Tāraka,
went to the abode of Svāyambhuva, placing Turāsāha at their head.

At the very moment when Girijā was worshipping Giriśa, the denizens of heaven—the gods—being harassed and oppressed by the Asura Tāraka, the son of Vajrāṅga, went to the self-born abode, the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka), placing Turāsāha Indra at their head. The word *div* also ends in the vowel *a*, as in "the arms are the quarters, the head is the sky" (*diśo bāhū divaṃ śiraḥ*).
Like *vainya* and other such words, the term *turāsāh* is also used in the vernacular.

Svayambhū is Brahmā; that which belongs to him is *svāyambhuva*. According to the rule "a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific designation is not invariably valid," the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel for *o* does not apply here.
Thus ends the absence of qualities. In this chapter, the meter is Anuṣṭubh. || 1 ||
To them, whose splendor of countenance had faded, Brahmā appeared,
just as the sun appears at dawn to lakes whose lotuses are closed.
Viriñca appeared before the gods, whose facial splendor had vanished due to the harassment of Tāraka;
yet no obstacle to their vision arose.
This is compared to how the sun appears at dawn before the reservoirs of water whose lotuses have closed.
By this, the brightening of his face due to the destruction of his grief is indicated. || 2 ||
Then, having prostrated themselves, they all approached the Lord of All, the Sustainer of All, whose face is turned in every direction, with meaningful words addressed to the Master of Speech.
Then all the gods, bowing down, approached and praised Brahmā, the Lord of Speech, with meaningful and truthful words.

Of what nature was he? He is the creator and sustainer of the entire universe, possessing faces on all sides—that is, four-faced—or alternatively, having many gates because he is praised in all the scriptures.
The Lord, the source and master of the words consisting of the Vedas and the Śāstras— as it has been said:
"Yoga, knowledge, as well as Sāṃkhya, the sciences, the arts, ritual action,
the Vedas, the Śāstras, and specialized wisdom— all this [originates] from the Grandfather."
"Arthyāḥ" means not deviating from the purpose, unshakable, meaningful, and free from superimposed meanings; [this is according to the rule] "not deviating from dharma, path, artha, and nyāya.
"Upatasthire" is [derived] from the rule "upa-āt deva-pūjā... [etc.].
Thus ends the third [section] on the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings.

He utters that very praise: "Obeisance to You, the three-formed one, who existed as the solitary Self prior to creation, and who subsequently underwent differentiation for the sake of the division of the three qualities. (4)
Salutations to you, who possess the forms of the three manifestations— Hari, Hara, and Brahmā; who, prior to creation, exist as the absolute self of undifferentiated form,
because the qualities (guṇas) have not yet been disturbed.
Then, for the sake of distinguishing the three qualities characterized as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*,
[the Lord] approached that which had subsequently attained the differentiation characterized by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;
for the qualities, when undivided, are not capable of performing any function.

It is not possible for [a single entity] to create progeny in the forms of gods, humans, and animals. Furthermore, through the differentiation of the qualities (guṇas), the state of being the threefold form (trimūrti) has indeed come about. As it has been said:
"Salutations to the one who partakes in *rajas* during creation, and to the one consisting of *sattva* during maintenance."
To the self-existent one, who consists of darkness, who is the dissolution, and who possesses a threefold form.
O Unborn One, since the infallible seed was sown by you within the waters,
you are celebrated as the source from which this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings arises.

O unborn and eternal one, because you have sown—that is, cast—the infallible and fruitful seed, which generates effects, into the midst of the waters within the ocean, from that seed arises the entire universe consisting of the moving and the unmoving, the stationary and the living. Therefore, you are celebrated by the sages as the source and the cause of that universe; as it has been said: [The verse continues: "Thou art the womb of all beings, O Puruṣottama; Thou art the creator of all beings, O Supreme Lord. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.69) "You are the origin of this world, O Infinite One; You are the support of all things, O Unborn One. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.70) "You are the father of this world, O Infinite One; You are the mother, the sustainer, and the great abode. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.71) "You are the ruler of this world, O Infinite One; there is no other cause for the existence of the universe. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.72) "You are the imperishable, the supreme, the eternal, the divine, the self-born, the lord of all, and the ancient one. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.73) "You are the beginning, the middle, and the end of all beings; You are the undecaying, the infinite, the supreme, and the eternal. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.74) "You are the unmanifest, the manifest, and the supreme; You are the cause of the world, O Lord of the World, and the refuge of the world. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.75) "You are the creator of the world, O Infinite One; You are the protector of the world, O Infinite One; You are the destroyer of the world, O Infinite One; there is no other cause for the world than You. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.76) "You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme light, the supreme goal, the supreme refuge, the supreme truth, and the supreme eternal. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.77) "You are the supreme bliss, the supreme peace, the supreme liberation, the supreme purity, the supreme knowledge, and the supreme power. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.78) "You are the supreme dharma, the supreme virtue, the supreme sacrifice, the supreme austerity, the supreme yoga, and the supreme meditation. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.79) "You are the supreme mantra, the supreme hymn, the supreme offering, the supreme oblation, the supreme fire, and the supreme wind. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.80) "You are the supreme water, the supreme earth, the supreme space, the supreme time, the supreme direction, and the supreme atom. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.81) "You are the supreme sound, the supreme touch, the supreme form, the supreme taste, the supreme smell, and the supreme mind. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.82) "You are the supreme intellect, the supreme ego, the supreme consciousness, the supreme bliss, the supreme self, and the supreme lord. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.83) "You are the supreme witness, the supreme knower, the supreme seer, the supreme hearer, the supreme thinker, and the supreme doer. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.84) "You are the supreme enjoyer, the supreme giver, the supreme receiver, the supreme protector, the supreme friend, and the supreme refuge. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.85) "You are the supreme father, the supreme mother, the supreme teacher, the supreme preceptor, the supreme guide,
Desiring to emit various kinds of creatures, he first created those [waters] from his own body through meditation,
and then cast his seed into them.
That from which the moving, the non-moving, and that which is both moving and non-moving originate is the Source (prabhava). || 5 ||
Manifesting your majesty through three states,
you alone have become the cause of dissolution, maintenance, and creation.

By means of your three states— those of Hara, Hari, and Brahmā— and your ten manifestations, you proclaim and declare your own majesty and greatness; thus, you alone have become the sole cause, having attained the status of the primary source for dissolution, preservation, and creation— that is, for destruction, protection, and emanation.
As it has been said:
"In his state as Brahmā, he creates the worlds; in his state as Kāla, he also withdraws them;
in his state as Puruṣa, he remains indifferent—these are the three states of the Self-existent One."
Abiding is the preservation of existence. 6.
Woman and man are the two portions of your own being, divided by your desire to create;
they alone are remembered as the parents of this procreative creation.
Woman and man are the *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, the two portions or parts of your own self;
for, when your body was divided into two by the desire to create, those very same woman and man are traditionally said to be the parents—the mother and father—of the procreative, womb-born creation.
As it has been said:
Having divided his own self into two parts, he became a man with one half and a woman with the other; through her, the Lord created Virāj.
The term "prasūtibhāj" (possessing procreation) is included because even creations such as those of Mānasas and others are possible.

"Strīpuṃsau" means a woman and a man; the form is derived according to the rule for words beginning with "acatura" etc. "Mātā ca pitā ca tau pitarau" (the mother and the father, these two are the parents); [this is governed by] the rule "pitā mātrā. (Pāṇini 1.2.70).
For you, whose day and night are divided according to your own measure of time,
sleep and waking are precisely the dissolution and emergence of all beings.
Your very states of sleep and waking are the dissolution and emergence, the destruction and manifestation, of all living beings.
As it has been said:
"When that God is awake, then this world moves."
When he, whose self is tranquil, sleeps, then everything is dissolved.
Of what kind is he? He is one by whom night and day—the day and night—have been distributed, that is, divided, according to his own temporal measure, his own standard of time. As it has been said:
"The wise know that the day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas."
Those people who know day and night understand that the night ends after a thousand yugas.
It is also stated elsewhere:
"That which has been enumerated as the first mortal cycle of four ages (caturyuga),
consisting of twelve thousand [years], is called an age of the gods."
A single day of Brahmā is to be known as consisting of a thousand divine yugas, and his night is of exactly the same duration.
In this *dvandva* compound,

the word *divā* functions solely as the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) and does not function as the locative case-meaning (*adhikaraṇārtha*). For if it were to always express the locative sense, [the form] would have been *doṣāmanyamahar*.
The state of being an object of action, as in "the day is [regarded] as night," is difficult to establish. || 8 ||
You are the source of the world, yet you are without origin; you are infinite, yet the ender of the world.
You are the beginning of the world, yet you are without beginning; you are the lord of the world, yet you are without a superior lord.
As Brahman, you are the womb and the source of the worlds; here, the suffix denotes the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*). But for you, there is no source whatsoever, because you are unborn.
Likewise, you are the ender of the universe through the form of Rudra, by means of its withdrawal.
But for you, there is no end, because you are indestructible;
likewise, you are the beginning of the world, because you are ancient. But for you, there is no beginning, because you are eternal.
