Likewise, you are the Lord of the world, because the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe depend upon you; but for you, there is none.

Someone might argue that [the Lord] is not the Sovereign because of being "complete" (paripūrṇa). The word "also" (api) should be connected with every term [in the compound], indicating a contradiction.
However, while there is a contradiction if one resorts to a *tatpuruṣa* compound for these words, there is no contradiction when using a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
You know yourself by yourself; you create yourself by yourself;
and through your own creative power, you dissolve back into yourself alone.
The meaning of the statement is that there is no other whatsoever who is your creator, destroyer, or knower.
Now, as for that which is eternal, what kind of creation and dissolution could it have of its own accord?
There is no fault here, as [these occur] through the distinction of incarnations (avatāras); for its parts (aṃśas) are produced for the sake of specific tasks.

And they dissolve. Or rather, this was stated thus because of the plurality of persons (puruṣa). By the "accomplished one" (kṛtin), meaning the skillful one who knows all; [the form] *pralīyase* is the present indicative (*laṭ*) in the active voice. 10.

You are fluid, you are solid through aggregation, you are gross, subtle, light, and heavy; you are manifest and the other than manifest; O Lord of manifestations, your power of irresistible will prevails.
In Your manifestations—the glories such as the earth and so forth—there is sovereignty, abundance, or the power to act according to Your will.
For instance, You alone are the liquid, whose essence is rasa;
and You are the solid, being either a composite (saṃghāta), which is an aggregate of atoms, or that which is hard and firm by means of such an aggregate.
The meaning is that it is "solid" (kaṭhina) because it consists of a composite form;
it is "gross" (sthūla) because it is composed of the great elements such as earth and so forth;
it is "subtle" (sūkṣma) because its essence is the power of the senses. Lightness and heaviness are likewise your two manifestations (vibhūtī).
Because Brahman consists of all powers, even that which is gross becomes light, like a boat and so forth;
even that which is subtle becomes heavy, like a separate piece of gold.
Likewise, you alone are manifest and perceptible, because you take the form of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest.
The unmanifest is both manifest and other than manifest, because it consists of both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
The meaning of the statement is that whatever is seen or unseen is but a mere fragment of Your glory. || 11 ||
Of those words whose opening is the Udgītha, whose utterance is by means of the three Nyāyas, whose ritual action is sacrifice, and whose fruit is heaven— you are the source of them.
You are the source, the place of origin, of those words and utterances. To the question "Of which ones?", he says: "Of those whose [source] is the Praṇava, the syllable Om, known as the Udgītha.
For in the Veda, this [syllable] is conventionally designated by the name Udgītha.

Some, however, say that the *udgītha* is both the beginning and the concluding part; for in the recitation, the syllable *oṃ* is necessarily employed at the very start and at the end. And for those [recitations] which are established by the three methods—namely, the high (*tāra*), low (*mandra*), and middle (*madhya*) pitches—or by the *saṃhitā*, *pada*, and *krama* modes of recitation.
Their utterance or pronunciation is performed through the high, low, and circumflex accents, or through the acts of studying and teaching, or through the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
and their function is sacrifice— the activity of the sacrificer— and their fruit is heaven.
The meaning is "of those Śrutis.
By this, it is stated that you are the first rememberer and promoter of the Vedas. || 12 ||
They declare you to be Nature (prakṛti), which sets in motion the goals of the person (puruṣa);
yet they know you alone to be the Person (puruṣa), the indifferent witness of that [Nature]. 13.

The Sāṃkhyas declare you to be *prakṛti*, and they call you *buddhi* and *manas*. Of what nature are you? You are that which "proceeds for the sake of the *puruṣa*" (*puruṣārtha-pravartinī*), meaning it functions for the purpose of the conscious self's goal; for all *prakṛti* exists for the sake of the *puruṣa*.

For the sake of enjoyment and for the sake of the knowledge of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. And it has been said: "Since the intellect accomplishes experience for the sake of the individual soul (*puruṣa*), it is that very intellect which again distinguishes the subtle difference between primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the *puruṣa*."

Moreover, those people know that very person (puruṣa) to be such: he is "the seer of that," meaning he perceives that primordial nature (prakṛti). For the followers of Kapila maintain that the person is the seer, while the intellect (buddhi) is the object seen. Likewise, he is "indifferent" (udāsīna), meaning inactive. As it has been said:
And from this absence of error, the witness-hood of this Puruṣa is established,
as well as his isolation, neutrality, state of being a seer, and lack of agency.
You are the father even of the ancestors, the deity even of the gods;
you are higher than the highest, the ordainer even of the ordainers.

The *pitṛs* are sevenfold classes of divine beings; you are their father as well, because they are to be gratified by you in the *śrāddha* rite. You are the deity even of the gods, such as Indra and others, because they are to be worshipped by you.
Furthermore, you are beyond even the subtle things, such as the senses, being the most subtle of all.
As it has been said:
"The objects are indeed superior to the senses; the mind is superior to the objects;
the intellect is superior to the mind; and the Great Self is superior to the intellect."
Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest; beyond the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal.

Likewise, you are the creator (vedhāḥ), the progenitor, even of the ordainers (vedhasaḥ), the lords of creatures (prajāpatayaḥ) such as Dakṣa, Manu, and others; the word "api" is used here to express wonder. 14.
You alone are the oblation and the priest, the food and the eternal eater;
you are the object of knowledge and the knower, the meditator and that which is the supreme object of meditation. 15.
This praise is based on the non-duality of the agent and the object:

"He who offers the oblation and that which is offered; he who eats according to the rules and that which is eaten; he who knows and that which is known, that which is to be known; he who meditates and that which is the supreme, most excellent object of meditation—all that is of your nature, you alone are Brahman, eternal and immutable."
This straightforward meaning for the purpose of praise has been explained concisely;
however, the detailed exposition [should be sought] from a thorough study of other treatises. 15.
Having heard these truthful and heart-pleasing praises from them,
the Creator, inclined toward grace, replied to the gods.
Having thus heard the hymns of praise from the gods, the Creator Brahmā, becoming well-disposed through his grace, spoke this to the deities.
Of what kind were they? They were "yathārthāḥ," meaning their subject matter was true;
for that very reason, they were "hṛdayaṅgamāḥ," meaning pleasing to the mind. [The suffix] *khac* is applied after the root *gam* in the sense of "reaching" (Pāṇini 3.2.49). 16.
For that ancient poet, as uttered from the mouth of the four-faced Brahmā,
the fourfold application of words became fully realized.
The poet says:

For that first poet, the omniscient one, the fourfold application of words— divided into substance, quality, action, and genus— uttered by his four faces became fully realized and accomplished its purpose,
because it was spoken directly by the Blessed One himself.

The collection of four faces is *caturmukham*; it belongs to the class beginning with *pātra* (Pāṇini 2.4.11). That which has four parts is *catuṣṭayī*, according to the rule *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap* (Pāṇini 5.2.42) and *hrasvāttādau taddhite* (Pāṇini 6.1.70).
Thus ends the section on the substitution of *ṣ*. 17.
What did he say? He says:
"Welcome to you, O you of abundant prowess, who have arrived simultaneously with arms as long as a yoke, having assumed your own offices by means of your powers. (18)

"O you of abundant prowess and great heroism, welcome to you! Through the act of honoring their arrival, a blessing is conveyed by means of these auspicious words. [The status of] "to whom" (the recipient) is established by the rule "there is also [the designation of recipient] when an action is mentioned. Of what sort are you?
Having assumed their respective offices and duties by virtue of their majesty, they simultaneously approached; for the Ādityas did not come there having abandoned their movement through the sky.
From those whose arms were as long as a yoke—that is, from those whose arms reached down to their knees.
Two pairs of hands constitute a yuga. || 18 ||
What is this, that your faces do not bear their own luster as before, like stars whose clarity is obscured by frost? 19.
Your faces do not possess today the same luster as they formerly bore;
they do not carry it now. Tell me, what is this?
Just as the stars—the luminaries whose clarity and purity are obscured and impaired by frost and mist—no longer possess their radiance, so too are your faces. 19.
Now he speaks of this very matter in detail:
"Due to the subsiding of its flames, this thunderbolt of the slayer of Vṛtra appears as if its edges have been blunted, no longer emitting the celestial weapon. (20)
This thunderbolt of Indra, the enemy of the asura Vṛtra, appears as if its edge is blunted and its point broken.
What is this?
It is for this very reason that, due to the subsiding of its flames and the extinguishing of its luster, it has neither discharged the weapon of the gods nor manifested the bow of Indra.
For they say that the rainbow arises from the spreading radiance of the lightning-flash; "aśru" means a stream. 20.
Moreover, this noose of Varuṇa, which was once irresistible to his enemies,
has now fallen into a state of wretchedness, its power neutralized by a mantra, like that of a serpent.

And why is this noose of Varuṇa, which was previously so difficult for enemies to resist, today reduced to a state of wretchedness and dejection by the power of the mantra—as if it were a snake whose venom has been destroyed? The meaning is that it has become one whose power is lost, like a serpent deprived of its poison. || 21 ||
With his mace cast aside, his arm resembled a tree with broken branches, as if proclaiming the mental anguish and defeat of Kubera.
The arm of Vaiśravaṇa, by whom the mace was cast away and abandoned, seems to announce his defeat by the enemy—a source of pain that has become a thorn in his mind.
For one who is not humiliated does not hurl his own weapon;
it is for this very reason that Kubera’s body appears withered, resembling a tree whose branches have been lopped off due to the abandonment of his mace.
Even Yama, scratching the ground with his staff whose luster has faded, treats this [staff] as if it were as light as an extinguished firebrand, even though it remains unerring in its power.

This son of Vivasvat, too, out of embarrassment, scratching the earth with his own weapon, the staff, displays a lack of regard—a lightness of hand—toward this fierce rod, as if it were a mere extinguished, tranquil brand of fire;
for it has lost its luster, its brilliance having set, like a fire extinguished where no wind blows.
And how is it that these suns, whose heat has been extinguished by cold, have become so utterly beautiful to behold, as if they were figures depicted in a painting? (24)
And why have these suns, due to their coolness caused by the heat of their radiance, become so exceedingly desirable to behold—attaining a state of visibility as if they were fixed in a painting?
For previously, even when glanced at slightly, they would have scorched the sight. || 24 ||
From the agitation of the winds, a break in their momentum is inferred,
just as the obstruction of a current of water is inferred from its flowing upstream.
The obstruction of the speed—the checking of the velocity—of the Maruts, the winds, is inferred or surmised.
Why? Because of their agitation, their clustering together, and their confusion;
for those spreading forth with speed do not become agitated.
Just as the obstruction of a flood of waters is inferred from its movement upstream. || 25 ||
Even the heads of the Rudras, with the tips of their crescent moons hanging from their bound topknots, seemed to proclaim their defeated "hum" sounds.
Even the heads of the Rudras— those distinguished deities of infinite power— proclaim that their wounds have vanished and their special *huṃkāra* sounds have ceased;
they have become such as these,
for the tips of the crescent moons hanging from their crowns of matted hair have been bent down.
The *jaṭā-maulayaḥ* are the matted locks themselves as crowns, because they have that shape;

or, the *maulayaḥ* are the hair in the form of matted locks; or, they are the crests of the matted locks. Those [clouds] upon which the tips of the moon hang, suspended from those matted-lock-crowns that are bent down and drooping.

For "having disheveled hair" (muktakeśatā) suggests humiliation; however, the reading "indicating the destruction of one's pride" (kṣatāhaṃkāraśaṃsinī), as found in the older manuscript tradition, is more appropriate here. 26.
For you have first been established by others who were more powerful,
just as general rules are set aside by exceptions.
And for this reason, why is it that those who were previously established and had attained their station have today been turned back by powerful enemies and deprived of their place?
They are like general rules (utsarga) set aside by exceptions (apavāda).
For a general characteristic, though first established in its own domain, is cast out from its own sphere by another, more powerful particular characteristic. || 27 ||
"Tell me, my children, what do you seek by having come here?
For while the creation of the worlds rests with me, their protection is vested in you. (28)

"O sons, if you have been defeated, then tell me: what do you request from me? What do you desire? The word *kim* (what) implies a question preceded by doubt. Between creation and preservation, if you request creation, that is well.
Since the creation of the world rests with the Creator,
while its protection lies with you, the guardians of the worlds, the reading "prārthayadhvam" (you should pray) is an error;
for in the context of a question expressing doubt, the imperative mood (*loṭ*) is not expressive of that sense.
For when the meaning of a sentence is intent upon negation, the sense of an injunction becomes appropriate; as for example:
"What could one of noble mind give, and what could he eat, even if he possessed the three worlds in their entirety, were he distressed by the need to support his dependents?"
And here, when there is doubt as to what object you gentlemen are requesting, the use of the present tense (*laṭ*) alone is logical. ||28||
Then Vāsava urged his preceptor with a thousand eyes that shone like a bed of lotuses stirred by a gentle breeze.
Perceiving his desire to hear the words "Tell that," Indra immediately urged the preceptor of the gods with a glance from the corner of his eye.

Consequently, due to the trembling [of his eyes], it was fitting— even for the gods who do not blink— that their eyes should move by the power of their will, possessing the beauty of a cluster of lotuses shaken by a gentle breeze.
The contraction of the eyes by means of missiles is difficult to accomplish. || 29 ||
Vācaspati, with palms joined in reverence, spoke thus to the lotus-seated Brahmā, whose two eyes were the eye of Hari and who surpassed the thousand-eyed Indra: 30.

Then Bṛhaspati, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to Viriñca (Brahmā). Of what nature was he? His eye was like an eye, being superior even to the thousand eyes of Hari (Indra), though [Indra] himself possesses only two eyes.
Indeed, as long as he does not see with those [eyes], he does not see even with his thousand eyes;
for this very reason, that [thousandfold nature] is an incitement.
Although these are qualifiers of the eyes, they are to be understood as qualifiers of the Teacher alone, because it is his very eye that is thus characterized.

A thousand eyes have been gathered together, thus [he is] "Sahasranayana" (the Thousand-eyed One). [This occurs] in the case of a compound for the sake of benefit, a descriptive determinative compound (*tatpuruṣa*), or a collective compound (*samāhāra*). A *dvigu* compound takes the singular number.
In common usage, the word *vācaspati* is optionally [used] like *vainya* and *giriśa*. 30.
What did he say? He says:
"O Blessed One, it is as you have said; our position has been refuted by others.
How could the Lord, whose self is engaged with each [object], not know it? (2.31)
"O Blessed One, it is exactly as you have said; you discern that we have indeed gained our footing.
For our domain has been seized, trampled, and taken away by our enemies.
And yet, O Blessed One, this knowledge of yours is not surprising."

Since He is the Lord who abides as the very self of all, how could He not know? He knows; for [the rule] "after the five beginning with *āṅ*, after *bruvaḥ*, and after *āho bruvaḥ*" applies here. "Bhagavan" is a term of reverence.
Sovereignty, complete virtue, fame, prosperity,
dispassion, and liberation— of these six, the word "Bhaga" is the traditional designation.
In the sense of "he will know" (jñāsyati), when used in the sense of denial (apahnava), the middle voice (ātmanepada) for the root *jñā* is optional by the rule *akarmakācca*.
Even regarding the present tense, they generally employ the *lṛṭ* (the periphrastic future);
for example: "May it be well with you; I shall go.
"In this weighty matter, I shall appoint someone equal to myself."
"I shall cause her to feel intense remorse," and so forth. || 31 ||
Having stated generally, "Our position has been seized by our enemies," he speaks specifically: "The great asura named Tāraka, emboldened by a boon obtained from you..."
He has arisen like a comet for the destruction of the worlds.
A great Daitya named Tāraka, the son of Vajrāṅga, having become arrogant through a boon obtained from you, has arisen like a comet for the purpose of afflicting the world.

For the rising of a comet portends calamity for the world. A comet that is smoke-shaped is a *dhūmaketu*; it is exceedingly formidable. The word *udīrṇaḥ* is derived from the root *ṛ* (to go) with the suffix *kta*.
From the root *ṛdh*, there is substitution of *r* for the vowel [of the suffix].
This substitution of *r* occurs in place of the vowel.
In this regard, he first describes its intensity: "In the city, the sun spreads its heat only to such an extent that it is sufficient for the blossoming of the lotuses in the long ponds. (33)
In his city, the sun shines only to such an extent that the blooming of the lotuses and water-lilies is produced;
it does not shine more than that, out of fear of him.
The suffix *kan* is applied to the word *dīrghikā* in the sense of a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*).
Whatever its measure may be, however great it is—from that [measure], the suffix *mātrac* is added in the sense of the word itself (svārthe). 33.
The moon always serves him with all its digits;
it does not withhold even the single digit that has been made into the crest-jewel of Hara.
The moon serves him incessantly with all its digits;
it does not withhold even that single digit which has become the crest-jewel of the Lord,
because of the god’s great majesty.
Thus, when the moon, having abandoned the world, out of fear worships that very [Hara] while remaining eternally full, then there is a calamity for the world.
The same applies hereafter.

And in this context, having perceived a difference in the moon, [the poet] said that he did not take up the crescent moon of Hara because, in his haste, he failed to consider what use it would be to him. || 34 ||
The wind, its movement checked by the fear of stealing the flowers from the garden,
did not blow at her side with a force greater than that of a palm-leaf fan.
In his presence, the wind does not blow with greater force than the breeze from a palm-leaf fan or a handheld fan;
for its movement has been checked out of fear of scattering the flowers of the garden.
For if it were to blow with vehemence, it might perhaps carry away the blossoms of the grove.
Then, punishment shall befall him. || 35 ||
Abandoning their seasonal rotation, the Seasons, intent on providing an abundance of flowers,
wait upon him like common gardeners.
The six seasons, beginning with spring, constantly attend upon and serve him like a gardener, setting aside their sequential order.
Having abandoned defects such as excessive heat or cold, they are solely intent on gathering flowers; thus, they are all equal and common.
It is not strictly logical here to employ the pronoun *tat* (that) when the word *tadpara* (intent on that) already contains the word *tat*.
Because that which is to be grasped is directly specified,
as in the example "your two hands are devoted to seeing you," and because of the repetition [of the word], an emphasis is understood. || 36 ||
The Lord of Rivers waits within his waters for some time before the gems suitable for presentation to him can be brought forth.
The ocean, amidst its waters, somehow awaits and searches for the jewels worthy of being a pillow for Tāraka;
that is to say, until their completion—that is, until the acquisition of such suitable gems.
In the phrase "pratīkṣate," the reading "apekṣate" (expects) is more elegant. || 37 ||
And at night, serpents headed by Vāsuki, with the crests of their jewels blazing,
attend upon him like steady lamps.
And because of the blazing crests of their jewels, the lords of the nāgas, such as Vāsuki and Takṣaka, treat it as a steady lamp and resort to it at night; for its steadiness—

Because it does not depend on oil and the like, and because it is free from affliction by wind and other elements; herein, connoisseurs should consider whether the presence of a serpent at night for the amorous Tāraka is appropriate or not. [The word] *enam* takes the form *enaḥ* in the second case singular and dual. 38.
Expecting the favor bestowed by him, even Indra daily gratifies him with ornaments from the wish-fulfilling tree brought by the charioteer.
Let the other gods remain;
even the Lord of the Gods daily honors him with ornaments from the wish-fulfilling trees sent by his messengers,
since he seeks the favor granted by Tāraka.
The root *harati* is used in the sense of "attaining" as well, and not only in the sense of "stealing. || 39 ||
Even when propitiated in this manner, the wicked man torments the three worlds;
he is pacified by retaliation, not by kindness.
In this manner described, although he is served by the sun, the moon, the wind, the seasons, the ocean, the serpent-king, and the lord of the gods, he continues to afflict the worlds.
And this is not surprising;
for a wicked person is pacified—that is, becomes tranquil—only by opposition, by harm, or by affliction, and certainly not by kindness.
The optative suffix (liṅ) is used in the sense of possibility (sambhāvanā), as in "liṅ evam-ādi-sambhāvane."
He describes that very same affliction:
"By him, the trees of the Nandana grove—whose sprouts were tenderly plucked by the hands of the immortal maidens—are made to experience the falling of their own severed branches. (41)
By him, the trees of the celestial gardens are made objects of his supernormal power through their being split, felled, divided, and uprooted;
that is to say, they are cut and cast down.

He says this so that they might perhaps become suitable for those [trees]—having their sprouts and tender shoots gently plucked by the hands of the immortal women, the hands of the celestial nymphs, for the purpose of ear-ornaments and the like.

Thus, by the destruction of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), a great calamity has been brought about. Who is it that possesses direct knowledge? [He is] one who knows directly; thus, he is called "one with direct knowledge" (abhijña). 41.
And while he slept, he was fanned by the captive celestial women with chowries that released showers of teardrops and emitted a breeze no different from his own breath.

And that asura, lying down, was fanned and cooled by the wives of the gods with yak-tail whisks. Of what kind were they? Those whose wind (breath) was common, shared, and mingled with his own breath. And likewise—
Those who shed and release showers of tear-drops and water-sprays indeed sigh and weep out of sorrow. A female enemy, captured by force as a captive—
[this refers to the root] *ij* in the sense of "to go."

The form *vījyate* is derived from the root preceded by the prefix *vi-* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), used in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*). Verbal roots have multiple meanings. The particle *ca* serves as a conjunction (*samuccaye*) in reference to what precedes it.
In the reading *hi*, the particle *hi* functions in the sense of *ca*.

In the expression "with chowries" (*cāmaraiḥ*), the third case is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). In the expression "by bards" (*vandībhiḥ*), it is used in the sense of an agent (*kartari*).

In the reading "of the bards" (*vandīnām*), the sixth case is used in relation to the chowries. However, regarding the act of fanning, by virtue of proximity, the object being fanned is indeed the [king] himself.
Or one who makes chowries. 42.
Having uprooted the peaks of Mount Meru, which were trampled by the hooves of the gods' horses,
he fashioned pleasure-mountains within his own dwellings.
Having uprooted the peaks of the mountain of the gods, he fashioned pleasure-mountains—play-hills—for his own residences;
they are called "pleasure-mountains" because people sport (*ākrīḍyante*) upon them. Of what nature were they?
They were trampled by the hooves of the green horses of the sun’s chariot.
The statement "ground" refers to their height. || 43 ||
Now, the waters remaining in the Mandākinī are turbid with the ichor of the elephants of the quarters;
her ponds have now become the abode for the crops of golden lotuses.

Today, only a remnant of water remains in the Mandākinī river; it is turbid and fouled by the ichor of the elephants of the quarters, for they come there for the sake of sporting in the water. As for where the golden lotuses have gone, he says: they are indeed the golden lotuses themselves.
Their crop is the fruit; their ponds are now their reservoirs. This is a statement regarding the extraction of the essence, because [the plants] were uprooted from there and planted there.
That which remains is the "residue" (śeṣa). The suffix ghañ, when devoid of verbal force (bhāva), has the gender of the word it denotes (vācyaliṅga).
*samprati* means "just now" or "presently. The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule beginning with *prajñādi*. 44.
The joy of beholding the world is not experienced by the celestial beings on their path through the empty regions, due to the fear of the falling of their aerial chariots. 45.

Satisfaction is not experienced by the celestial beings through the beholding—that is, the seeing—of the worlds. Why is this? He says: because the path of the celestial chariots in the sky has become entirely empty and void.
The falling of Tāraka is his assault; from that comes fear. For while they are moving about without hesitation, he might at any moment arrive and suddenly fall upon them from above.

That master of illusions snatches away from us, while we look on, the sacrificial offerings prepared by the performers of sacrifice during their extended rituals, through the mouth of Jātavedas (the Fire-god). 46.

While we were looking on—winking and competing with one another—he, by means of his illusory power, snatches away and carries off from the mouth of the fire the sacrificial offerings, such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and the like, which have been won during the sacrifices performed by the frequent sacrificers (*yajvabhiḥ*) and those who perform sacrifices repeatedly (*yāyajūkebhiḥ*).
One who performs sacrifice is called a *yajvā*;
[the suffix] *ṅvanip* is applied after the root *suyaj*.
"Maya" refers to rice and other such grains. The word "na" is used with the genitive case either in relation to the oblation (*havya*) or in the sense of disregard. || 46 ||
And he carried off the excellent horse Uccaiḥśravas,
who was exceedingly noble, as if he were seizing the long-earned glory of Indra, which was firmly established among the gods.
That best of horses, named Uccaiḥśravas, was seized by him from Indra with a loud cry;
it is imagined to be like the embodied fame of Hari, acquired over a long time and now bound to a physical form.
The suffix *luṅ* is used for the past tense (*ahāri*) in the sense of an action. || 47 ||
Now, as to why the employment of means such as conciliation was not applied there, he says:
"Against that cruel one, all our means of policy were rendered ineffective, like potent medicines against a disorder caused by the simultaneous derangement of all three humors (sāṃnipātika). (48)
Against that star, all four of our expedients— conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force— have been rendered ineffective and have lost their power.
For just as potent medicines fail against a cruel and severe complication arising from the three humors (sāṃnipātika), becoming fruitless due to its virulence, so too are these means thwarted.

Because of the mutual opposition of the *dhātus*, that which provokes their combination (*saṃnipāta*) is called *sāṃnipātika*. The suffix *ṭhak* should be stated [after the word *saṃnipāta*] according to the rule "and after *saṃnipāta*. (Pāṇini 4.3.48)
He speaks of that very state of having one's action frustrated:
"That very discus of Hari, by the flames arising from its impact, has been placed upon his neck like a golden necklace (niṣka), wherein our hope for victory was struck down. (49)

Upon which disc we always had our hope for victory, thinking, "Surely by this we shall conquer our enemies"—that Sudarśana, the discus of Hari, was placed upon his neck like a golden ornament (niṣka).
Though hurled to sever his head, it became as if adorned with a niṣka, meaning it proceeded deprived of its power.
It was such that its flames arose merely from the impact against his throat.
Because his neck was like a diamond, the ornament on his chest was a golden necklace (niṣka). 49.
Today, his elephants— having already conquered Airāvaṇa— practice their frontal blows against the clouds, such as Puṣkarāvartaka and others.

The celestial elephants of the stars, having surpassed the elephants of the gods, now practice the sport of tossing their banks against the clouds of the world's end, such as Puṣkarāvartaka; for they alone are capable of withstanding those blows.
Having thus exposed the insult, he states the purpose of his arrival:
"Therefore, O Lord, we desire that a commander be created for his pacification, just as those seeking liberation seek the Dharma that severs the bonds of karma for the sake of Bhava. (51)
Therefore, O All-pervading Lord, we desire and entreat you to create a commander-in-chief;
for you have said to me, "Indeed, the creation shall be through me," so that there may be peace for this worldly existence.
Yogins who desire liberation long for that merit which severs the bonds of karma;
for by the fire of knowledge, the fuel of karma is consumed. In the phrase "sṛṣṭim icchāma," the suffix denotes a connection with the verbal root. Or else:
One who is full of energy and pride is said to be "created" (*sṛṣṭa*).
For example: "By him, having obtained from Śiva a weapon difficult to acquire, he was created for the conquest of Indra’s world."

The reading "sraṣṭum" (to create) is indeed a corruption. One who leads an army is a "senānī"; the substitution of "yaṇ" is according to the rule "satsūdviṣa...". The form "icchām" is in the imperative mood (loṭ) expressing a request. || 51 ||
Placing him at the head, the breaker of mountain peaks (Indra) will recover from his enemies the goddess of victory, like a captive woman, he who is the protector of the celestial armies.
Of what sort is the commander-in-chief?

He whom Indra, the breaker of mountains (Gotrabhit), having placed at the front as the protector of the divine armies, will bring back from the presence of his enemies the Goddess of Victory, like a captive woman forcibly abducted—indeed, he will recover both. The word *puraskṛtya* is derived from the indeclinable *puraḥ*.
In the word *gotrabhit*, there is the substitution of *s* for *t* according to the rule "namaspurasorgatyoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.40), because it denotes a direction.
Since they protect the earth (*gām*), they are called *gotrāḥ*, meaning mountains; Indra is the "Mountain-Splitter" (*gotrabhit*) because he split them. || 52 ||
When those words had been uttered,
the Self-born One (Brahmā) spoke a speech that surpassed in excellence the rain that follows a thunderclap.
When that speech of Bṛhaspati had been concluded and finished, Brahmā, the self-born, uttered a word; he spoke these words:

"That voice which, through its excellence and fruitfulness, has surpassed the subsequent rain that was to come after the thundering—this is because it has rendered fruitful the grand display of the preceptor’s prayer."
In the word *jigāya*, there is the substitution of *k* for *g* according to the rule *san-liṭorjer*. || 53 ||
He spoke to that very mountain:
"This desire of yours shall be fulfilled; wait for some time. However, I will not personally undertake the task of creation for its accomplishment. (54)
The desire characterized by the emergence of a commander-in-chief shall be fulfilled for you; however,
wait now for a short while, because I myself do not undertake the creative activity for the sake of accomplishing this task.
Why is this so? He says:
"For this reason, that Daitya, having attained prosperity from this very source, does not deserve destruction from this same source;
even a poison-tree, having been nurtured by oneself, is unfit to be cut down by that same person. (55)

This son of Vajrāṅga has attained prosperity through me by virtue of his excellent conduct; therefore, he does not deserve destruction at my hands. For while other fruit-bearing trees may be cut down after they have been brought to maturity, it is improper and unfitting for even a poisonous tree to be felled once it has grown.
This word *sāmprata* (proper/fitting) signifies what is appropriate by its very nature, as it inherently contains the power of the action.
Since the object has already been expressed by that very [action], there is no need for a second accusative case, as in the case of a poison tree (*viṣavṛkṣa*) and the like.
Even with respect to the action of nurturing, this [tree] does not require it,
because the primary object has already been expressed.
For it has been said thus: "When the power of the primary element (pradhāna) is expressed, the power of the subordinate element (guṇa) appears as if it were already expressed.

For example: "Let this woman, the enemy's wife, be killed. And even though [the term] is a qualifier of a specific tree, because the general [term] was introduced first, it is not appropriate [to change it]; therefore, the indication is given according to its established state. || 55 ||
Now, he explains why this calamity was brought about by you yourself: "This very boon was chosen by him previously, and it was promised to him by me;
for that ascetic power was sufficient to burn the worlds, yet it was neutralized by the boon. (56)

Long ago, that Tāraka chose this very boon: "May I be invulnerable to the gods, with the exception of infants seven days old. I likewise promised and accepted it for him, because his ascetic power, if not quenched by the granting of a boon, would be capable of consuming the worlds.
The fruit of asceticism must necessarily come to pass;
and if it is not rendered inert by a boon, then it will be capable of causing even greater affliction.
[The rule] "asmā iti pratyāṅbhyāṃ śruvaḥ" applies here.
The state of being the recipient (sampradāna). || 56 ||

"Let the power of destruction be ordained against us alone," he said: "Who could withstand him, the warrior prepared for battle, were it not for a portion of the seed of Nīlalohita infused [into him]? (57)

Who among you would be able to withstand him when he has exerted his prowess in battle? Except for Nīlalohita Śarva— that portion, part, or incarnation of his bright seed which was cast into the field— excluding him.

The meaning is that even the son of Hari (Kārttikeya) would be unable to conquer him; for he was *sāṃyugīna*, skilled in battle. The suffix *khañ* is applied after *pratijana* and other words in the sense of "good" (*sādhu*).
The ablative case ending [in the word *aṃśāt*] occurs due to its connection with the word *ṛte*. 57.
Now, as to how the wrestler who is a portion of Hara could prevail where even Indra, Upendra, and the others were not capable, he says:
"For that god is the supreme light, established beyond darkness."
The extent of his radiance and supernatural power has been measured neither by me nor by Viṣṇu.
Because that Mahādeva is the supreme, most excellent, subtle light— the splendor known as the Supreme Self— established beyond darkness, which is without beginning or end;
and because the abundance of his powers and greatness has not been fully delimited or determined by either me or Viṣṇu, he is described as such.
And therefore, how could he who is a portion of such a Great God not be one who tears asunder his adversaries? || 58 ||
And regarding the possibility of attaining a portion of that [state], he states the means:
"By means of the form of Umā, you must strive to draw out the mind of Śambhu, which is stilled by self-restraint, just as a magnet attracts iron. (59)

In the form of Umā, with the body of Gaurī, you all must strive—exert yourselves—to attract and seize the mind of Śambhu, which is rendered motionless by meditative absorption (samādhi) like iron, as if it were a magnetized piece of metal.
By the use of the pronoun "you" (te), he indicates their dedication to this effort.
An "ayaskānta" is a magnet, that which attracts iron (ayas).
Therefore, although the rule *kṛ-kam-i* does not apply here, the treatment [of the visarga as *ś*] occurs because of its inclusion in the *kaska*-type list. 59.
He says— whether it is possible or not for another young woman to attract the heart of Hara in the absence of Gaurī:
"Both [of them] are indeed capable of enduring the power infused by both."
Whether it be Śambhu himself or his water-formed manifestation, it is mine.
The seed, which is the virility belonging to both, having been deposited and cast, is capable of being endured and supported by both women alone. To the question "Which two? Which ones? he says:
"She, the Śāmbhavī form of Śambhu, and my own body in the form of a woman; for by Brahmā..."

Vīrya was cast into the waters; ... and the emission (visarga) is indeed a form of the Eight-formed One (Aṣṭamūrti). This has been stated incidentally with the desire to establish a point of comparison.
The meaning is that just as water is capable of enduring my virility, even so does Gaurī alone endure the splendor of Hara.
Here, the word "vā" is used in the sense of conjunction (samuccaya).
Furthermore, this is the principal view, wherein the indicators are equal to the indicated.
Even when summoned by his companions, even though he has cast off sleep,
and even though he is intent on departing, the traveler does not loosen his reluctance.
His soul, having attained the command of your army, shall release with the splendor of his prowess the braided locks of you women held captive in heaven.
The son of that very Hara, the blue-throated one, having attained the leadership of your armies, will release the braided tresses of the captive celestial beauties by means of his abundant power.
For it is the custom that the untying of a woman's hair, once bound by her husband, must be performed by him alone.
Śiva’s throat has become blue due to the consumption of the Kālakūṭa poison.
Having thus addressed the gods, the Source of the Universe vanished;
and they too, having resolved upon their duties, returned to heaven.
Having spoken thus to the gods, the Creator, the source of the universe, vanished and disappeared;
the gods, too, having accomplished their purpose, returned to heaven.
Having resolved upon that matter, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) went to Kandarpa with a mind whose speed was doubled by the urgency to accomplish his purpose.
Then, having deliberated with his ministers on how the union of Hara and Gaurī was to be brought about in that celestial realm, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, called Smara (Kāma) to mind.
With what kind of mind?
With one possessing double the speed—that is, with great impetuosity—due to the haste for the successful accomplishment of the task characterized by the union of Hara and Gaurī.
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, the root *gam* takes the substitute *aṅ* due to its being marked with the *ḷuṭ* indicator;
he is called Pākaśāsana because of his slaying of the asura named Pāka.
Then, having slung around his neck a bow whose beautiful tips were curved like the playful eyebrows of lovely women and which was marked with the footprints of Rati’s bracelets,
he took as his weapon a mango sprout offered by the hand of his companion, the Spring.
With palms joined in reverence, the flower-bannered god approached Śatamakha.
Then, being remembered, Kāma, having formed a *añjali* (salutation with joined palms), approached and presented himself before Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
The *taṅ* suffix is used here in the sense of "bringing about a meeting. Having done what?
Having placed his bow upon his neck because of his state of *prāñjali-tva* (having joined palms). Of what nature was he?

The beautiful peaks [of the mountain] are like the creeper-like eyebrows of those women who are graceful and full of charm; this is due to their lovely curvature and their power of enchantment. On what kind of neck?
Rati is his wife.
What kind of flower-bannered god (Kusumadhvaja) was he, whose very mark or sign was the impression of her bracelets— the patterns of her bangles— due to the force of his embrace?
He whose weapon—an arrow—is the mango sprout itself, which was placed and entrusted into the hand of his companion and friend, the sweet Spring.
[This is composed in] the Mālinī meter.
65. Thus ends the second canto in the commentary on the *Kumārasambhava* composed by Vallabhadeva, son of Ānandadeva.
The Third Canto.
Upon him, Indra’s thousand eyes fell simultaneously, having abandoned the thirty gods;
for the respect shown by masters toward their dependents is generally fickle, depending as it does upon the presence of some purpose.

Then, a thousand eyes of Maghavan Indra fell upon that object simultaneously; the meaning is that he beheld it with his full complement of one thousand eyes. "Having abandoned the Tridaśas" means having left behind the gods.
And this is appropriate, since the respect shown by masters toward their dependents and servants is generally fickle and unstable;
for what reason? Because it is subject to the requirements of utility and driven by necessity. As it has been said:
"They abandon even their own biological sons if those sons fail to provide assistance."
In this composition, the meters used are almost exclusively upajāti. || 1 ||

Having been granted the space by Vāsava with the command

Then that Smara, having greeted the favor of his lord with a bow of his head, began to speak thus to Ākhaṇḍala in private. He [Indra] granted him a place, saying, "Sit here near my seat," thus personally assigning him ground by Śakra himself. The phrase *āsanasannikṛṣṭam* means "in the vicinity of the seat," that is, close to the seat.
The Ātmanepada ending is used because of the rule "prākramateti propābhyāṃ samarthābhyām" (Pāṇini 1.3.42).
What did he say? He says:

"Command me, O Knower of the distinctions of men; whatever must be done by you among the worlds, I desire to increase that favor which has been set in motion by your remembrance through your command. (3)
O you who know the distinctions among men, the most excellent in knowledge among all persons in the worlds—that is, among all beings—command that which is to be done by you. How so?
By your grace, that is, by your favor, [this work] has been set in motion, impelled by the mere remembrance of you.
By your command, I desire to cause it to increase and bring it to growth. || 3 ||

By whom, desiring the fruit of their actions, has this envy been produced through their exceedingly long austerities—that they should remain subject to the command of this bow of mine, upon which an arrow is already fixed? 4.
By whom, desiring liberation, has envy been provoked against you through excessively long and long-accumulated austerities?
Let him become subject to the command of my bow, with arrow fixed and drawn.
This is what is meant: "There is no obstacle for you; give the command. The sense is: "I shall carry out the command this very moment. || 4 ||

Who would disagree with you? For one who has entered the path of liberation out of fear of the afflictions of rebirth, let him remain bound for a long time by the side-long glances of beautiful women, playful with arched eyebrows. (5)
Who is it that, being disapproved of by you— being undesirable to you— has entered the path of liberation, the way to release characterized by knowledge and detachment?

Out of fear of the afflictions of renewed existence— that is, out of fear of the afflictions such as ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life which belong to *punarbhava*, or rebirth in the cycle of *saṃsāra*— and thus out of further fear of the sufferings of cyclic existence.
Let him remain bound for a long time, for many ages, by the side-long glances and sidelong looks of those beautiful, excellent women;
"bound" means as if truly bound, just like one who is actually fettered. As one who is bound...
Being unable to go anywhere else, he remains right there; thus, bound by side-long glances, he becomes one who desires women and does not attain the path to liberation previously described.
It is compared by the word "bound" (baddha) due to its similarity to a physical bond.
Of what kind are these side-glances? "Ārecita" refers to the action of the eyebrows, namely the knitting of the brows;
it is so called when they are raised at one point and then cast down with grace.
"Command him: 'Let him remain bound right here for a long time,' by means of the graceful arching of your eyebrows, adorned with the dancing of your line of body hair. (5)

Tell me, for which of your enemies—though he has been taught statecraft by Uśanas and though his passion and secret agents have been employed—shall I now afflict his wealth and virtue, like a swollen flood attacking the two banks of a river? (6)
Speak; tell me—of which of your enemies, of which adversary, shall I afflict both wealth and virtue? Wealth and virtue are "wealth-and-virtue. Of what kind of enemy?
Even of one [as wise as] Uśanas, that is, Śukra.

Of one who has been taught, read, and instructed in *nīti*—that is, the science of polity (*nītiśāstra*) characterized by the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) and the means such as conciliation (*sāma*) and the rest. This is what is meant: for he who is disciplined by Uśanas necessarily pursues the three aims of life (*trivarga*); but I, on the other hand, [pursue] his...
"Even for one of such a kind, I shall afflict both wealth and virtue. Furthermore, that very person is further specified: "Of what sort is he?
To this, he says: "one whose application is directed toward passion."
"Whose [enemy]— one whose resolve is passion, whose thought is a resolve of passion,
for whom a resolve of passion is applied, or for whom passion itself is an applied resolve and a spy— whose such enemy shall I afflict with wealth and desire? Who indeed?"
To whom does this belong? He says: Just as the flood—the swelling mass of water—of a river like the Indus, having increased and reached full growth, afflicts both banks or shores; even so am I.
The meaning is: "Whose wealth and dharma shall I, having grown so excessive and fierce, now afflict? || 6 ||

Do you desire her—who is devoted to the vow of having only one husband, whose character is disciplined by hardship, and whose fickle mind has been captivated by your beauty—to cast off her shame and place her hanging arms around your neck of her own accord? 7.
You desire—that is, you long for and wish for—a woman of passion clinging, hanging, and embracing your own neck with her own body.
Of what sort?
One whose arms are clung to like two crocodiles (*grāha*), due to the common quality of firmness.
Her two arms, like crocodiles, were entangled; she whose arms were thus ensnared by crocodiles—do you desire such a woman as this?

To the question, "How could she have disregarded Indra who sought her? he replies: "She was ill-disposed toward the vow of a devoted wife. One who has but one husband is called *ekapatnī*, a virtuous woman who chooses her own husband.

The vow and restraint of those who have but one husband is the "ekapatnīvrata"; she whose character (śīla) or nature (svabhāva) is such that it consists of, or is caused by, the suffering of that very vow is "ekapatnīvrata-duḥkha-śīlā"—her [the speaker addresses].
Now, is it not indeed the case that she is of such a kind?
He explains why Indra desired her: "Your fickle mind has entered [her] because of her beauty. "Fickle" (lola) means either moving or longing.
How did it enter? Because of her beauty.

"By its being beautiful to behold" means by its loveliness. That very [city] is further qualified: what is it like? "Abandoned shame"—that by which shame (*lajjā*) has been abandoned or cast off is "abandoned-shame"; that [city] is one from which modesty has been discarded. || 7 ||

O amorous one, by which angry woman were you, having committed an offense, rejected while prostrate at her feet—she whose body I shall now cause to suffer intense remorse, finding refuge only in a bed of tender leaves? (8)
O lustful man, by which woman have you been spurned, disregarded, and insulted? What sort of person are you?
You are one who has bowed at her feet, fallen prostrate at her feet.

To the question "Why is he called *avadhūta*? he says: because he is one whose offense is fresh and moist (*sarasāparādhaḥ*), meaning his transgression is perceived as having just occurred. Of what kind was she?
She was "irascible" (*kopanayā*), meaning prone to anger; that is to say, she was wrathful.
That woman whose body I shall make my refuge upon a bed of young shoots, making her intent on a couch of tender leaves— she indeed,
disregarding your request, will be lamented by me.
Her limbs tormented by my arrows, she longs for a bed of flowers and tender leaves to soothe her fever.
Be gracious; O Hero, let the thunderbolt rest; by my arrows, which enemy of the gods shall fear, his prowess of arm rendered futile, even by women whose lips quiver with anger? (9)

O Hero, show favor! Let this thunderbolt, your weapon, rest; let it remain as it is. Which enemy of the gods, of what lineage, would fear even women with lips quivering in anger, once his own strength of arm has been neutralized by our arrows?
For when angry women, trembling their lower lips, look upon him, at that very moment he sets aside all business and becomes intent on pleasing them.
In the request "Be gracious; let her rest," the *loṭ* suffix is used;
in "Let her fear," it is used in the sense of the time being appropriate (*prāptakāle*).
Because the enemies of the gods—the Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and others—are numerous, [the destruction] occurs as something inherent to their very nature;
the suffix *-tam* (in *katama*) arises in the sense of "which one? || 9 ||

Now, if you ask, "Why do you possess such power?", he says: "By your grace, even the flower-armed god, having obtained only Madhu as his companion, could cause even Hara, the wielder of the Pināka bow, to lose his fortitude; what then of other archers compared to me? (10)

"Even I, whose weapon is the flower, by your grace alone and having secured Vasantasena as my sole companion, could cause even Śiva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, to lose his composure. Therefore, what are other wretched archers and wielders of bows compared to me? The meaning is that they are utterly ineffective."
The meaning is: "Where I am capable of conquering Hara with bow in hand, what could other wretched archers do to me? The phrase "by your grace" is intended to express a lack of arrogance.
*Madhu* is Caitra; by it, spring (*vasanta*) is indicated, because that [season] consists of *madhu* and *mādhava*.
"I shall act" (*kuryām*)—this is the optative (*liṅ*) used in the sense of possibility or deliberation. *Pināka* is Śiva’s bow and trident. The word *dhanuḥ* denotes a weapon.
Those who possess those [bows] are called *dhanvinaḥ*; the suffix *-in* is applied according to the rule for the *vrīhy-ādi* group. || 10 ||

Then Śakra spoke this which was about to be said; he declared:
"In whatever matter is intended or desired to be done, I shall manifest my own power—that is, explain my innate majesty—so as to cause even a hand to lose its fortitude."
Therefore, out of an excess of reverence, he spoke while lowering his foot from his thigh.
Of what sort was the foot? It was one by which the footstool—having been honored and graced by its placement through the act of treading upon it—was elevated to a state of dignity.
This very act—placing one's feet upon him—is itself a favor bestowed upon him. || 11 ||
Encouraging him, he said:
"Friend, all this is fitting for you; both my weapons—the thunderbolt and yourself—are at hand.
The thunderbolt is blunted against the great through the power of their asceticism, but you are all-pervading and effective. (12)

The address "friend" is for the sake of showing respect. O companion, all that you have said is entirely appropriate and well-founded in you; for my two weapons are indeed the thunderbolt and yourself. He states the distinction between the two: the thunderbolt [is superior] among great beings by virtue of its ascetic power and heroism.

It is blunted and bent against those who are difficult to conquer, namely the ascetics, because it is impossible to strike them with it. You, however, possess a preeminent weapon that reaches everywhere and encompasses all objects, since it can even arouse passion within ascetics; and it is effective.
It accomplishes its task because it remains uninjured by weapons. || 12 ||
I know your strength; therefore, I shall indeed appoint you, who are equal to myself, to this weighty task.
Just as Śeṣa is commanded by Kṛṣṇa to bear his body, having regard for his status as the upholder of the earth.
And when I know your essential strength, then I shall employ you—appoint you like my own self—in a great task;
just as Viṣṇu, having considered Ananta’s capacity to support the entire earth, commands him to assume his own body.
The form *niyokṣye* is the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) because it is preceded by the prefix *ni*.
He who supports the earth is Bhūdhara; the elision of the causal suffix (ṇi) occurs here by the rule "it is frequent elsewhere as well in names and Vedic meters. 13.
Since you have declared that the flight of your arrows against the Bull-bannered Lord has become as good as accomplished for our purpose, now understand this:
the high desire of those who enjoy their share of the sacrifice, yet are our enemies, must be thwarted here.
O Hari, by your now describing the discharge of arrows, our purpose has already been effectively accomplished.
Therefore, O Hari, understand and recognize that this is the desired object of the gods who partake of sacrificial portions;
by the phrase "of the high enemies," he indicates that meaning through the device of referring to powerful foes.
From the root *budh* meaning "to awaken," the form *nibodha* arises from its svarita-accented vowel. || 14 ||
Why is their purpose dependent upon you? He says:
"For these gods desire the General of the Army, who is born of the seed of Śiva, for the sake of victory;
and he can only be accomplished by the falling of a single arrow from you, since his soul is united with Brahman and he is born from the body of Brahmā. (15)
These gods, desiring victory, wish for a commander born from the seed produced by the virility of Hara;
and that Hara can be subdued by a single discharge of your arrow— that is, he can be moved—
since his mind is fixed and his consciousness is absorbed in the Brahman, which is the Self and pure knowledge.
And therefore, who else besides you could possibly be capable of bringing [him] under control?
"Brahmāṅgabhū" means one whose son is Brahmā as his own body;
some, however, say it means one who is born from the body of Brahmā.

We, however, say: the Brahmans and the limbs (of the sacrifice) are specific mantras well-known in the Śaiva tradition; "earth" (bhūḥ) is their source, because the mantras originate from that. [The word] "uśanti" [is used] in the sense of "desiring" (vaśa kāntau). || 15 ||

Therefore, strive to win over the daughter of the Himālaya, who is self-restrained and pure, for your own sake; for it has been ordained by the Self-born Creator that among all women, she alone is fit to be the soil for the sowing of his seed. 16.
Therefore, strive—that is, exert effort—to cause Pārvatī to take pleasure in, or to desire, that Hara;

for it has been ordained by Brahmā, or is indeed observed, that among women, the earth of Hiraṇyagarbha alone is capable (kṣamā)—that is, worthy—of being the soil for the sprinkling of his seed, the field for the discharge of the semen of the Three-eyed One.
By the phrase "the self-restrained one" (*prayatām yatātmanaḥ*), he expresses the very capacity for such an undertaking.
For there is no spontaneous activity on the part of two things that are already subject to a restriction.
Therefore, by the rule "the one who is pleased is the recipient (*sampradāna*)" for verbs meaning "to please," the status of the recipient applies to the word *tasmai*. || 16 ||
Nor is she situated at such a distance that the *rocanā* would be difficult to obtain; thus he says:
"And by the command of my preceptor, the daughter of the Lord of Mountains attended upon Sthāṇu as he performed austerities on the mountain plateau.
I have heard this from the mouths of the Apsarases—that group [of them] was my secret emissary. (17)

I have heard from the mouths of the Apsarases that Pārvatī attends upon and serves Pinākin as he performs penance on the mountain slope at his father’s command. Since this company of celestial damsels is my emissary and my spy, they shall ascend the mountain’s tableland—the uppermost ground—according to the rule: "The suffix *tyakan* is used after the words *upādhi* and *upari* in the senses of proximity and ascent."
The word "ca" (and) indicates a conjunction with respect to the preceding sentence; the same applies elsewhere. 17.
Therefore, go for the sake of success and perform the work of the gods; O you who are supreme in purpose, this goal is indeed destined to be realized.
It requires a causal condition to attain its auspicious fulfillment, just as the sprout of a seed requires water before its emergence.

Therefore, O Kāma, pursue this goal for the sake of success; perform the task required by the gods, for this matter, characterized by the birth of a prince, is destined to come to pass. It requires only a cause as a sign for the attainment of auspiciousness and for its own manifestation.
It requires [auxiliary causes], just as water is required for the emergence of a seed-sprout.

For the seed-sprout must arise from its material cause (upādāna-kāraka); however, since it cannot come into being without water as a cooperative cause (sahakārin), there is a dependence upon that [water] in that case.
The word *bhavya* is derived as a noun denoting the agent. || 18 ||
Encouraging him, he speaks these two verses:
"In this means for the victory of the gods, the mastery of weapons belongs to you alone; you are indeed accomplished.
For even an unknown deed, if it is unique to a man, leads to his glory. (19)
In this means of victory for the gods, the reach and application of the weapon named after you alone is possible,
and not that of any other; therefore, you are successful, one who has achieved his purpose, and proficient,
since even a task that is unestablished or very slight [is accomplished by you].

Even that which is unique, not shared by others, and impossible for another to perform, brings glory to the doer; how much more so, then, a great deed? The word *nāma* is used here in the sense of possibility;
the meaning is that this deed of yours is indeed possible. In this context, [the power of] Hara serves as the means for victory.
Because he is the cause of causes; one who has "done" (kṛta) is "one who has done" (kṛtī), meaning one who has accomplished his purpose. || 19 ||
These gods are your petitioners; the task of all three worlds rests upon you.
With your bow, your deed shall not be excessively violent—oh, how marvelous! You are truly one whose prowess is enviable.
Oh, how wonderful! You are one whose prowess is truly desirable;
for all these gods of great power are seekers after the purpose of the three worlds, and even in that task, your role consists merely in wielding your bow.
That too is not of a violent nature; on the contrary, it causes delight.
The two words "aho" and "bata" here express an excess of wonder, as they possess the same meaning. || 20 ||
Aiming to express "by your grace," he says:
"O Manmatha, because of your association with Spring, he is indeed your companion even though not explicitly mentioned. Who needs to command the wind to be the fanning assistant of the fire? (21)

O Madana, even without your command, Spring is indeed your companion by virtue of his constant association with you; for who could ever command the wind, "Become the kindler of fire"? These two are surely companions, for it is not so.
Fire burns without wind; he who acts together with another is a companion (sahāya). || 21 ||
Saying "So be it," Madana accepted his master’s command like a subordinate and set forth;
Indra then touched his body with a hand made callous by the slapping of the elephants of the quarters.

"So be it; let it be thus. I shall carry out your command," saying this, he took his master's instruction upon his head like a garland and departed—just as Smara (the God of Love) takes a command. "The remaining [instruction] was given as a favor for the sake of auspiciousness. This is a *sahokti* (simultaneous expression), comparing it to that [garland].
The meaning is "taking that [garland] as well.
It is the established custom that a garland is given at the time of departure.
And as he was departing, Śakra touched or stroked his body—either his back or his head—with his hand for the sake of indicating affection.
Of what kind? Rough and harsh due to the striking—that is, the impact—of the world-elephant Airāvaṇa for the purpose of increasing his own splendor. 22.
Followed with apprehension by his beloved friend Mādhava and by Rati, he—
whose success in his undertaking was sought at the cost of his own body— went to the hermitage of Sthāṇu in the Himavat mountains.
Then that Kāma went to the penance grove of Śiva on the Himavat; what sort of man was he?
He was followed by his dear friend Vasanta and his wife Rati, who were apprehensive, thinking, "This task is difficult and its outcome uncertain. Thus, even at the cost of his own body...
He by whom the accomplishment of the desired task was sought even at the cost of destroying his body— thinking,
"Even accepting death, I must certainly perform the work of the gods"—
for this very reason, the words *āśaṅkā* and *mādhava* are used; [the suffix] *ñ* is applied after *magha*.
Thus, terms such as *madhu*, *mādhava*, *iṣu*, *ūrja*, and so forth, are employed even in the vernacular by the tradition of great poets.
In that forest, Madhu, acting as an adversary to the penance and meditative concentration of the self-restrained sages,
expanded himself by assuming the form of the ego-principle (abhimāna) born of creative volition (saṃkalpa).

Then, in that hermitage, Madhu, having manifested himself in the form of flowers and other such things, expanded and blossomed; an untimely spring appeared. Of what nature was it? Even for those who are tranquil...
He is the adversary who acts as an obstacle to the ascetic concentration (*tapas-samādhi*) of the sages,
because he generates longing.

He is the very embodiment of pride belonging to that Mind-born one (*manobhuva*) whose source is volition (*saṃkalpa*), for he is like intoxication (*darpa*) and is difficult to conquer due to his power over them.
Concentration is one-pointedness. || 24 ||
He begins to describe that very honey with further honeyed words:

When the sun, transgressing the proper season, set out to travel toward the quarter favored by Kubera, the southern direction exhaled through her mouth a fragrant breeze as if it were a sigh born of resentment. (25)
The southern direction, with her face turned downward, released—that is, emitted—the fragrance-bearing wind;
for during the spring, the Malaya breeze blows. When?
When the sun had set out to travel toward the quarter inhabited by Kubera, the Giver of Wealth, having transgressed the proper time—that is, having overstepped the appointed hour.
For in spring, the sun moves toward the northern quarter;
yet at that time, it is not the proper season for him to resort to her, since the context concerns his southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). Therefore, it is figuratively imagined as follows:
She released a sigh like a reproach, as it were, or a very deep breath, in this manner.
For when the hero, having transgressed the agreement and oath, approaches with passion the woman of loathsome form served by Kuvera, then the heroine, favorable toward him, sighs in resentment.
*Vera* means the body. *Vyalīka* is the offense committed against a beloved.
Gandhavaha and the others are to be understood as occurring in the fifth and subsequent positions. || 25 ||
The Aśoka tree immediately produced flowers along with new leaves starting from its very trunk;
it did not wait for the touch of the feet of beautiful women adorned with tinkling anklets.
The Ashoka tree suddenly produced flowers along with new leaves, beginning from its very branches;
yet, due to the power of time, it neither avoided nor desired the blow from the feet of a young woman adorned with tinkling anklets—
for indeed, struck by such a foot, it blossoms.
When the arrow of the fresh mango blossom— charming with its emerging sprouts as its feathers— had reached its completion,
Spring placed the bees upon it like the syllables of the name of the Mind-born God.
The arrow was indeed a fresh mango fruit; when that [fruit] was completed, Madhura placed [the name] upon it.
It is imagined as if they were the syllables of the name, the letters of the designation, of his friend, the Mind-born (Cetobhū).
For on an arrow the master’s name is inscribed; an arrow ought to be provided with feathers.
But in this case, there is the emergence of young shoots—the very sprouting of tender leaves—which constitute its beautiful wings. 27.
When its color was at its peak, my heart felt pain that the karṇikāra flower lacked fragrance;
for generally, the Creator’s disposition is averse to the complete assembly of all virtues.
The flower called *karṇikā*, despite its beauty and loveliness, pained—that is, oppressed—the mind because it lacked fragrance.
To the question of why it was not made fragrant, he says: generally, the flow of the Creator’s activity is averse to the arrangement—that is, the bringing together—of all qualities.
He does not place every quality in a single place.

This should be understood as an appearance of a different meaning (*arthāntarābhāsa*), and not as an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by another fact), because it lacks the essential purpose of that figure.
For an *arthāntaranyāsa* is a corroboration of the primary subject through similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Here, however, one thing is introduced and a different matter is established elsewhere.
Therefore, it should be said as follows: "What conscious person would not feel distressed upon seeing one who possesses virtues surpassed by another's superior virtue?
Or rather—everyone delights in that very virtue by which other virtues are quickly made to shine. (28)
The extremely red palāśa flowers, curved like the crescent moon due to their lack of full bloom,
shone like nail-marks on the forest grounds that had just been visited by Spring.
The Palāśa flowers shone brilliantly. Of what sort were they?
Because they had not yet blossomed—that is, due to their lack of full expansion—they were curved like the crescent moon, resembling a digit of the moon;
and by their very nature, they were intensely red. Therefore, it is poetically imagined that [the flowers] appeared as if... through their resemblance to a husband.
The curved and reddish nail-marks left upon the slopes of the forests, where they have come into contact with the fragrant [wind], appear as if they were fresh wounds inflicted at that very moment.
Having applied to her face a tilaka of the beauty of spring, variegated with the decorative patterns of bees clinging to it like collyrium,
the Goddess of Spring adorned her lip— resembling a mango sprout— with a glow as tender as the morning sun.

Madhuśrī—the Fortune of Spring—having placed or fashioned a flower called the *tilaka* (or a *tilaka* tree) at the beginning, that is, at the onset [of her arrival], then adorned the lower lip of the mango sprout with a redness resembling fresh sunlight. Of what sort was the *tilaka*? It was a variegated *tilaka*, wonderful due to the streaks of collyrium (*añjanabhakti*) consisting of bees (*dvirepha*) clinging to it because of their blackness.
The sense of the sentence is that the mango tree, being laden with pollen, is frequented by swarms of bees, and thus the mango has put forth its sprouts.

Even a woman endowed with grace, for the sake of beauty, applies collyrium, a tilaka mark, and decorative painting (viśeṣaka) to her face, and adorns her lips with the dye of betel and other substances; [her lip] is soft and symmetrical. 30.
The deer, their vision obstructed by the particles of pollen from the clusters of priyālu blossoms,
wandered through the forest glades against the wind— intoxicated with rut and shedding rustling leaves.
Intoxicated and fierce with rut, the lions wandered and roamed through the forest ranges facing the wind;
this was because they were facing the wind. Of what sort were they?
Their range of vision—the casting of their eyes—was obstructed and hindered by fragments of pollen from the blossoms of trees known as *priyālu*.
Because of the wind's intense whirling of pollen; what kind of grounds? Those upon which there is a rustling sound (*marmara*) from the falling of leaves (*parṇapāta*).
For at that time, dry leaves fall and new ones are born. (31)
The sweet cry that the male cuckoo uttered, its throat made hoarse by tasting the mango sprouts,
became the very speech of Love, skilled in not thwarting the hearts of high-minded women.

Because its throat was purified by tasting the mango sprouts, the young male cuckoo uttered a sweet cry; that very sound became the speech of Love, skillful in destroying the pride of haughty women, and turned into a collection of words of entreaty, for upon hearing it, lovers become inclined toward their beloveds. Just as there are colors, there are also tastes such as astringent (*kaṣāya*);

and the designation of the throat and other parts as "astringent," "sweet," or "pungent" is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). In the word *puṃskokila*, the term *pum-* (male) is used for the sake of clarity. || 32 ||

With the departure of the snow, fresh perspiration appeared upon the decorative leaf-patterns on the faces of the Kimpuruṣa women, whose lips had become clear and whose facial complexions had turned pale.
Fresh sweat made its appearance and took its place upon the leaf-shaped tilaka marks of the Kinnarīs; this was because their skin was so exceptionally fair. Of what sort were they?
Their lips were stainless due to the departure of the cold and the onset of heat following the end of winter.
For indeed, due to the absence of natural luster on the lower lips caused by the cold, a discoloration arises;
likewise, the complexion of their faces has become somewhat pale.
But surely, since the onset of spring does not occur out of season, and since such a time did not exist prior to that, how can this be so?
Regarding that description of the qualities of the Dharma: this is true.
However, there is no fault in first stating its non-temporality merely by way of introduction, and subsequently describing it in a general form. || 33 ||
Seeing that untimely onset of spring, the ascetics dwelling in the forest of Sthāṇu found it difficult to remain masters of their minds,
even though they had restrained their emotional agitation through great effort.

The sages dwelling in the forest of Sthāṇu and those residing in the hermitage of Hara, though masters of their own minds, found it difficult to maintain self-control upon beholding that untimely and unseasonable manifestation of spring; for,
despite their efforts, their mental agitation and transformation had been suppressed only by the sheer force of time,
they who were lords and masters.
That which exists at the wrong time is *ākālikī*. The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied because the word belongs to the *adhyātma* group.
However, the rule *ākālikaḍādyantavacane* (Pāṇini 4.3.23) is not applicable here, as its meaning would not be consistent with the context. || 34 ||
When Madana, with his flower-bow strung, had entered that place accompanied by Rati,
the pairs [of lovers] revealed their inner state through their actions, permeated by a surge of passion that had reached its peak.
When Smara, together with his wife, arrived at that hermitage— having strung and made ready his bow composed of flowers—
the pairs of bees, deer, elephants, and other creatures [became agitated].

They revealed—that is, they declared and made manifest—such a state of being, namely their intention, through the performance of actions; that is, by the completion of their deeds. Of what nature was it?
It was a love and a passion that had reached the ultimate limit, the highest pinnacle.
Passion is permeated and cultivated by those two; the meaning is that it contains within it the passion for delight.
It was stated that [the sages] revealed [the truth] through action; he explains that very point in detail:
"The two-repelled bee (the bumblebee) drank honey from the single vessel of the flower while following his own beloved;
and the black-spotted deer scratched with his horn the doe whose eyes were closed at the touch. (3.36)
A single flower served as a common vessel— a cup—
in which the honeybee shared the sweet nectar with a female bee;
likewise, a deer known as the *kṛṣṇasāra* scratched his beloved, whose eyes were closed from the sensation of touch, with his horn.
Drinking together and scratching one another indicate their desire for sexual play; the same applies to what follows.
"Anuvṛtti" means capturing the heart or winning over. In the phrase "he scratched," the suffix *ñi* is used in the active sense (*kartari*).
The suffix *yak* is applied according to the rule *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak*.
Having analyzed [the compound] as "he who is both black and brindled," the compound is formed by the rule *varṇo varṇena*. || 36 ||
The female elephant gave mouthfuls of water, fragrant with the pollen of lake-lotuses, to her mate;
and the Cakravāka bird honored his wife with a lotus-fiber stalk that he had only half-eaten.
The male elephant gave mouthfuls of water to his mate; how [was it]?
It was that from which there arose the fragrance of the pollen—the dust—of the lotuses (*paṅkaja*) in the lake. The ruddy goose (*rathāṅganāman*, *cakravāka*), having eaten only half, [remained].
With a lotus stalk, he honored his beloved and won her over.

And amidst the singing, the kimpuruṣa kissed the face of his beloved, which was beautiful with eyes rolling from the intoxication of flower-liquor and whose leaf-designs were slightly revived by drops of perspiration.
Out of passion, the Kinnara kissed and drank from the face of his beloved as she sang; what kind of face?
One upon which the leaf-like lines [of her eyebrows] were slightly revived—that is, blossomed—by drops of perspiration.
Likewise, it is so described because she shines with eyes that are reeling and whirling from drinking liquor infused with flowers;
"in the midst of song" means during the singing of a song. || 38 ||

Even the trees received the embrace of the arms of their vine-wives— arms formed by branches bent low, whose breasts were clusters of full-blown flowers and whose lips were charming, quivering sprouts.

Let alone those possessed of consciousness; even the trees, which are stationary by nature, then received from their vine-wives—their creeper-consorts—the embrace of the arms of their bending branches, that is, they were embraced by the coils of their curved tendrils. For these [trees]:

They embrace and climb them by means of their branches. To what kind of branches? He states a point of similarity with the bride (*vadhū*): those whose breasts are full and complete clusters of flowers (*puṣpastabaka*), as well as trembling young shoots (*pravāla*).
Their lower lips were indeed young sprouts, making them more enchanting than those [already] beautiful. || 39 ||
Even though he had heard the song of the Apsarases at that moment, Hara became intent on profound meditation;
for obstacles never have the power to break the concentration of those who are masters of themselves.

At this moment, during the manifestation of spring, the Blessed One—though the sound of songs sung by celestial nymphs was being heard around him—remained intent on contemplation and established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), his mind not at all perturbed.

For those who are masters of their own minds, seasonal festivals such as the spring celebration can never become obstacles to the highest good, hindrances to spiritual welfare, or causes for the disruption of concentration and the breaking of one-pointedness;
it is only for one whose mind is wavering that such obstacles arise.
Although discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) and other such states take specific forms, in poetic works they are characterized by one-pointedness of mind.
Here, by the word "self" (*ātman*), the six sense-faculties are indicated. (40)
