The first drops of rain rested for a moment on her eyelashes, struck her lower lip, were crushed by the pressure of her swelling breasts, and having slipped down her folds, reached her navel only after a long time.

The first drops of water from that Gaurī, those tiny droplets, reached the region of her navel only after a long time. For instance: first they rested for a mere moment upon the eyelashes—the hairs of her eyes—and because of their density, they did not fall downward; then, having struck her lower lip, they were shattered by the impact against the elevation of her breasts; thereafter, due to the concavity of the three folds of her waist, they faltered; and finally, they sank into her navel.
By describing the nature of the onset of the first monsoon in this way, the poet indicates the extraordinary beauty of the Goddess.
*Udabindavaḥ* means drops of water; there is a substitution of *uda-* [for *udaka-*] in the compounds *mantha*, *odana*, and *saktu*. *Utsedha* means height or elevation. || 23 ||
During the incessant downpours of rain, they watched her— who slept on a stone slab and dwelt without a shelter—
through flashes of lightning that seemed to stand as witnesses to her great asceticism throughout the nights.
The nights gazed upon that Pārvatī with glances flashing like lightning;
it is suggested (utprekṣyate) that they were as if standing as witnesses to the great ascetics. For a witness indeed observes repeatedly. Of what sort was she?

"She who sleeps on rocks" (*śilāśayā*) refers to her who reclines upon a stone slab; for at that time, there was indeed the presence of mud on the bare ground (*sthaṇḍila*). She was "dwelling without a home," staying outdoors.
When? During incessant rains falling between the intervals.
The meaning is: "while rains consisting of hailstones—those whose interval or interior consists of water—are falling," that is, while showers of thunderbolts are descending.
For in this way, the greatness of his ascetic power (*tapas*) is manifested.
Although the words *varṣa* and *vṛṣṭi* have the same meaning, a specific distinction is understood here from their joint usage.
The state or the activity of a witness is "sākṣya" (testimony). 24.
Devoted to dwelling in the open air, she passed the nights of the month of Sahasya, which were intensely cold with northern winds;
she was filled with compassion as she saw before her a pair of cakravāka birds separated from one another and crying out to each other.
That queen spent—meaning she passed—the nights of the month of Sahasya, the exceedingly cold nights of Pauṣa, remaining intent on dwelling in water.
Of what sort were they? They were nights in which the wind was "exceedingly full of frost," that is, a breeze even more intense than snow;
the word *uttara* (exceeding) expresses an intensification and thereby implies a mixture [of cold].

For example: "O timid one, your embrace is followed by trembling; under the power of passion, they float amidst the afflictions, surpassing even the sprouts of durva grass and barley, and the unopened leaf-buds of the plakṣa tree."
In such passages as these, *utkara* and *utkira* are indeed corrupt readings. What kind of goddess is she?
She is compassionate and merciful toward the pair of cakravāka birds that are separated before her, because she herself experiences the pain of separation;
they cry out and warble to one another on account of their parting.
For even when two things are situated in the same place, their mutual non-perception is indeed separation (*viyoga*).
"Living in water" (*udavāsa*) means dwelling in water; the substitution of *ud* for *uda* occurs by the rule "in the case of *peṣam*, *vāsa*, *vāhana*, and *dhi*."
Because autumn and spring are neither hot nor cold, they are not described;
furthermore, winter shares the same conditions as the cold season (hemanta). (25)
At night, with her lotus-fragrant mouth, its lower lip beautiful as it trembled,
she seemed to restore the wealth of lotuses destroyed by the fall of frost to the waters.
That goddess, standing within the water,

created, as it were, a lotus-arrangement by means of her face, fragrant like a lotus, through her presence there among the waters whose beauty of blooming lotuses had been destroyed by the sprinkling of frost.
The lotus should be surrounded by petals;
there, because of his absorption in recitation (*japa*), he appears beautiful even with a trembling lower lip as if it were a petal.
By the word "night" (*niśi*), it is indicated that even then, he does not abandon [the practice] while in the midst of the water.
In the word *niśa*, there is the substitution of *niśā* for *niś*. || 26 ||
Indeed, subsisting on the leaves of trees that have fallen off by themselves is the supreme limit of asceticism;
because she has even abandoned that, those who know the past call the sweet-spoken lady "Aparṇā" (the Leafless One).
This is the highest pinnacle and extreme point of austerity: when the maintenance of the body is carried out using a tree leaf that has fallen of its own accord.
But when she had discarded even that leaf, having cast it away, those who know the past call her Aparṇā, the one who speaks kindly;
for they say she did not eat (na bhuktaṃ) the leaf (parṇaṃ). Indeed, Gaurī’s name is Aparṇā.
As it is said: "Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā."
Thus [it is asked]: "Why is there the accusative case in *aparṇām*?

For since the word *iti* establishes [the preceding element] as being merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), it would be logical for the nominative case to occur, as in: *kramādamuṃ nārada ity abodhi saḥ*. This must be considered further.
Or, if there is no connection with Yati for those who know the past, [then] they call her Aparṇā; this is the meaning of what those who know the past say. || 27 ||
By means of such vows as making her limbs as delicate as a lotus stalk, she emaciated her body day and night;
thus, she cast far below the ascetics who had acquired their merit through bodies hardened by penance.

By means of such austerities as the five-fire penance and others, the Queen— afflicting her own body, which was as delicate as a lotus stalk and as tender as a lotus fiber, day and night— far surpassed and conquered the accumulated ascetic merit of the aged sages, even though their bodies were hard.
According to some, the word *pelava* is considered vulgar, but not by all.

Then, wearing a deerskin and a cloth of bark-fiber, with bold speech and blazing as if with the splendor consisting of the Veda, a certain man with matted hair entered the penance grove like the first stage of life incarnate. (29)
Then once, a certain brahmin with matted hair came to Gaurī’s hermitage. Of what sort was he?
He was one who wore an *ajina*, a deerskin, and carried an *āṣāḍha*, a staff made of *pālāśa* wood; he was eloquent and talkative, and seemed to blaze with a divine luster.
Thus, he is described through poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
Bound to his body, he was embodied like the first stage of life, namely brahmacarya;
he was composed of Brahman, having arisen from Brahman by means of that splendor born of the Veda.
Pārvatī went out to meet him with a hospitable reception preceded by great respect;
for even in those whose minds are fixed on equanimity, their actions display profound reverence toward those distinguished by their physical form. (30)
The queen went out to meet that brahmin, honoring him with a reception preceded by great respect;
that is to say, she went forth before him for the purpose of worship,
because she was virtuous toward guests (*ātitheyī*), being skilled in the service of guests.
[The suffix] *ḍhañ* [is applied after the words] *pathya*, *atithi*, *sāti*, and *svapati*.

Now, she too is herself an ascetic (*tapasvinī*) and not inferior to him; therefore, one might ask: "What weight does he place upon her worship? To this he says: Even among those whose minds are settled and whose hearts are tranquil, when there is equality in external appearance, yet a pre-eminence in form, their gestures proceed with great respect.
Indeed, ostentations are worthy of honor, and he possesses such distinction because of his possession of the deerskin and other [emblems].
But some say that even though there is equality, and even though there is an equal vision,
[the form *saparyā* is derived] because the root *kaṇḍū* and others include the word *sapara*, from which the suffix *yak* is applied to form *saparyā*.
Having accepted the hospitality offered according to the prescribed rites and having dispelled his fatigue for a moment,
he gazed at Umā with a straightforward glance and proceeded to speak without abandoning the proper sequence.
Then that matted-haired ascetic, having properly performed his worship and rested for a short while, began to speak;
he did so without abandoning the proper sequence and by following the established order, because he spoke the subject matter in its correct progression.
He beheld the Goddess with a straightforward gaze, for she is free from passion and hatred.
Immediately thereafter, he will surely display passion and hatred.
He states that very sequence:

"Is sacrificial wood and *kuśa* grass easy for you to obtain for the sake of ritual acts? Are there also waters suitable for the procedure of bathing? Do you apply yourself to austerity according to your own capacity? For the body is indeed the primary instrument of dharma. (32)

Regarding the inquiry into what is not desired: Is fuel, *darbha* grass, and so forth easily available for the purpose of oblations and other rites? Are your waters fit for ritual ablutions because they are not defiled by poison or other pollutants?
And do you perform your vows after considering the physical capacity of your body, rather than out of foolish obsession?

Because the body is primarily the instrument for performing dharma; and since *samit* (sacrificial fuel) and *kuśa* (sacred grass) constitute *samit-kuśa*; and because [the term] "jāti" (genus/class) applies to non-living things. 32.
Moreover, the young shoots of these creepers, nourished by the water poured forth by you,
continue to grow until they attain a resemblance to your lip, which is naturally rosy even when long since divested of red lac.
I hope that the fresh sprouts produced by the water you have given for their irrigation have grown continuously upon these creepers and climbing vines. Of what sort are they?

They attain—that is, touch—the likeness or equality of your lip, which, though its redness was long since lost through the application of astringent (yāvaka), has become pale-red (pāṭala) from being clothed by your teeth;
for both possess a natural redness.
It is called "concomitant" (anubandhin) because it follows along with and arises together [with its object]. || 33 ||

Is your mind also gracious toward the deer, who commit the offense of fondly grasping the darbha grass held in your hand—deer who, with glances flickering as they cast off lotuses, seem to vie for the mastery of your eyes? (34)
"Is your mind gracious and full of affection toward the deer?
"From what cause, then, is there a suspicion of lack of grace? He says: "Toward those who have committed an offense by stealing the kuśa grass held in the palm of your hand.
He states another reason: "Those deer who, because of their flickering nature, seem to engage in rivalry or even emulate the co-wifehood of your eyes with their glances."
By what kind [of eyes]?
By those trembling with a tossing—that is, a casting forward or a shaking—of blue lotuses;
for a tossed blue lotus possesses an exceeding beauty due to its continuous trembling.
The reading *ākṣepa* is indeed a corruption; *praṇaya* means entreaty. *Sapatna* means an enemy; its quality (*dharma*) is *sāpatnya*, which refers to enmity and rivalry. || 34 ||

O Pārvatī, that which is said—that beauty does not lead to sinful conduct—is a statement that is never false; for such is your character, O lady of noble vision, that it has become a source of instruction even for ascetics. (35)

O Pārvatī, as for this which is said by those who know the marks (*lakṣaṇajña*)—that beauty does not exist for the sake of sinful conduct (*pāpavṛtti*)—whereby "sinful conduct" means a wicked way of life or behavior, and that beauty is not for its purpose, according to the saying, "Where there is form, there dwell virtues," that statement is now proven true and unerring.

Why? He says: "For thus, O large-eyed one, your character has become a teacher, having reached the state of being an instructor even for sages. The meaning is that even those most devoted to dharma (*dharmiṣṭha*) learn from your conduct.
If those who possess beauty were to be of immoral conduct, then your ladyship would not be devoted to dharma;
and her possession of beauty is already implied by the very fact of her having large eyes. (35)
This mountain, along with its lineage, has been purified not so much by the waters of the Ganges falling from heaven— which mock the offerings scattered by the Seven Sages—
as by your own stainless deeds.

This Himavat, along with its sons and grandsons, has been purified by your stainless and unblemished deeds and actions in a way that it could not be by the pure waters of the Ganges fallen from heaven, nor even by the clear waters of the Sun or the Sindhu.
For the Ganges did not fall upon his head directly from the sky;
rather, [the mountain is purified] by the offerings of flowers and other gifts scattered and strewn by the Seven Sages, which seem to smile because they are white.
O beautiful lady, through this [practice], the Dharma today appears to me as the preeminent essence of the three goals of life (trivarga),
since it alone is embraced and cultivated by you, who have turned your mind away from the objects of wealth and desire.

O proud and beautiful lady, although Dharma was previously understood by me as the essence, today—by means of this matter about to be spoken—it appears to me with particular clarity that Dharma is the supreme essence of the three aims (trivarga), characterized by virtue, wealth, and pleasure. For you have disregarded both wealth and pleasure, and having accepted that alone, you practice it;
if that [Dharma] were not the most excellent of all, why would you, seeking virtue, perform such ascetic penance? (37)
Having stated that this austerity is a cause for dharma by means of the "elephant's wink" (a sign of indifference), he now speaks out of a desire to know the specific details:
"O lady of graceful limbs, you ought not to regard me as a stranger merely because I have personally offered you special honors;
for it is said, O fair-limbed one, that among the virtuous, friendship is formed by walking seven steps together with wise men. (38)
"O lady of graceful limbs and slender form, you ought not to understand me as being intent upon another;
for what kind of person am I?
I am one by whom a special honor—a preeminent act of worship—has been personally extended, and not through the mediation of another."

Even if one has honored [the teacher] for oneself, what follows from that? He says: "Since" (yataḥ) friendship (saṅgatam)—that is, friendship consisting of walking seven steps—is said by the wise (manīṣibhiḥ), meaning by the learned (paṇḍitaiḥ), to be [the mark] of the virtuous (satām), meaning of the good (sādhūnām).
"Sāptapadīna" means friendship; the sense is that he with whom seven steps have been taken is a friend.
As it has been said: "They say that a relationship is preceded by conversation. And a meeting of our words has indeed already occurred. (38)

Therefore, O lady rich in asceticism, this person, whose fickleness is justified by his status as a twice-born, now desires to ask you something for which you are very patient; if it is not a secret, you should grant me an answer.

Therefore, because of our friendship, I desire to ask you—who are so very patient and capable of enduring such importunity—about that fickleness and curiosity which are appropriate and easy to find in one's status as a twice-born Brahmin; the meaning is: "I ask out of youthful curiosity."
If this is not a secret to be hidden, you ought not to speak against it,
since you are very patient— the suffix *ṇi* being applied according to the rule *īkṣikṣamibhyāṃ ca*. One whose mind is inclined to ask is *praṣṭumanāḥ*.
In the sense of necessity, the suffix *tumun* is used after the roots *lup*, *pad*, *vas*, and *am*, as well as after *kāma* and *manas*; furthermore, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *m*. || 39 ||

Birth in a noble family, a body that has arisen like the very beauty of the three worlds belonging to the First Creator, unassailable sovereignty and happiness, and fresh youth—what could be the fruit of asceticism beyond this? Tell me. (40)
What greater fruit of asceticism could there be for you than this?
The meaning is that whatever is to be sought through penance, all of that is already yours.
For instance, your birth was in the lineage of the first Creator, the primordial Lord of Creatures, Śambhu.
The traditional teaching (*āgama*) is that the Himalaya is the creation of Śiva;
likewise, Bhāravi [states] that it was fashioned as a representative of the worlds, as if by Śambhu himself, in order to manifest his omnipotence.
Others, however, say that the first creator is Brahmā.
"Indeed, these mountains are the first offspring of Prajāpati," so says the Śruti. And your form is embodied, as if the beauty of the three worlds had arisen in person;
moreover, the bliss of sovereignty is not even to be sought after, because you are the daughter of the King of Mountains.
Your age, too, is fresh and new because you have attained youth;
therefore, what could be the fruit of asceticism greater than this for you?
"Triloka" refers to the three worlds, numbering three. 40.
"O slender-waisted one, such a resolve indeed arises in high-minded women even from an undesirable and unbearable situation;
yet, by a mind directed toward the path of discernment, that [resolve] is not seen in you. (41)
Moreover, for proud women, such a course of action—characterized by ascetic practice—is undertaken out of unbearable adversity in the form of widowhood.
And that adversity, O slender-waisted one, is not perceived by you whose mind has been cast onto the path of discernment. 41.
Why is this so? He says:
"O fair-browed one, whence could this form of yours suffer the onset of grief or humiliation in your father's house?
There is no insult for you; who would stretch out a hand toward the needle that guards a serpent's jewel? (42)

This form, this physical appearance, is such that it is impossible to obtain and unfit to be attained; it is one that is overwhelmed and assailed by grief. Indeed, widowhood is not appropriate for this form;
even from the humiliation of another, one might attain detachment.

He says that even this you do not have: "O fair-browed one, whence could there be insult in your father's house? Even an assault committed by another leads only to destruction; for you, there is no physical touch [of such a nature].
For who would stretch forth his hand to grasp the tip of the jeweled crest-ornament of a serpent?"
For one who causes you humiliation does not remain at ease.
In the word *subhrū*, the short vowel [in *bhrū*] arises from negligence due to the prohibition of the designation *nadī*. 42.

Why have you cast aside your ornaments in your youth and donned the bark garment that graces old age? Tell me, if the night, with its moon and stars shining bright at the onset of evening, can ever be fit for the dawn? 43.
And for this reason, why have you abandoned ornaments at the very height of youth and taken up the radiant bark-garment of an elder?
That which is indeed appropriate for the fourth stage of life is improper for youth.
Furthermore, tell me: when the night begins with the moon and stars clearly visible, does it turn toward dawn by changing its hue to redness?

Because the bark-garment (*valkala*) is red, it serves as the object of comparison. The dative case is used according to the rule *kḷpi sampadyamāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.13). The moon and stars serve as the objects of comparison for the ornaments.
The state of being old is *vārdhaka*; the suffix *añ* is applied because the word denotes an age (*vayas*).
*Vārdhakam* is simply *vārddham*.
Some read the word *vṛddha* among the *manojñādi* group [of words]. 43.
Having raised other possible motives for her asceticism, he says in order to refute them:
"If you seek heaven, your labor is in vain, for the regions of your father are the very lands of the gods.
Or, if you seek a husband, enough with this meditation; one does not search for a jewel by seeking it out, for a jewel is sought after [when it presents itself]. (44)
If you desire heaven through austerity, then this hardship is useless, for the cities of the gods are already within the domain of your father.

Or, if you seek a husband as your spouse, then enough with this meditative concentration; do not impose restraints upon yourself. For a jewel does not search for a taker, nor does it think, "Who will seek me out to take me?"
Rather, it is sought and desired by another through force; thus you are to be desired, but you do not desire [him].
One who takes [a wife] as his own, i.e., accepts her, is a "bridegroom" (*upayantā*);
*alaṃ samādhinā* (enough with composure) takes the third case ending because it belongs to the class beginning with *prakṛti*.
But in the formulation of the fourth case, the term *alam* is understood in the sense of sufficiency (*paryāpti*).
Then, at the moment of discussing the groom, Gaurī, perceiving her sigh, said:
"My heart is informed by this warm sigh, yet it plunges into doubt.
Your suitor is not seen; how could he be one who is sought after and yet difficult to obtain? (45)
"By your hot sighs, it has been indicated that you desire a husband;
yet even in this matter, my mind remains doubtful,
for he whom you desire does not even exist— how much less could he be obtained even if requested?"
The sense is: "because you are a jewel among women. The suffix -tavya is used here in the sense of a reason (hetu). || 45 ||
Then, concluding from her silence that she was indeed praying for her husband, she said:

"Aha! What a steadfast youth must be your desired one, since he neglects for so long those matted locks—tawny at the tips like ripened rice—and which hang down with loosened bonds from your cheek, now that it has long been bereft of its ear-lotus. (46)

Oh, how strange! There is some steadfast, cruel, and youthful man desired by you whom you wish to obtain, yet he ignores your matted locks as they hang down from your cheeks—cheeks now bereft of the blue lotuses that once adorned your ears—simply because their binding has loosened;
he does not rearrange them, for they have become tawny and reddish-brown like the awns of the *kalamā* rice-plant due to the absence of oil treatment.
Whose heart would not break upon seeing you, emaciated by the vows of a sage, your ornaments scorched by the sun, like the crescent of the moon seen by day? (47)

The "vows of the sages" refers to the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such ascetic observances. Seeing you, who have been exceedingly emaciated by them like a digit of the moon on a [waning] day, whose sensitive heart would not break? The sense is: "Therefore, my mind suffers pain upon seeing you."

Her places of ornamentation were scorched and burnt by the sun because of her extreme delicacy; the form "pluṣṭāni" is derived from the root *pluṣ* (to burn), and "dīryate" is used in the reflexive passive sense (the object acting as its own agent). 47.

I know that your beloved is deceived by the intoxication of his own good fortune; for he does not make his own face—possessing curved eyelashes—the steady target for the eyes of you who look so skillfully. 48.
I understand that you have been deceived and deluded by pride in your own loveliness;
for you do not make your own face the object of observation by placing it in proximity to this eye of yours—meaning, you do not look at it. For by your looking [at it], its...
The fulfillment of one's birth: of what kind of eye?
Of one that looks with skill and beholds with sweetness;
for the eyebrows possess a certain cleverness through their slight upward arching and a sweet, elongated grace.
For this very reason, her eyelashes are curved and her eyebrows are arched, because she gazes downward. || 48 ||
"How long have you been exerting yourself, O Gaurī? I too possess ascetic merit accumulated in my former stage of life.
Therefore, obtain the desired boon by means of half of that; and I wish to know it well. (49)
"O Gaurī, how long have you been wearying yourself? From what time have you begun your penance?

Or rather, for how much longer will you continue to practice penance for such a long time? For me too, there exists penance accumulated during my previous stage of life, acquired through my period of celibacy."
"By half of that portion,
may you obtain a beloved husband as your chosen boon"— this was either a blessing or a command.
And I wish to know well and correctly who that chosen husband of yours is.
The sense is that if he is worthy, then this is approved; "ardhabhāga" means a portion that is half. || 49 ||
Having been thus addressed by the twice-born man upon his entrance, she was unable to express what was in her mind;
then she cast a sidelong glance at her friend standing beside her, her eyes turned and their collyrium unsmudged.
Having spoken thus from within, she was unable to express her intention due to her modesty;
thereupon, for the sake of speaking, she glanced toward a female friend standing nearby. How?
With her eye—unadorned with collyrium—turned and moving.
"Tell him this"—by means of a wink of the eye, she thus incited her friend; this is the meaning.
"Paripārśvam" means "right by the side. || 50 ||
Her friend spoke to the ascetic: "Listen, O holy man, if you have curiosity as to why she has made her body—an instrument of penance—like a lotus for warding off the heat. (51)

Then the goddess’s friend spoke to the ascetic: "O virtuous one, listen if you have curiosity or interest as to why she has undertaken this body—a means for penance and a performer of vows—which is like a lotus provided with a parasol;
for just as a lotus suffers distress from the warding off of the sun's heat, so too does this body suffer from the practice of austerity. (51)
It is said that this proud lady, having disregarded the lords of the four quarters, Indra and the others who possess great majesty,
desires to obtain as her husband the wielder of the Pināka bow, whom even the God of Love could not captivate by his beauty due to his previous punishment.

This high-minded lady, having looked with contempt upon the guardians of the quarters—Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Dhanada—who have acquired their respective splendors, desires indeed to obtain Hara as her husband.
By the word "indeed" (kila), she indicates his unattainability. He is "unseizable by form" (arūpahārya) because of the burning of Smara; that is, he cannot be captivated by beauty.
For if she were subject to physical form, this passion would not burn her because of that [beauty].
By calling her "the proud one" (māninī), he also implies her readiness to conquer Śiva.
All that needs to be asked has been stated by this much. 52.
Now, by way of digression, he describes her state of passion:

Long ago, the arrow of the Flower-Bowed God, turned back by an unbearable roar before it could reach the face of the Enemy of Smara, struck this woman in the heart with a wide-reaching impact—even though the God’s body was shattered to pieces. (53)
Formerly, the arrow which was discharged by Madana toward Hara struck this very woman in her heart instead, for it failed to reach the enemy of Smara; this was because Śambhu was invincible.
He was turned back and forced to retreat by the weapon of the syllable *huṃ*;
though his body was shattered and his form consumed by fire— indeed, he was burnt by Hara immediately following the discharge of the arrow— he made a long and far-reaching descent into [the earth].
The form *akṣiṇot* is derived from the root *kṣi* (to destroy). *Aprāptamukhaḥ* means one whose face has not been reached; here, *prāpta* is used in the active sense.
In the term *smarārimit*, the accusative case is used in relation to a quality or action (*guṇakriyā*), just as in the expression *kṛtapūrvī*.
"Kaṭam" means "eaten before"; "odanam" means "rice. He whose bow consists of flowers, or who has flowers as his bow, is "Puṣpadhanvā.
According to the rule *dhanuṣaśca*, there is the substitution of the form *anaṅ*. || 53 ||
From that time forth, the young girl, intoxicated with passion in her father’s house, her curls greyed by the sandal-paste on her forehead,
found no peace at all, even upon stone slabs as cold as masses of snow.
From that time on, because of her suffering from love, she never found relief or happiness even upon surfaces of stone as cold as a mass of snow.

To dispel her torment, she applied sandalwood paste to her forehead in the form of an ornamental mark; thus, her curls became greyish-black with the *lalāṭikā-candana*. [The term] *karṇalalāṭāt* refers to an ornament for the ear and forehead.
The word "tadā" functions in the sense of the ablative case (pañcamī). || 54 ||
When the conduct of the wielder of the Pināka bow was praised in words faltering with tears in her throat,
this daughter of the Kinnara king made her companions in the forest concert weep many times.

In the grove at the edge of the forest, this kinnarī, afflicted by separation, repeatedly wept before her companions who were engaged in musical practice; by whom [was she seen], and like what, with a throat choked with tears?

With faltering and stumbling steps and words—when? When the heroic exploits of the wielder of the Pināka bow, such as the destruction of Tripura, were being sung with their praises fully expressed and described;
and thus, because the exploits of her beloved were being celebrated, tears arose due to the manifestation of redoubled passion, causing the indistinctness of her speech.
And there is the weeping out of compassion for her friends;
the musical notes (varṇas) are those well-known from the treatises on song, such as the stationary (sthāyin), ascending (āroha), and so forth. 55.
When three-quarters of the night remained, she closed her eyes for a moment and suddenly awoke;
with her arms cast around his neck, she spoke words that were indistinct: "O Blue-throated One, where are you going? (56)

In this fourth watch of the night, having somehow closed her eyes for a mere moment under the power of sleep, she suddenly awoke with wide-open eyes. "O beloved, where are you going? she asked indistinctly, while that which is unreal and not ultimate remained [unrealized].
She by whom the arm-noose was placed around his neck— that very same man was seen by her in a dream as he had arrived.
"How is it that you, whom the wise declare to be omnipresent, do not perceive this person standing before you?"—
thus was the moon-crested Lord reproached in secret by the simple girl, who had herself written these words with her own hand.
And this innocent girl, having herself painted the moon-crested Lord in a picture, reproached him thus with indignation.
To explain how: "When you are described by the wise as omnipresent and all-pervading, how is it that you do not know this person—me—who am situated in my inner state, devoted, and full of passion?
Having recognized me as one in such distress, it is right for you to offer protection"—this is the meaning.
"Existence" (*bhāva*) refers to latent predisposition (*vāsanā*); "abiding in existence" (*bhāvastha*) means that it resides therein. "This" (*imam*) is a reference to the self (*ātman*).
The particle "and" (*ca*) serves as a conjunction in relation to what precedes; the same applies elsewhere. "Censure" (*upālambha*) means being subject to reproach.

And when, searching for no other means to attain that state of the Lord of the World, she perceived none, she then came with us to this grove of asceticism for the sake of penance, having obtained the permission of her guru. (58)

When she, seeking the means to attain that Hara, the Lord of All, could find no other expedient even after searching, she then came to this hermitage with us at our father’s command for the sake of penance.
For indeed, desired objects do not come to pass without merits. || 58 ||
To the question "How long have you been wearying yourself? she gives this reply:
"By her own friend, the trees who witnessed her asceticism, fruit has been borne;
yet her desire for refuge with the Moon-crested Lord is not seen to be even on the verge of sprouting. (59)
Fruit has indeed been formed and produced upon these very saplings planted by her own hand; yet that desire of hers which is directed toward Śiva,
though it has sprouted and even begun to grow, is not yet visible before the witnesses of her asceticism.
Among the perceivers, because [the seeds] were previously planted in them. || 59 ||

I do not know when he, so difficult to obtain even when sought after, will take as his wife this friend of mine— emaciated by penance, gazed upon by her companions with tears in their eyes, and like Sītā when she was parched by drought, waiting for the rain.

And for this reason, I do not know whether he, though entreated, will rescue and protect this friend of mine who is so weak from her religious observances; she whom her companions have seen with eyes full of tears and a path of weeping.

Just as the bull Śakra rescued Sītā—who was afflicted by the drought caused by his withholding of rain—by means of a downpour, so too might he protect her. "Tadavagraha" refers to his (Indra's) withholding of rain; for the root *grah* with the prefix *ava* signifies the obstruction of rain.
"Emaciated by asceticism" (*tapasā kṛśā*) is [called] *tapaḥkṛśā*; the absence of the *aluk* compound in *ojaḥ-saha-ambhas-tapobhis-tṛtīyāyām* is to be considered. || 60 ||

When she who was skilled in interpreting gestures announced, "His true nature is not concealed," Naiṣṭhikasundara asked Umā, "Is this indeed so? or "Is it a joke?", while he himself did not betray any sign of joy.

Then, when her friend—who was skilled in reading gestures and understood her intention—had thus related the matter, making the hidden truth manifest and revealing the ultimate reality, that beautiful lifelong celibate student asked Gaurī.
What did he say? "Is this which has been said by her true, or is it a jest, a joke? Even though there was no second interrogative word present, [the meaning is understood].
The comprehension of that meaning arises by virtue of a specific recitation,
as in the case of "Is the Lord perhaps a kinsman?
where [the intended meaning] is "one who observes the lifelong vow."

And he is both beautiful and fortunate; thus he is "Naiṣṭhika-sundara" (the eternally beautiful one). His status as a *naiṣṭhika* (one who has reached the final goal) arises from his adoption of that [ascetic] dress, while his beauty arises from the fact that he himself is the object of longing.
He is so described because the signs of joy, such as horripilation and the like, were unmanifested and unrevealed by him;
for it is logical that their arising would occur upon hearing of his own good fortune. 61.
Then, offering a crystal rosary with her fingers folded into a bud-like shape in her outstretched hand,
the daughter of Atri spoke with measured syllables, her speech having been composed with great effort over a long time.
Then Pārvatī spoke in measured words with difficulty. Of what sort?
She was placing a circle of white gem-beads upon the tips of her fingers, which were like budding flower-stalks; she was thus joining them together.
This is a manifestation of her bashfulness.
By her speech, they were established [in their state] after much difficulty and without being exhorted.
What did he say? He says:
"O best among the knowers of the Vedas, as you have heard, this person is eager to leap to a high station;
indeed, this penance is the means for attaining it, for there is no limit to the reach of one's desires. (63)

O best of the twice-born, it is exactly as you have heard. For this person is intent on ascending to a high station. Why is this so? He says: "This, indeed, is the austerity that accomplishes the attainment of Hara."

The word "kila" (it is said) indicates that he is not easily attained through this austerity. To the objection, "If he is not obtained, what is the use of this hardship? he replies: there is indeed nothing that does not fall within the scope of one's desires; for hope impels one everywhere.
The use of the pronoun "that" (tat) is due to the influence of modesty;
however, the specific meaning is understood from the literal hearing [of the word]. The phrase "as heard" (yathāśrutam) consists of two words. 63.
Then the student said: "Maheśvara is well known to me; yet you continue to behave toward him as if he were still an object of your desire.
Considering him to be devoted to inauspicious practices, I cannot bring myself to continue my attendance upon you."
Then the religious student spoke again. He said: "Maheśvara is known.
The meaning is: "I know him according to his true nature.
The term "Maheśvara" is used here as a form of derision.

He speaks with anger within: "Once again you remain desirous of that. Indeed, before the burning of desire, you were already seeking it; and having experienced such humiliation, even now you pray for that very same thing. However, if the reading is *pura eva*, these two sentences are sarcastic.
"It is improper to say that you desire him;
for since the previous time, you have been desiring him.
Nevertheless, you stand right there before me—meaning you do not flee out of shame."

But I am unable to satisfy your heart by granting your request through compliance with you, having reflected upon and observed that husband of yours who is devoted and attached to inauspicious practices such as dwelling in cremation grounds;
for he is not a suitable husband for you. 64.
Now he speaks of the fault in that [position]:
"How indeed will this hand of yours, with its marriage-thread still bound on it, endure being grasped for the first time by the hand of Śambhu, which has a serpent coiled as a bracelet? (65)

O you who invoke the impossible through your prayers! How will this hand of yours, with the wedding bracelet bound upon it, endure being first grasped—that is, held—as an armlet by Bhava’s arm, which is encircled by serpents?
For he is indeed adorned with ornaments of snakes.
Reflect upon this yourself for a moment: could these two ever possibly be joined?
A bride’s silken garment marked with swans and an elephant hide dripping with drops of blood! (66)

Let others be set aside; you yourself first consider this: whether the union of a bridal silken garment marked with a swan drawn in yellow pigment and an elephant hide dripping with drops of blood is appropriate.
For the Blessed One is indeed clothed in an elephant skin.

Who else indeed would approve of your feet—marked with red lac—leaving their prints upon the grounds of the dead strewn with disheveled hair, when they are already covered by heaps of fourfold flower offerings? 67.

Who, even an enemy, would approve of—would permit—the footprints marked with red lac upon your feet as you step in succession through the cremation grounds, those lands of the departed where hair and bones are strewn? One might think that perhaps your feet are indeed suited for such places; thus he says: in a *catuṣka* (a particular type of mansion), there is a scattering of flowers, and it is upon these that your feet are cast. Thus, those feet which are stained with lac and accustomed to walking amidst the flower-arrangements of the dwelling of Indra—how utterly cruel is their wandering upon the ground of the cremation grounds, which is thick with the hair and bones of corpses!
For Bhava dwells in the cremation ground;
in the word *catuṣka*, the suffix *kan* is applied to the sense of a four-winged building (*catuḥśālā*).

Tell me, what could be more improper than this: that even upon these two breasts of yours, which are the abode of yellow sandalwood and are easily reached by the chest of the Three-eyed Lord, the dust of funeral ashes shall leave its mark? 68.
Tell me, what else is improper or impossible? For the dust of funeral ashes placed upon the chest of Śiva will remain even upon this pair of breasts of yours, which are worthy of divine unguents;
for by virtue of your embrace, it moves there as well.

And this other mockery awaits you before you: when the great multitude beholds you—who were once carried by the king of elephants—mounted upon an old ox, they will have their faces turned toward smiles.
And this mockery, appearing in the form of ridicule, stands right before you:

for when people see you—who have married her—mounted upon the aged bull that is the vehicle of Hara, even virtuous folk will have their faces turned toward laughter. He says that perhaps she might indeed be worthy of him: "by the king of elephants, Airāvata, to be carried—that is, to be attained."
It is proper for you to go with Indra, who is like a lordly elephant;
and since that bull is old, he is called "vṛddhokṣaḥ" (an old bull), according to the rule beginning with *acatura-*. 69.
Now both have fallen into a state of lamentability by their longing for union with the Skull-bearer (Śiva):
that radiant digit of the Moon, and you, who are the moonlight for the eyes of this world. 70.

Out of a desire for union with Paśupati, both have now fallen into a state of lamentability. What are these two? That digit of the moon, endowed with beauty, which delights the eyes of people, and you.
"Of one possessed of art" is a term of derision; for he is indeed "possessed of art," meaning he is clever. 70.

O fawn-eyed one, is there anything among the boons sought that exists even in part within the Three-Eyed God? His body is deformed, his birth is untraceable, and his wealth is revealed by his nakedness. 71.
O Hari, let alone all those things—beauty, lineage, wealth, and so forth—which are sought and searched for in excellent suitors for a maiden; does even one of them exist in you?
It does not exist at all.
For instance, his body is indeed misshapen, with eyes that are terrifying due to being tawny like fire.
Even his birth is not perceived; from where was he born?
Even his wealth is described by his state of being sky-clad—that is, his nakedness. (71)
Turn your mind away from this unconsidered course; where are you, such as you are, and where is she of auspicious marks?
For virtuous people do not expect a Vedic consecration for the sacrificial post of a funeral stake.
Since this is so, therefore turn your mind away from this unconsidered course and make it look elsewhere;

for where is that unfortunate man of the aforementioned nature, and where are you, endowed with auspicious marks and excellent characteristics? The meaning is that a union between the two of you is entirely unsuitable.
He confirms this very point by means of an illustration:
the virtuous people, the world of the twice-born, do not look toward nor do they seek the sacrificial consecration prescribed in the Vedas for the stake of the cemetery—the pillar of restraint.
For that honor which is accorded to a sacrificial post is never performed for a thief’s stake by anyone who is wise.
And if you offer yourself to him, then he will be consecrated.
Regarding this latter half-verse, three or four variant readings are current;
yet in all of them, the substance remains the same: here, the queen’s honor is equal [to that of the king]. 72.
Thus, as the twice-born man spoke in opposition, she, her anger betrayed by her quivering lower lip,
cast her eyes askance with their corners reddened, her creeper-like brows knit together.
While that student was speaking such unpleasant words, Gaurī knit her brows and cast oblique glances from eyes reddened with anger;
for one possessed of dignity does not look directly at someone who is angry. Her wrath was evident from her quivering lips.
For in anger there is a trembling of the lips; and in that [emotional] state where the two creeper-like eyebrows are contracted and made crooked.
And he said to him: "Surely you do not know Hara in his true essence, since you speak to me thus;
for the dull-witted hate the conduct of the Great-Souled ones, which is beyond common worldly experience and whose causes are inconceivable. (74)
And thus he spoke to the Brahmin. He said: "In truth, you certainly do not understand Śiva, since you speak such harsh words to me."
For those who are dull-witted and ignorant hate and revile the conduct of the great, which is entirely unlike their own and whose underlying cause is incomprehensible;
if you were wise and had realized the ultimate truth, you would not speak thus. 74.
Now, regarding what was said [by him], "delighting in the practice of inauspicious things," etc., he provides the reply in due order:
"Auspicious rites are practiced by one intent on averting calamity, or by one eager for prosperity.
But for the virtuous one who is the refuge of the world and free from desire, what need is there for these things which corrupt the natural functioning of the self with hope? (75)

In this world, auspiciousness is pursued by two kinds of people: by one who desires the destruction of calamities such as disease, and by one who longs for prosperity. Yet, for him who is the refuge of the worlds and the remover of suffering, no misfortune is conceivable.

And since he is free from desire and devoid of longing because of his perfection, what prosperity could he possibly desire that he has not already attained? Therefore, what use have these auspicious rites for Hara, the refuge of the world, who is free from longing? [The phrase] "by those whose own nature is censured" refers to those whose very being is afflicted by worldly expectation;
for such hope belongs only to the small-minded.
Whether the use of the singular number in the expression "maṅgalam" (auspiciousness) is appropriate or not, the wise are the authority;
for it is a general designation.
He is called *śaraṇya* because he destroys (*śṛṇāti*) fear; thus he is a protector. Another [scholar] says it is from the roots *śṛ* and *raṇ*.
Alternatively, he is *śaraṇya* because he is excellent (*sādhu*) in providing refuge (*śaraṇa*), which is protection. 75.
Referring to Virūpākṣa’s body, he says:
"Though possessing nothing, he is the source of all prosperity; though his abode is the cremation ground, he is the Lord of the World;
though of terrifying form, he is proclaimed as Śiva. There are none who truly know the Pināka-wielder as he really is. (76)
For those who know the true nature of Śarva, there exist no [notions of] things according to their own specific forms;
for even though he is without anything and devoid of worldly power, he is the source and cause of all prosperities and sovereignties.
Though he is without possessions, free from desire, and poor, and likewise dwells in the cremation ground, he is the Lord of the World, the sovereign of the seven worlds.
Even though he possesses terrifying forms such as Bhairava and others, he is proclaimed to be Śiva.
But how could one who is fearsome be the bringer of welfare?
Therefore, because of the perception of these various contradictory forms, there are no true knowers of the Pināka-wielder’s essential nature.
Whether shining with ornaments or encircled by serpents, whether wearing an elephant hide or a silken garment,
whether bearing a skull or having the moon as his crest— no single form can be discerned in the body of the Universal Form.
In short, it cannot be ascertained—that is, determined—that the body of the God, whose form is the universe and who is the self of all, is of such-and-such a kind alone.

For instance, whether it be resplendent with ornaments or bound by serpents, or even strung with snakes—the meaning is that it possesses both these seemingly contradictory forms. The same applies to what follows.
Whether he wears an elephant hide or a human skin, whether he is clad in fine silk garments,
whether he holds a skull-cup or bears the moon upon his crown—
this one is sometimes seen as terrifying and sometimes as gentle.
The meaning is that [the Lord] is the one whose form is the universe; by this, the objection "you yourself first...
has been answered. || 77 ||
To answer the question of how [the ashes] will become the dust for his footprints, he says:
"Having obtained contact with his limbs, the dust of the funeral pyre will certainly serve for purification;
for it is smeared by the crests of the dwellers of heaven as they fall during their performance of dance and dramatic gestures. (78)
Having obtained contact with the body of that deity, even the dust of the ashes of the funeral pyre certainly becomes pure.

Why is this so? He says: For indeed, those dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) consisting of the employment of hands, feet, and so forth, which occur during the performance—by virtue of the performance of those gestures, the [ashes] fallen from them are smeared upon and rubbed onto the heads of the gods (*nākin*).
If it were inauspicious, how could Śakra and the other gods, competing with one another for precedence, bear it upon their crowns?
And this is the definition of perception. || 78 ||
When he goes out on his bull without [the usual] retinue, Indra— whose vehicle is the elephant Airāvata with rent temples—
approaches him on foot and, with his crown, touches his feet, the toes of which are reddened by the pollen of blossoming Mandāra flowers.

Because that god has a bull for his mount, even though he possesses no wealth and his riches consist of but an old ox, Śakra approaches his feet and makes them red with the pollen of blossoming Mandāra flowers—his fingers reddened by the pollen of the blooming celestial blossoms.
If one such as this is still poor, then let it be so;
"lacking wealth" is said from the perspective of others' standards. By this, [the poet] implies: "having seen the aged bull."
And it was replied: "The wealth has been offered by way of nakedness. What kind of bull?
He whose vehicle is the world-elephant Airāvaṇa, who is "prabhinnah"—that is, one whose temples are bursting with rut-ichor.
Having approached and descended from the lord of elephants, || 79 ||
O Lord, although you intended to point out a fault, you have spoken well with your mind undisturbed:
"How could he, whom even the Self-born Brahmā acknowledges as his own cause, have originated from a visible source? (80)

Although you, having lost your composure under the influence of reviling Hara and with your mind deranged, spoke of the fault of his "unperceived birth," you have nonetheless uttered one truly auspicious and beneficial word directed toward Śiva:
that they declare him to be the source even of Brahmā. For it is said:
"Kāma, Brahmā, the Veda, and the Brāhmaṇas—all this, both the stationary and the moving, has originated from you, O Sthāṇu."
Thus, how could that God have his origin in a perceptible object or be known by birth? Therefore, his "unbornness" (ajātva) is merely a matter of praise. 80.
Enough with this dispute; let him remain exactly as you have heard him to be, in every respect.
My mind is established here with its sole essence in devotion to Him; the movement of desire does not regard what is said about propriety.
Or rather, what is the use of this insistence?
Let him be exactly as you have perceived him; let him be everything he may be.
As for me, my mind has become fixed upon the Lord with a single flavor and a single form through its inner disposition, love, and devotion; it has become composed entirely of that passion.
The meaning is that it cannot be turned back by you;
for one whose conduct follows desire—that is, one who acts according to their own whim—does not take account of what is censurable or blameworthy.
As it has been said:
What is the remedy for false attachment, and what is the restraint for addiction?
By what means can those who perceive things perversely be joined to the path of the virtuous?
The word "entirely" (aśeṣam) is an adverbial modifier of the verb "to exist" (asti). || 81 ||
"O friend, let this boy be stopped; he wishes to speak something further, as his upper lip is quivering.
Not only is he who speaks ill of the great a sinner, but he who merely listens to such speech shares in that sin as well. (82)
Saying, "I shall go from here," she, whose bark garment was pressed by her breasts, began to move away;
but he whose banner bears the bull-king, assuming his own form and smiling, took hold of her.
Speaking thus, the goddess moved forward;
the god, appearing before her with a smiling face, took hold of her and restrained her.
He said, "What are you saying? O friend (āli), let this young brahmin boy (vaṭu) be released."
Because he desired to speak something else even more significant that remained unsaid—
evidenced by his upper lip quivering and moving upward,
for the trembling of the lips occurs through the desire to speak.

If you ask why he is being restrained when he wishes to say something, he says: "Because not only is he who speaks ill of—that is, reviles—the great and the excellent a man of sinful fortune and blameworthy, but even he from whom that slanderer is heard incurs demerit.
If he does not desist, then I myself shall depart from this place. As it has been said:
"Indeed, the censure of others should never be uttered, nor should it ever be heard."
One should either cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.
As she was speaking thus, the moment she rose with the desire to depart, the God revealed his true form and seized her.
The phrase "with the bark-garment torn at the breasts" is intended to demonstrate the agitation of her heart;
for either by the force of his touch or by the heaving of her body, the binding of the bark-garment was loosened.
Beholding him, the daughter of the mountain king— her limbs and joints trembling, her feet raised only to set them down again—
neither went forward nor stood still, like a river obstructed by a mountain on its path.

Then, having seen the God in person, Pārvatī, overcome with trembling and perspiration, neither moved forward nor remained still; for she held up her foot, which had been raised for the purpose of stepping, bearing it right there. For if she were to go, she would have to place her step in another location.
Moreover, even if she were to remain there, her rescue would be futile; therefore, he should leave her right where she is.
Her arrival there was not possible because the cause for it had ceased to exist, yet she does not stay put either, as she has become agitated by witnessing unprecedented events.
Just as a river like the Sindhu, overwhelmed by contact with a mountain on its path, neither flows forward nor stands still due to the obstruction of its current, so too is she.
For by her, one must go downward. 84.

When the moon-crested Lord said, "From this day forward, O lady of peerless limbs, I am your slave, purchased by your ascetic penances," she immediately cast off the exhaustion born of her observances; for hardship does not produce renewed vigor once its fruit has been attained.

Speaking thus to the moon-crested Lord, the Goddess instantly, at that very moment, cast off the exhaustion arising from her ascetic observances and abandoned her weariness. Why did she say this? She spoke thus: "O lady of faultless limbs, O you of auspicious body, from this day forward I am your slave, purchased by the price of your penance.
Why did she abandon her weariness? She explains: because when there is fruit, suffering no longer possesses its freshness.
The meaning is that [the affliction] perishes upon seeing the fruit.
For this indeed is the "newness" of the affliction: the manifestation of physical exhaustion and so forth.
The word *ahnāya* is a particle resembling a dative case ending, functioning in the sense of "at that very moment."
The meter is Vasantatilakā; this is the figure of speech known as Arthāntaranyāsa (Corroboration by a General Truth). || 85 ||
Thus ends the fifth canto in the commentary on the Kumārasambhava composed by Vallabhadeva, the son of Ānandadeva.
The Sixth Canto.
Then Gaurī privately instructed her friend regarding the Self of the Universe:
"Let the Lord of the mountains, my suitor, be made the final authority. || 1 ||
Immediately thereafter, Pārvatī, being restrained by Hara, secretly instructed her friend, saying to Śiva, the Soul of the Universe:
"My father is the giver and the master; therefore, let him be the authority in this matter, let him be empowered here.
For a daughter is dependent upon her father. (1)
Having been addressed with that message, she shone silently before her beloved like a mango branch near a cuckoo in the springtime.

With that friend standing near her beloved, she to whom the message had been delivered shone—indeed, the queen appeared radiant—precisely because she was reserved; for, due to her modesty, she was humble.
The meaning is that by not speaking herself, she attained beauty while remaining reserved.
For bashfulness is indeed the ornament of maidens. Like what did she shine?
In the spring season, when it is close at hand, the mango creeper shines like a female cuckoo acting as a messenger with her mouth;
for the purpose of conveying his message, the cuckoo’s mouth is metaphorically employed.
This figurative use of the term "message" implies that Hara is the suitor, Madhu (Spring) is the comparison, Gaurī is the mango creeper, and her friend is the female cuckoo.

Although terms such as *parabhṛtā* (cuckoo) denote the kokila bird, the basis for the application of the action [of naming] is not the genus (*jāti*), and thus, by the rule *jāter astrīviṣayāt*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur. || 2 ||
Having promised "So be it," and having with great difficulty dismissed Umā,
he who was the punisher of Smara called to mind the seven seers, whose abodes were the celestial lights.
Having promised "So be it," and having said "I shall do so," the Enemy of Smara (Śiva) requested the Lord of Mountains;

and having thus consented and released Gaurī with great difficulty, he called to mind the sages. The absence of the genitive case [in "ṛṣīn"] is due to the lack of intention to express the remainder (*śeṣatva*).
Whom? The sages. Whose home or abode (*dhiṣṇya*) consists of the luminaries, that is, the stars—the meaning is "the Seven Sages" (*saptarṣi*). The root *śas* has the sense of "to injure.
One who has chastised (*śāsitavān*) Smara is "Smara-śāsana" (the Chastiser of Smara). The lengthening [of the vowel] is as in the word *kulapāṃsana* (a disgrace to the family).
Or the form [of the root] *śās* [is used].
Illuminating the sky with their circles of radiance, those ascetics,
accompanied by Arundhatī, suddenly appeared before the Lord.
Then those sages, together with Arundhatī, immediately after being remembered, appeared and manifested themselves before the Lord, illuminating the sky with their own circles of splendor. || 4 ||
They bathed in the currents of the celestial Gaṅgā, where the waves were covered with mandāra flowers from the banks, and which bore the scent of the ichor of the elephants of the quarters.
What are those seven sages like? They are bathed—having performed their ablutions—in the currents of the celestial Ganges, in the flows of the divine river.
In what kind of currents? Those in which the northern waves and ripples are increased by the *mandāra* flowers along the edges of the banks.
In the reading *utkireti*, it refers to those [waves] in which the quarters (of the sky) are strewn—that is, scattered—with flowers;
likewise, they possess the scent of rut belonging to the elephants of the directions who have come for water-sports. 5.
Wearing pearl girdles and sacred threads, clad in golden bark garments,
and holding rosaries of jewels, they had taken up the life of mendicants like wish-fulfilling trees.
Wearing sacred threads made of pearls, they are "hemavalkalas," meaning those whose bark-garments are of gold;
and those whose rosaries are made of jewels are "ratnākṣasūtras.
From this, they are compared to the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas).
Those who have resorted to the life of renunciation are the renunciants (*pravrajita*). For them, indeed, jewels are easily obtained.
"Renouncing" (*pravrajana*) is "renunciation" (*pravrajyā*); the suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of the action of the roots *vraj* and *jay*.
In the word "bearing" (*bibhrataḥ*), [the elision of *n*] does not occur because of the rule "not after a reduplicated stem before the suffix *śatṛ*" (*na abhyastāc chatuḥ*).
The state of being non-existent. || 6 ||
They were constantly gazed upon with respectful salutations by the thousand-rayed sun, whose horses were directed downward and whose banner was bent low.
They were constantly gazed upon by Ravi with a gesture of salutation from above,
for their station is indeed near Dhruva;
it was for this very reason that the horses were made to stand below them.
By whom the banner and the flagstaff were bent down and brought low.
With their coiled trunks resting upon the earth as it was lifted up together with the tusk of the Great Boar,
they found repose during the calamity of the dissolution.
Likewise, the statement regarding their imperishability is that they remain resting upon the tusk of the Primordial Boar during the calamity of dissolution, at the time of the world's destruction.
To the question, "Are they resting there alone? he says: "together with the earth that was uplifted."
For she was lifted from the water by the Blessed One and carried upon his tusk; she who, out of fear of the sudden onset [of danger], clung to him like a creeper to a branch. 8.
Because they brought forth the remainder of creation immediately after the Source of the Universe,
those ancient ones are celebrated by the knowers of antiquity as the "Dhātṛs" (the Sustainers).

The ancient knowers of the past, such as Mārkaṇḍeya and others, have proclaimed them to be the "ancient, primordial creators" (purātanā ādyā dhātāraḥ). Why? Because they carry out all the remaining tasks for Brahmā, the source of the universe.
For after Brahmā has fashioned something, they are then appointed to the work of creation. || 9 ||
The ascetics were enjoying the fruits of their former, pure, and fully matured austerities.

They were consuming the fruits of the austerities of former ascetics—those who existed in the past—who were stainless and fully ripened through their penance. For in other cases, the fruit of austerity is bestowed in a future birth;
but because these [ascetics] lived for so long, it was granted even in this very life. The word "api" (even) expresses wonder. It is truly marvelous now!
Even while practicing austerities, they are enjoyers of the fruits of those austerities.
Standing in their midst, that virtuous woman, her eyes fixed upon her husband’s feet,
shone like the personified perfection of asceticism, appearing as if she were many Arundhatīs.
Among those sages, Arundhatī shone most brightly; she was resplendent,
her eyes fixed upon the feet of her husband Vasiṣṭha, for she was a virtuous woman who regarded her husband as a deity,
and her gaze never wandered elsewhere.
Therefore, it is imagined: she is like the perfection of asceticism (tapas-siddhi) itself in embodied form; for the perfection of sages must indeed be personified. 11.
The Lord beheld those sages with a lack of reverence; for he was indifferent as to whether she was a woman or a man, since it is conduct alone that is honored by the virtuous.
The Lord beheld Arundhatī and the sages with an impartiality that was free from partiality, through a realization that transcends conventional distinctions;

for [the thought] "this is a woman" and "this is a man"—such a lack of fixedness is secondary when it comes to showing respect. Nevertheless, the conduct of the virtuous is honored and their character is revered, even if it is not currently of practical utility.
The meaning is that the virtuous honor conduct;
and who else is superior to Arundhatī in terms of character? 12.
And for this reason:
Upon seeing her, Śambhu felt a great longing for a wife;
indeed, virtuous wives are the primary means for performing dharma-oriented rites. (13)
Upon beholding that virtuous Arundhatī, Śiva made a great effort to bring about a wife for himself;
for virtuous wives alone are the primary means and cause for religious rites such as sacrifices. || 13 ||
Even though Śarva had been made to grant a boon to Pārvatī in accordance with dharma,
the mind of Kāma, fearing his previous offense, began to breathe a sigh of relief.
The meaning is that the mind of Kāma is the swelling and blossoming [of desire]; that is to say, the Mind-born (Manobhū) has manifested in the form of power. When?
When Śarva was made to fix his foot—that is, to make an effort—upon Pārvatī.
The meaning is that when Hara desired to marry Gaurī;
for it has been stated thus: "When he shall marry Pārvatī," and so forth.
That he was impelled by dharma has already been explained by the passage beginning with "upon seeing him," and so on.
Of what kind of desire?
Of one who is afraid of a previous offense characterized by having agitated the mind of the Lord. The word *api* (even) is used for the sake of emphasis.

It is a marvel that Kāma was made by Dharma to set foot upon Umā through righteousness and not through passion; nevertheless, Kāma fears his former offense, while the Lord fears further harassment due to His own fierce anger. 14.
Then all those sages, learned in the Vedas, having honored the Teacher of the World,
spoke these words, their skin bristling with joy.
Then those seven sages, having honored the Blessed One with prostrations and other marks of respect, spoke these words that are about to be related.
Of what nature were they?
They were learned in the Vedas (anūcānāḥ), humble, obedient to his commands, or alternatively, students of the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (sāṅga).
Then, out of love and devotion, their skin became bristling and their limbs were covered in horripilation. || 15 ||

What do they say? He says: "That Brahman which has been correctly handed down by tradition, that which has been offered into the fire according to the rules, and that austerity which has been practiced—the fruit of all that is ripened for us today. (16)
O Sovereign of the worlds, we have been placed by you upon a path that lies beyond even the reach of desire, yet remains within the range of your own mind.

Whatever Veda or knowledge we have properly recited and studied according to the rules, whatever Agnihotra sacrifice we have duly performed, and whatever discipline we have correctly observed— of that [may there be the fruit].

Now the fruit of everything has ripened, in that we have been brought—placed—within the range of the mind and the sphere of the heart of you, the teacher of the world; that is to say, we have been remembered by you. Of what kind is he?

It is beyond even the path of one's desires and outside the scope of the imagination; for even the most fervent wishes of anyone do not extend so far as to think that the Blessed One would remember [them].
Whoever dwells in your heart is already the best among the accomplished; how much more so he who, being of Brahmanic origin, dwells within your heart! 18.
He in whose mind you dwell would indeed be the best among the accomplished and the foremost among those who have achieved their purpose;
for those endowed with a store of merit remember you.
How much less could he who dwells in your heart, whom you remember— that foremost among those who have accomplished their purpose— not be so? [This applies] even to Brahmā Virañci, or to the Supreme,
the source of knowledge, your own progenitor.
Truly, we abide in a state higher than both the sun and the moon;
today, however, through the grace of your remembrance, that state of ours has become even loftier. 19.

"By dwelling near Dhruva, we certainly occupy a station far higher than that of the sun and the moon; yet today, through the grace of your meditation, that station of ours has become even more exalted. For it is by meditating upon you that we have become so exceedingly high.
[Note: The reading *uccaistarām* with the suffix *-ām* is not logical, as a word (*pada*) is a substance (*dravya*). 19.
We hold ourselves in high esteem because of your appreciation; for generally, the highest honor inspires confidence in one's own merits. (20)
We hold ourselves in high esteem and know ourselves to be excellent because you have honored us, respected us, and known us according to the truth as we truly are;
for such supreme honor inspires, awakens, and establishes confidence in one's own virtues, which are essentially the worship of God.
Indeed, it is through the respect of great men that we truly come to know ourselves as being endowed with virtue.
Even though "much" functions as an adverbial modifier of the action, it is understood as the excellence of the self alone. || 20 ||
O Virūpākṣa, what need is there to describe to you that joy of ours which arises from meditating upon you,
for you are the inner self of all embodied beings?
O Virūpākṣa, O Piṅgalanetra, why should we inform you of that satisfaction which has arisen in us from remembering you?
For you abide within all living beings; therefore, you yourself know everything. 21.
Now, by way of a digression and out of a desire to know the true nature of the Blessed One, they say:
"You have been seen directly, yet we do not truly know you.
Be gracious and tell us of yourself; you do not abide within the path of the intellects. (22)
It is a marvel that, although You have been directly beheld by us, we nevertheless do not know You immediately and in their entirety according to reality.
Therefore, please be gracious;
tell us of Your own nature—what is Your form?
He says: "Why do you not investigate for yourself?"—for you do not travel on the path of the intellects. And how can that which is not an object of the intellect be understood by itself? (22)
Having spoken thus in general, "Tell us of yourself," they asked specifically:
"Is it that by which you create the manifest, or that by which you sustain it?
Or is it that which is its destroyer? Which of these is this portion of yours? (23)
"Which of these parts of yours is visible to my direct perception?

Is it that part by which you create the universe from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—that you are Brahmā? Or is it that by which you sustain and protect it—that you are Viṣṇu? Or is it that which is the destroyer and devourer of this manifest world—that you are Rudra?

Which of these parts is this one of yours? If it is asked, 'Even though your nature as Rudra is understood, what occasion is there for doubt?', the answer is simply your possession of many forms. (23)
Or rather, O Lord, let this very great request rest;
for now, command us regarding those things that come to us as soon as they are thought of—what shall we do?

Alternatively, O Blessed One, let this request not be too great, since it reveals the secret meaning: "We have become meditators and have attained [the goal]; command us, what shall we do? What shall we accomplish? The verb is used in the imperative mood (*loṭ*) to express a prayerful entreaty. 24.
Then the Supreme Lord, augmenting the slender luster of the moon resting upon his crest with the bright rays of his teeth, replied: (25)
Then the god replied with words contrary [to the truth]. What was he doing?
Increasing the meager moonlight of the moon situated upon his head by means of the stainless rays of his teeth.
The use of the verb *āha* (he said) in the present tense (*bhūte*) is an error arising from the confusion of it being a form ending in *-nal*. 25.
To dispel the suspicion that his state of being at the end of his life was caused by his pursuit of a maiden, he says:
"It is known to you that none of my activities are for my own sake;
indeed, I am indicated as being such by these eight forms. (26)
This is surely understood by you all: that whatever activities or functions belong to me are not for my own sake, but rather for the sake of others.
For it has been declared that I am oriented toward the welfare of others through these eight forms known as earth, water, air, fire, the sacrificer, ether, the moon, and the sun.
Indeed, the functions of the earth and the other elements are exclusively for the sake of others.
The genitive case [is used] by the rule "vo viditam" (Pāṇini 2.3.67) and "ktasya ca vartamāne" (Pāṇini 2.3.67), meaning "it is known by you. || 26 ||
Thus, like a rain-cloud besought by cātaka birds parched with thirst,
I was entreated for offspring by the gods who had been oppressed by their enemies.
Acting for the sake of others, I was entreated and petitioned by the gods, who had been humiliated by their rivals: "O Blessed One, procreate a son upon Umā, who shall become our general for victory.

Just as the cloud (*vidyutvān*) is entreated for rain by *cātakas*—a specific type of bird, afflicted by thirst and longing to drink—so too, because the secondary objects (*apradhānakarman*) [the gods and the *cātakas*] are expressed by the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), the accusative case occurs for the primary objects (*pradhāna*), namely the procreation and the rain.
[The term *vidyutvān* means] he in whom lightning (*vidyut*) exists; [it is formed with the suffix *matup*] in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).
Thus, because it is a *bha* [suffix], there is an absence of *pada*-status; consequently, there is an absence of *jaś*-substitution. || 27 ||
Therefore, I desire to bring Pārvatī for the birth of my own son,
just as a sacrificer brings the fire-drill wood for the production of the consumer of the oblation.
Since I have been requested for a son, for that reason I desire to bring Gaurī here to obtain a wife for the sake of procreating a son,
just as one consecrated for the manifestation of fire desires to fetch the wooden fire-drill.
Therefore, you must request Himālaya on our behalf;
for relationships properly established do not admit of alteration. (29)
Therefore, you must request Pārvatī for my sake from the Lord of Mountains.
He asks why this matter is not sought through his mediation:
"Alliances that are well-performed and firmly resolved by the virtuous do not undergo change; they remain stable. (29)
To the question, "How can the Lord of All enter into a relationship with one who is unequal [to Him]? he says:
"Know me also to be uncheated, for I have entered into a relationship with him who is elevated, established, and who bears the burden of the earth. (30)
Know me also to be one who has not been deceived, but rather one who has achieved his purpose through that king of mountains;
for the meaning of the word "also" (api) is that just as he is praised by me as a son-in-law, so too am I by him as a father-in-law.
For indeed, he is preeminent by virtue of two forms.
In that regard, first, in the case of the stationary [mountains], he is one who, being elevated, touching the sky, established, and firm, bears the burden—the weight—of the earth;
for mountains are so called because they support the earth (*mahī-dhara*).

Even in the case of the moving [beings], he is one who, being elevated through great majesty, established, and possessing moral boundaries, upholds the burden of the earth—that is, its security and prosperity (*yoga-kṣema*).
Because he is the king of mountains; "know" (vitta) is the imperative (loṭ) of the root vid. || 30 ||
"You should speak thus for the sake of the maiden; this is not being taught to you as a new rule, for the virtuous follow the conduct established by you. (31)
It is not being said to you that this should be spoken by you to the father of the girl regarding her excellent qualities for the sake of the marriage;
for the wise declare that the legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is established by you, since you are indeed the creators of the immortal law (*amṛti*). 31.
The noble Arundhatī also ought to take part in this matter;
for generally, in such affairs, housewives possess great confidence.
In this matter, the venerable Arundhatī should also provide assistance by performing her duty in the house of Himavat;
for in such a task as seeking a bride, the skill of matrons is generally required, as they know how to urge even an unwilling father of the maiden. (32)
Therefore, let us set out for Oṣadhiprastha, the city of Himavat, for the sake of success;
at this Mahākośa precipice, we shall surely meet again.

Therefore, for that reason, go to the city of Himavat called Auṣadhiprastha to accomplish our purpose. Furthermore, there shall be a meeting with us at this great precipice named Mahākośa to report the success of our mission;
here I shall await you—this is the meaning. || 33 ||
When that foremost of self-restrained ones had become eager for marriage, the ascetics devoted to the procreation of offspring cast off their shame regarding the acceptance of wives.

Then, when that Blessed One, the foremost of those who practice self-restraint, had become intent upon marriage, the sages—the sons of Brahmā born of Prajāpati—cast off their shame regarding the taking of a wife; they abandoned their embarrassment over the wedding. For they were always ashamed in the presence of Śambhu, thinking, "How wretched is our asceticism compared to those of us who have experienced union with women!"
But when even he becomes impassioned, then, due to the equality of all [in that state], there is the abandonment of shame.
Then, having said "So be it," the circle of sages departed;
the Blessed One also reached the first designated location.
Immediately thereafter, having said "So be it," he went to the circle of the Seven Sages; the god also proceeded to the Mahākośī waterfall. *Paramam* signifies agreement;
others say it refers to words of benediction (*puṇyāha*). (35)
Those supreme sages, born of the mind and possessing minds of their own, leaping into the sky as dark as a sword, reached Oṣadhiprastha.
Those seven sages, created by the mind (mānasa), having ascended into the sky as dark as a sword-blade, reached and entered the city of Oṣadhiprastha.
"With the mind" (manasā) is a clever expression meaning "like the mind" (mana iva);
the sense is that as soon as the mind was resolved to go, they arrived. || 36 ||
Now he describes the region of Oṣadhiprastha: "As if surpassing Alakā, the abode of the wealth of the Vasus, it was established as if by the very outpouring of heaven vomited forth. (37)
What kind of city was it?
It was as if constructed after surpassing, crushing, and plundering Alakā—the abode and refuge of riches, treasures, and increasing wealth, the city of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Likewise, it was fashioned as if by taking the essence and overflowing abundance of heaven itself and vomiting it forth.
The meaning is that it was as if constructed by taking the very essence of Alakā and Amarāvatī, the two most excellent [cities].
For it has been said: "One should establish a city by bringing in people from foreign lands, whether they have lived there before or not, and by attracting those from one's own country. (37)
Encircled by the stream of the Gaṅgā, with medicinal herbs glowing at the edges of its embankments,
and possessing great walls of precious stone, it was enchanting even in its state of seclusion.
