Why else would it not be delightful? It is charming and fit for habitation even in its secluded areas and its surrounding outskirts.
For instance, it is surrounded and encircled by the flow of the Gaṅgā; thus, it possesses a water-fortification (*jaladurga*).
Furthermore, with medicinal herbs blazing at the edge of the embankment near the riverbank, it possesses the nature of a fire-fortification (*agnidurga*).
Where the walls and the rampart consist of massive gem-stones, that is "protected by a rampart" (*prākāragupti*).
In other cities, however, protection by water, fire, or ramparts becomes terrifying and unfit for habitation. || 38 ||
There, the elephants had conquered the fear of lions; the horses were born from the womb of serpents;
the Yakṣas and Kimpuruṣas were the citizens; and the women were forest deities.

This describes the excellence of the army: there, elephants, having conquered the fear of lions, do not tremble before maned beasts; and horses born from the womb of caves emerge from the forest thickets.
There, the *puṇyajanas*, *kiṃnaras*, and others are the citizens and country-folk, and the forest deities themselves are the women.
Now, are there no women of other castes among the citizens in that forest?
How great indeed is this praise!

If that is so, then since the *kiṃpuruṣas* are equal to the citizens and the forest deities resemble women, yet no one has any sense of esteem for them or for them, this is praise for the citizens and their women. 39.
There, the sounds of drums produced by the instruments are distinguished from the echoes of clouds clinging to the mountain peaks, being rendered uncertain by the latter's thundering.
In that place, the sounds of drums belonging to the houses are manifested and determined by means of musical instruments and rhythmic beats, but not of their own accord;
for since the clouds are attached to the peaks— remaining upon the lofty summits—
they are therefore rendered uncertain by the resonance of the thunder, which is the echo of the sound of the clouds.

"Is this the thundering of clouds, or the sound of a drum?"—in such a doubt, the sense organs possess a manifesting capacity; for indeed, there is no presence of rhythmic beats within the sounds of rain clouds.
There, by the very wish-fulfilling trees with their swaying branches and foliage,
the splendor of household mechanical devices was produced without the labor of craftsmen.
In those dwellings, the splendor of mechanical banners—the beauty of artificial victory standards—is produced by the *kalpavṛkṣa* trees alone;
that is to say, the celestial trees themselves produce in the houses that very splendor which ought to be created by mechanical banners.
This is because they possess fluttering silken cloths upon their branches—that is, they have silken garments waving and moving upon their trunks (*viṭapa*).
For a banner ought to be made of cloths;
therefore, it was fashioned and created by human effort alone, even without the regard of the citizens. 41.
Where, in crystal palaces at night in the banquet halls,
the reflections of the stars serve a useful purpose.

Wherein, at night, upon the drinking terraces arranged upon crystal palaces, the reflections of the stars themselves serve as offerings of flowers, attaining the state of flower-clusters due to their whiteness and similarity to them. 42.
There, by the light of medicinal herbs, women going to meet their lovers could travel at night with their paths revealed; they were unaware of darkness, even on a cloudy day.

Where, even at night, even on a cloudy day, even during a torrential rain, the playful women going to meet their lovers (*abhisārikā*) are unacquainted with, and have never experienced, the darkness of the gloom;

that is to say, they know no fear of the dark. This is because the path upon which they travel has been revealed by the radiance of medicinal herbs. A "path" (*saṃcara*) is so called because it is that wherein one moves.
Darkness itself is *tamisra*; a rainy day is *durdina*. And it has been said:

"She who, unable to endure the arrival-time of her messenger, goes forth as if parched by the pain of the heavy fever of love, out of longing to drink from the lip of her beloved—that woman is called an *abhisārikā* by the best of poets."
In that [state], youth is the limit of life; therein lies the affliction of the flower-armed god (Kāma), and sleep arising from the exhaustion of passion, which is a reversal of consciousness.
Elsewhere [the text speaks of] the end of old age (*sthavirānta*) as the limit of life, but here it is the end of youth; this is a statement regarding the absence of afflictions such as senility.

Furthermore, where the only affliction or calamity is the god of love (*madana*) himself due to the discharge of his arrows—and not one caused by disease and the like—and where the resulting state is sleep arising from the exhaustion of sexual pleasure, which is a reversal of consciousness or insensibility rather than death resulting from the departure of the vital breaths: thus is their freedom from old age and death expressed. || 44 ||
Where, by means of anger characterized by knitted brows, trembling lips, and the pointing of graceful fingers, beloveds were made to seek their wives' favor.
Where young men, rendered unwilling to seek favor by the anger of proud women, do not even ask for their grace—because the very state of being angry is more delightful.

For indeed, [they are captivated] by those [women] who possess lovely and charming gestures of finger-pointing, accompanied by the knitting of eyebrows, the contraction of brows, and trembling lips with quivering lower petals. 45.
And his outer pleasure grove, fragrant as Mount Gandhamādana, was filled with travelers— Vidyādharas— sleeping in the shade of the Saṃtānaka trees.
And his external worldly pleasure grove was the mountain named Gandhamādana.
Of what sort was it?
It was a place where travelers were, in fact, Vidyādharas sleeping in the shade of the celestial trees known as Saṃtānas.
For the external garden is to be enjoyed by all; it is fragrant with scents.
The word *Gandhamādana* is neuter in gender. || 46 ||
Then those divine sages, beholding the city of the Himavat,
considered it to be like a deception of their own well-earned merit intended for the attainment of heaven.
Then those seven seers, beholding such a city of medicinal herbs and aiming toward heaven, perceived their own well-performed asceticism as a deception:
"Why was asceticism not practiced by us with this city in mind? For indeed—"
Beyond this is Surapura, which is even more delightful. 47.
At the palace of Śiva, they were gazed upon by the gatekeepers with upturned faces;
they descended with masses of matted locks as motionless as painted fires.
Then those sages descended from the sky and alighted at the house of Himavat;
they were observed by the doorkeepers stationed at the entrance, who wondered, "Who might these be?"—
men distinguished by their matted locks that were motionless like painted flames.
"Those who stand at the gate" (dvāsthāḥ) are so called because they stand there at the gate (dvāra). || 48 ||
Descending from the sky,
that succession of sages, led by the eldest, shone like a row of suns within the waters.
The garland of the Seven Sages descended from the sky, the region of space, and shone forth;
it was like a row of suns reflected in the midst of water—this describes its brilliance. It was that [garland] which had the elders as its leaders, each according to his seniority, moving in front.
A succession or row preceded by the elders according to seniority. || 49 ||
Taking up priceless offerings for those who were themselves beyond price, the mountain went out a long distance to meet them,
bowing the earth with his footsteps heavy as solid timber.
*Argha* is worship; for that purpose, water and other materials are called *arghya*.

Having taken those, the King of Mountains went out and advanced toward those lords of sages who were worthy of honor (*arghya*) and worship (*arcya*). What was he doing? [He was advancing] with his essence, that is, with his strength.
Causing the earth to sink downward with his heavy, difficult-to-bear footsteps.
With lips as copper-red as the mineral ore, tall in stature, and with arms as large as devadāru trees, he was by nature broad-chested like a rock; thus he was clearly recognizable as Himavat.

Of what nature is he? He is easily manifested—that is, easily known—as "the Himalaya by his very nature," because of the similarity between the two forms [of the mountain and the person]. The suffix *khal* is applied according to the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu*. For instance, in the case of the stationary [mountain], it is simply the minerals such as copper that constitute its lower lip.
He whose arms were tall, lofty, and as large as *devadāru* trees,
and whose chest was like a rock; yet,
being mobile, he possessed lips as red as minerals (*dhātu*), arms as tall and long as *devadāru* trees, and a chest that was rough, broad, and hard like a stone.
At this juncture, this verse is not so purposeful. || 51 ||
The teacher of the path himself, accompanied by those of pure deeds who offered honors according to the prescribed rites, caused him to enter the inner apartments.
He caused those sages to enter the inner apartments, the private quarters;
he led them there by those who had performed the prescribed rites of hospitality and honor. But he himself was the guide of the way, the instructor, saying, "Go by this path."

Since the root *kram* here has the sense of "attaining" with "going" as a subordinate element, it does not possess its primary meaning of "going"; therefore, there is no use of the accusative case in the word *taiḥ*. || 52 ||
There, having taken his seat upon a throne, the Mountain, with palms joined in reverence, addressed these words to the lords seated on cane chairs: || 53 ||
There, at the end of the night, the Lord of Mountains spoke these words to those self-controlled lords;
thus the verb *vac* takes two objects (*dvikarmaka*). Some, however, interpret the construction as "he spoke words to those lords," meaning he addressed those masters of speech (*vācaspati*).
They were seated—that is, sitting—upon thrones made of *vetra*, a particular kind of wood.
He too, having taken his seat at his command, stood with palms joined in reverent salutation. || 53 ||
What did he say? He says:
"Your appearance, occurring unexpectedly, seems to me like rain without the rising of clouds, or like fruit without visible flowers. (54)
"The appearance of you all—unexpected, unhesitating, arrived, and brought about—appears to me like a rain from a cloudless sky and like the flowers and fruits of unseen [merit];

this is the ornament of *rūpaka* containing a comparison (*upamā*) based on the impossibility [of the comparison]. The inclusion of the word "to me" (*me*) in the phrase "it appears to me" is for the purpose of indicating a conceptual distinction (*vikalpa*).
The absence of a second [self]. || 54 ||
Through your grace, I consider myself to be like a fool who has become enlightened, like iron that has turned to gold, and as if I have ascended from the earth to heaven. (55)
Through the grace of your vision, I perceive myself as such:
though formerly a fool, now awakened like a wise scholar;
though made of iron, transformed as if into gold; and having risen from the earth as if unto heaven.
Because of the equal satisfaction resulting from that. || 55 ||
From this day forward, I am accessible to all beings for the sake of purification;
for that which has been occupied by the Arhats is indeed declared to be a sacred ford (tīrtha). || 56 ||
From this moment forth, I am to be approached by people for the removal of their sins;
for that which is practiced by the worthy and the wise is called a *tīrtha*, and indeed, through your arrival, I have become a *tīrtha*. 56.
O best of the twice-born, I consider myself purified by two things alone:
by the descent of the Gaṅgā upon my head and by the water from the washing of your feet. 57.

"O best of brahmins, I consider myself purified in both ways; I know this by what two? He asks: 'By the spray of the Bhāgīrathī on my head and by the water from your washed feet—by the water that has cleansed your feet.
For as pure as the water of the Gaṅgā is, so too is the water from your feet."
For the wise have declared that one should wash the feet of Brahmins and carry that water upon one's head. || 57 ||

The mobile [form] was placed on your side as servants, while the immobile [form] was marked with your footprints; thus, having distributed grace between the two, you have indeed created for me a state of duality. 58.
"You have divided my two forms, bestowing favor upon one and extending grace to the other;
for my moving form, my body, has been placed among the servants in the task of servitude, while even my stationary form is marked with the impression of your feet. Thus it goes exceedingly far."
The suffix *jaṅgama* follows [the rule] for that which ends in a nasal (*anunāsika*).
In the case of *preṣaṇīya*, *praiṣya*, and *prādūhoḍhoḍhyeṣaivyeṣu*, there is *vṛddhi*. The state of having exactly two forms is called *dvairūpya*. || 58 ||
My limbs, though they pervade the very ends of the quarters, are not sufficient for the swelling joy that arises from your high regard for me. (59)

My limbs, though they pervade the very limits of the quarters, are not capable— indeed, they lack the power— to bear that swelling joy and rapture arising from your high regard for me, born of your affection for me, which increases until it reaches a state of fainting. To carry that [joy], they are insufficient.
The meaning is "they are able. This is a statement regarding the abundance of satisfaction.
The dative case is used because [the word] *paritoṣāya* has the sense of "sufficiency" (*alam-arthatva*), as in "not being sufficient for satisfaction."
Not only has the darkness situated within the cave been dispelled for you by my radiant vision, but even the darkness beyond the realm of Rajas has been cast out from within me.

By your radiant and luminous vision, not only has the darkness within my cave been dispelled, but even the internal darkness residing in my heart, born of the quality of passion (rajas), has been driven away.
But that which is called delusion has been cast aside; for by beholding you, I have indeed become free from delusion. 60.
Now, wishing to inquire about the purpose of their arrival by way of a different approach, he says:
"I see no task for you to perform; if there were one, what would not be possible?
I suspect this departure of yours is solely for the sake of purifying me. (61)
"Because of your asceticism, I see no purpose for you to have come into my presence. Even if there were such a purpose, would it not be accomplished by itself due to your great power?
Therefore, I know that this arrival of yours is solely for the sake of purifying me. (61)
Nevertheless, you ought to grant me a command for a while;
for servants exist by the grace of being employed by their masters. 62.

Although everything is accomplished for you by yourselves, nevertheless, give me a command in some matter; for those who are servants and bondsmen are recipients of the favor of being employed by their masters, and it is the master's command alone [that they obey].
Their favor consists in the application [of power] residing in those who possess sovereign power; thus, the locative case here should be understood as expressive of the locus. || 62 ||
"Here am I, here are my wives, and here is this maiden, the very life of our lineage.
Tell me what you wish to do with these; have no concern for external things. (63)

What is the use of much talk? Here we are; here are these wives; and here is this maiden, who is as dear to us as our own family and life. Tell us, Father, what you require from among these, for what need have you for land, gold, or other such things?

He says it is "concealed": because there is no attachment or regard for external objects such as land, gold, and the like; for one who gives away even his own self, sons, and wife, what esteem could he possibly have for wealth? (63)
Having spoken thus, Himālaya expressed that very same meaning by means of an echo alone, which spread from the mouth of the cave. 64.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Mountains, as if to confirm that very point, spoke again through the echo spreading from the hollows of the caves.
Then the sages urged Aṅgiras, the foremost among those cited as authorities on illustrative matters;
he, in turn, replied to the Mountain.

Then the sages urged the seer Aṅgiras, who was preeminent and proficient in the modes of exposition regarding illustrative subjects. And that Aṅgiras spoke to the Lord of Mountains: "It shall be illustrated."
"That which is told" is the example (udāharaṇa), and that very thing is the "subject matter of the example" (udāharaṇavastu). || 65 ||
He says what [the mountain] spoke: "All this is appropriate for you; even beyond this, your loftiness is equal to that of the mind and of mountain peaks. (66)

All that you have said, beginning with "We are these [people]," and even more than that, even further than that—all this is fitting and easily established in your case; for your mind is lofty and noble like mountain peaks. Indeed, what is difficult for one of great magnanimity? (66)
It is fitting that they call you Viṣṇu, whose nature is stable;
for indeed, you have become the receptacle containing within your belly all beings, both moving and unmoving.

Vyāsa and others describe you as Viṣṇu, whose nature is stationary, or as being joined with a station— that is, a specific object— as they say, "Himālaya is the foremost among stationary things. For this reason, yours...
Your belly is the womb, having become the support for all beings, both moving and unmoving;
for all creatures, whether stationary or mobile, dwell within you.
Indeed, it is well known that even Viṣṇu is called the "Abode of the World. 67.
How could the serpent have supported the village with his hoods, which were as delicate as lotus stalks,
had you not held it up from the very base of the netherworld?

How could the serpent Śeṣa have supported the earth—the ground—with his heads as tender as lotus stalks, and how could he sustain it down to the depths of the netherworld (pātāla), were it not for you holding it up?
For it is by your assistance alone that Śeṣa endeavors to bear the world. This is the meaning.
Since there is no occurrence of the non-actualization of the action (kriyātipatti), the use of the conditional (lṛṅ) suffix in "adhāsyat" is to be considered problematic.
With their stainless lineages unbroken and like the waves of the ocean that cannot be obstructed,
your fame and your rivers alike purify the world through their merit.
Your glories and the rivers purify and cleanse the world because of their holiness. Of what sort are they?
Both possess an unbroken, uninterrupted, stainless, and bright continuity, a connection, and a flow; yet both have their progress obstructed by the surging waves of the ocean. 69.
Just as the Gaṅgā is praised for being touched by the foot of the Supreme Lord, so too is she praised for her second source— yourself, whose head is uplifted.
Just as the celestial river is praised for originating from the supreme foot of Viṣṇu, the progenitor,
so too is she praised by you, O one with uplifted neck;
for the Viṣṇupadī indeed originates from Himavat, but [the other] from the foot of Hari.
"At the time of traversing the three worlds, one should go forth"—such is the sacred tradition (āgama). || 70 ||
The greatness of Hari is all-pervading—horizontally, upwards, and downwards;
yet that which belongs to you as you prepared for the three strides was innate.
The all-pervading majesty that belonged to Hari-Viṣṇu occurred during his three strides when he was intent upon traversing the three worlds, but it was not eternal; however,
this all-pervading majesty of yours is natural, innate, and everlasting.
The specific explanation:
the three strides, which are the placements of the feet, taken together constitute the "Three-Strider" (Trivikrama). || 71 ||
By you, who have taken your place among those who partake in the sacrificial offerings,
the lofty golden peak of Sumeru has been rendered futile.

Among the gods who partake of sacrificial portions, you have established your station by receiving a share of the sacrifice; yet, by doing so, you have rendered the peak of the mountain of the gods—though made of gold and though lofty—vain, fruitless, and rendered false. For he (Śiva) does not partake of a share of the sacrifice; therefore, what is the use of that peak, even if it be of gold?
You have bestowed all your hardness upon your stationary body;
but this form of yours is for the worship of the Arhat, bowed down in devotion. 73.

Your duality consists of two forms distinguished by softness and hardness. In that case, in a stationary body made of stone, you have established total hardness; but this mobile [body] of yours, because of its softness, is tender and bowed in devotion.
Therefore, one should perform the honoring and service of the Arhats, who are worthy of worship; however, there should be no stubbornness in this regard. 73.
Hear now the purpose of our coming; that task is yours alone, yet we too shall share in its merit through the instruction of what is beneficial.
The word "tat" (that) serves as a conclusion: enough with this proclamation of your greatness;
first hear the purpose of our arrival. As for that purpose, since it is something you must request, it belongs to you alone and not to us.

However, because both of us participate in the determination of the path to the highest good (śreyas) and thereby attain auspicious results, the meaning is that this task is also our own duty. || 74 ||
He who bears aloft the crescent moon together with the sound "Īśvara"—a sound that gives rise to the qualities such as *aṇimā* and remains untouched by any other person. (75)
By means of its own natures—earth and the rest—which possess mutually imagined capacities, this manifest world is stretched out, like a carriage drawn by draft animals upon a road. (76)
Those wise yogins who investigate that which resides within the field—the state of which the sages call the station free from the fear of rebirth. (77)
Śambhu, the bestower of boons and the direct witness of all deeds, chooses your daughter for himself through words transmitted by us. 78.
That Śambhu, the bestower of boons upon you, directly chooses [as his] daughter—that is, he requests her—by means of words and phrases transmitted through us and directed toward us.
Who is he? He says: "He who is such a Lord."
He bears a sound that is loud and pervasive, shaped like a half-moon; the meaning is that he also carries a crescent moon. What kind of sound?
It is the source, the origin, of the qualities (guṇas) known as aṇimā, mahimā, ladhimā, prāpti, prākāmya, īśitva, and vaśitva.
One who is endowed with qualities such as *aṇimā* (atomicity) and so forth is called the Lord (*īśvara*).
"Arising" (*utthāna*) means that from whom [all things] arise.
Likewise, he is one by whom another person—the Self (*ātman*)—is untouched and not made an object.
The Lord is indeed a distinguished person;
he is either exceedingly lofty or possesses great power.
By his own selves—his forms consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether—this manifest universe, the cosmic egg, is stretched out.
It is extended, that is, it is accomplished. Here, the vehicle—the chariot—is on the path by means of draft-horses.
Of what kind are they?
They are those by whom a mutual capacity, a support of power, has been fashioned and bestowed.
Indeed, by means of their functions—supporting, gathering, digesting, arranging, providing space, and acting—they are capable of creating the worlds, for they bestow power upon one another.
Even those who bear the primary burden [of the body] govern the vehicle [of the body] while depending on each other's power.

That deity whom the knowers of the supreme self (adhyātmavid) investigate as dwelling within the field, situated inside the body, and known as the Supreme Self (paramātman)—[it is he who presides over these elements].
They seek that state which they call the fearlessness of non-return—the state where the fear of returning, the terror of saṃsāra, no longer exists;
for having reached that place, one is not born again. Thus [they seek] the world...
He is the witness and observer of the auspicious and inauspicious actions of the world because he resides within the heart; he is the bestower of boons, the giver of desired objects.
Such is Maheśvara himself, who exists for his own sake before you.
He requests Umā as his daughter. This concludes the group of four verses (kalāpaka). || 75–78 ||
You ought to unite that purpose with your daughter Bhāratī;
for a daughter bestowed upon a virtuous husband is not to be grieved for by her father. 79.
Therefore, you ought to unite that Śambhu with your daughter,
just as one joins meaning with speech;
for word and meaning are eternally connected through their mutual non-deviation.
Moreover, by that gift, the merit belongs to you alone;
for a maiden bestowed upon a virtuous and noble husband becomes no longer a source of grief to her father.
He states another quality as well: "As long as there are dualities among beings, both stationary and moving, they conceive of her as their mother; for the Lord is the father of the world. (80)

"Give this maiden to him, so that these two types of beings, the moving and the unmoving, may regard this Gaurī as their mother. To explain how she becomes the mother of the world through that gift, he says: because the Lord Mahādeva is the father of the worlds.
Because he creates [the child], and because he provides for his welfare and security, and because she who is the wife of one's father is called "mother. (80)
Immediately after that, let the gods color the feet of this [goddess] with the rays of the crest-jewels of Śitikaṇṭha, who is composed of the syllable *praṇava*. 81.

Moreover, having bowed to the blue-throated Lord (Śiva) according to the procedure for the Goddess's daily rites, let them likewise color and adorn the feet of this Gaurī with the rays from the crest-jewel upon her head. [The mantra:
"Having bowed to the Blue-throated One... (praṇamya śitikaṇṭhāya).

Since a case ending denoting a *kāraka* (syntactic relation) is stronger than a case ending used for a secondary word (*upapada*), the accusative case would be the logical one; however, the dative case is employed, as seen in usages such as "having paid homage to Svayambhū" (*svayambhuve namaskṛtya*). || 81 ||
Umā is the bride, you are the giver, and we here are the suitors;
Śambhu is the groom—indeed, this is the destiny sufficient for the exaltation of your lineage. 82.
This rite is sufficient and adequate for the arising and prosperity of your lineage.
To the question "Who are these?", he says: Umā, that is Gaurī, is the bride; you are the giver; Maheśvara is the groom; and we are the petitioners.
Even though the virtues have not been explicitly disclosed, they are understood through the suggestive power of the words.
"Just as Rāma said, 'I shall endure everything. || 82 ||

Become the father of the Father of the Universe, who is worthy of praise though he praises none, and who is worthy of worship though he is worshipped by none, through the rite of conferring a son upon you. 83.

By giving Gaurī even to Śambhu, the Lord of the Universe, may you become a father-in-law worthy of supreme honor; for a father-in-law is indeed like a father. Of what kind [of a lord]? One who is praised and worthy of salutation due to his being the most excellent of all.
He says that he might even praise or bow down to some others: "of one who does not praise or worship," because there exists no one superior to him. 83.
While the celestial sage was speaking thus, Pārvatī, standing at her father’s side with her face cast downward,
began counting the petals of her play-lotus.

While Aṅgiras was speaking thus near the Himalayas, Gaurī, bowed down with modesty, began counting the petals of her play-lotus; by this concealment of her bashfulness, she indicated the intensity of her longing. 84.
Although his desire was fulfilled, Śaila looked toward the face of Menā;
for householders, regarding the matter of a daughter, generally have their eyes fixed upon the eyes of their wives.

Himavat, too, his desires fulfilled, looked toward the face of his wife, wondering what could possibly be said; for those householders who live as family men generally rely upon the eyes of their housewife—their wife’s very sight—regarding the matter of a daughter. To her...
The meaning is: "They do whatever pleases you. || 85 ||
Having reflected with his intellect that this was the proper reply in this situation, at the conclusion of their words, he took hold of his daughter, who was adorned with auspicious ornaments.

Then, having resolved in his mind that "the gift of the daughter alone is the proper response here, and nothing else," and having said something relevant to the matter at hand, he took his daughter—who was adorned with auspicious ornaments—at the conclusion of his speech.
"Come, child; by this offering to Śarva, you have been designated as alms.
The sages are my petitioners, and I have attained the fruit of being a householder. (87)
Having said this much to his daughter, the Mountain spoke to the sages:
"This wife of the Three-eyed One bows down before you all."
"Come, daughter; you have been offered to Śarva, and for the sake of Hara, you have been designated by me as alms.
The Seven Sages are the path.
Thus, the fruit of being a householder has been attained by me today."
"For a householder, a daughter should indeed be given to one possessed of virtue.
Having thus addressed Umā, he spoke to the Seven Sages:
"This [girl], who bows to all of you, shall be the wife of Śarva"—by this, the giving away of the bride was indicated.
That to which something is offered is "arpaṇa"; [this is derived] according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.
That in which Śarva is the object of offering (*arpaṇa*) is "śarvārpaṇā.
Those who meditate upon (*medhante*), that is, associate with, the home (*gṛha*), the dwelling (*veśma*), and the wife (*dārāḥ*) are "gṛhamedhinaḥ," namely, householders.
Those who seek [something] are called "seekers" (arthinaḥ). || 87–88 ||
Having rejoiced at the words of the Mountain, which were noble in their fulfillment of desired aims,
they gladdened Ambikā with blessings that bore fruit immediately.

Then those sages, having welcomed and rejoiced at the words of Himavat—which were of great significance for the attainment of their desired object—strengthened and gladdened Ambikā Gaurī with blessings.
Of what kind?
With those whose fruit, characterized by her husband’s favor, was "pureḥpāka," meaning its ripening was imminent or its success was near at hand.
Arundhatī took upon her lap that bashful woman, whose golden ear-ornament had slipped from its place due to the intensity of her prostration.
Vasiṣṭha’s wife took Ambikā onto her lap as she was ashamed by news of her husband;
she was one whose golden ear-ornament—a golden earring—had slipped and fallen due to the effort of bowing and the respectful salutation at [her mother-in-law's] feet.

And by means of his virtues, he dispelled the grief of his mother, whose face was bathed in tears and who was overwhelmed with affection for her daughter, as well as that of the bridegroom, who had never before been wedded to another.

Thus, he made Menā—who was weeping, distressed by affection for her daughter—free from grief through the virtues of her son-in-law, who had never before been with another and had not yet taken another wife.
He said, "Your son-in-law has become the Lord of All, omnipotent, and kind to his devotees; since this is a cause for great joy, what occasion is there for sorrow?
The term *ananyapūrva* means one who has no other [wife] before him; it is a statement intended to dispel the fear of a co-wife.
The compound is *sup-supā* (noun with noun). || 91 ||
Questioned at that moment by the kinsman of Hara regarding the auspicious date for the wedding,
they— clad in bark garments— informed him that it was three days hence and then departed.
Then those sages set out; they rose up to depart. Of what sort were they?
At that very moment, they were asked by the kinsman of Hara—the father-in-law of Śaṅkara—regarding the auspicious date for the wedding: "When shall the marriage take place? They too...

After three days had passed, they set out on the following day. "Those whose possession and wealth consist solely of rags and bark garments" is a statement intended to show their lack of desire; for generally, those who arrange marriages for maidens are full of longing. She for whom marriage was the sole purpose [was thus described].
Relating to marriage. 92.
Having taken leave of the Himalaya and beheld the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva) before them,
and having reported the matter accomplished to him, they departed by way of the sky, dismissed by him.
Those sages, having taken leave of the Lord of Mountains and bid farewell to Śiva, beheld him;
and having informed him of their acquisition of Gaurī, they were dismissed by him and rose into the sky, departing for heaven—thus concludes the story with brevity.
Even Paśupati passed those days with difficulty, longing for union with the Daughter of the Mountain;
for what other person, however independent, would these emotions not disturb, since they affect even that Lord? (94)

The sages departed for their own abodes. The Blessed One also, longing for union with Pārvatī, passed those three days with difficulty. This is an instance of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle). Where:

Even these states— passion, hatred, and the rest— touch and assail that Blessed One, the All-pervading Lord and Master; how then could they not disturb or afflict another who is powerless and has not conquered his senses?
The meter is Puṣpitāgrā. || 94 ||
Thus ends the sixth canto in the commentary on the *Kumārasambhava* composed by Vallabhadeva, the son of Ānandadeva.
The Seventh Canto:
Then, for the increase of the Lord of Herbs (the Moon), on a lunar day endowed with the quality of being in a favorable position relative to the zodiacal sign...
The Himalayas, whose kinsmen had assembled, presided over the ritual of his daughter’s marriage initiation.
Immediately thereafter, the Lord of Mountains presided over and completed the rites for his daughter’s marriage initiation, beginning with the *godāna* ceremony and the performance of her vows.
When? During the waxing phase of the moon, when the lord of medicinal herbs—the Moon—was increasing; on an auspicious lunar day endowed with the quality of being in the *jāmitra* position.
Here, the word *jāmitra* is used figuratively to indicate excellence.

For the seventh house from the ascendant is primarily known as the *jāmitra*; and that *jāmitra* is favorable. "Accompanied by kinsmen" means surrounded by one's own people; such is the nature of a festival. || 1 ||
With the preparations for the wedding festivities, the womenfolk in every house were busily occupied;
through their affection, the city on the mountain and the inner apartments seemed like a single household.
The city and the inner apartments of the snowy Himavat mountain became like a single family and resembled one undivided lineage;
the entire city was perceived as being like the inhabitants of his own private chambers. This was because of their affectionate attachment.
In that city, groups of women and crowds of matrons were busily occupied and lacked leisure in every house with the preparations for marriage festivities and various auspicious rites;
for "kautuka" refers to those auspicious acts such as the smearing of lime-wash and so forth performed for the sake of prosperity. || 2 ||
With its great highways strewn with *saṃtānaka* flowers, its rows of banners fashioned from Chinese silks,
and its golden archways blazing with light, that other place shone like heaven itself.
It shone like another region of heaven,
for there the great highway— the royal road— was strewn thick with divine flowers called *santānaka*,
and there the rows of banners were fashioned from *cīnāṃśuka* cloths produced in the land of China.
And another place, a different location, blazing and shining with the radiance and luster of golden archways. || 3 ||
Although there was a row of sons, Umā alone— seen after a long time as if risen from the dead—
became the cause of an especially intense sighing for her parents at the time of her marriage.
Because her marriage was imminent—meaning her wedding was near—the maiden Gaurī became, as it were, the sole object of her parents' affection despite having many other children;

for such affection did not exist toward the others. Likewise, although she was constantly present before them, she seemed to be seen only after a long time, due to the arising of longing; even while they were alive, she was as if dead.
As if risen from the dead; likewise, it has "breathed forth with distinction," meaning it possesses an extraordinary vitality, because life itself depends upon it.
Such an inference arises because of the manifestation of even denser affection at the time of separation. As it has been said:
The gaze wanders as if filled with longing; the mind goes somewhere in utter agitation;
and the heart, bound by a bond of unswerving love, trembles at the time of separation.
Receiving one blessing after another from her husband, she enjoyed one ornament after another;
though their relationship was different, the affection for the mountain’s lineage became focused solely upon her.
Addressed with blessings by her kinsmen, that queen moved from one lap to another;
and when an ornament had been placed by one person, she would take up another decorative arrangement brought by someone else. Thus it was with the lineage of the mountain.

Affection, though diverse due to the nature of its relationships and manifold in form, attained a single direction and a single basis. For affection has many subdivisions according to the difference in relationship; for example, it is of one kind toward a son, another toward a grandson, and yet another toward a daughter.

The meaning of the sentence is that the affection felt by kinsmen toward a daughter's son, a daughter-in-law, and a female friend is indeed of a different kind; there is no such joy for them toward her as they do not feel toward those others.
And in this case, the very fact of having performed the marriage ceremony is the cause.
That alone is the single path and the station for him; he is "one whose path is that" (tadekāyana); the state of being such is "the condition of having that as one's path" (tadekāyanatā). || 5 ||
At the auspicious moment when the moon entered conjunction with the Uttaraphalgunī asterism,
the female relatives who had sons and husbands performed the funeral rites for her body.
Upon the body of that Pārvatī, the non-widowed and fertile wives of her kinsmen performed the rites of adornment and decoration. When?
At the time when the moon had entered into conjunction—that is, connection—with the Uttaraphalgunī constellation; for [the rite is performed] during the conjunction with the moon.
The state of being a constellation belongs to the stars; at the auspicious hour presided over by the deity Maitra (the Moon). 6.
Beginning with the anointing, he describes the grooming of her body:

She adorned herself with the attire for anointing— consisting of a silk garment that reached down to the navel and was fastened by a bodice— which displayed a variegated hue, like white mustard seeds nestled among the tender sprouts of dūrvā grass.
Anointing is the application of oil. There, the queen adorned herself with finery and attire;
yet, the statement that she was not "adorned" by it expresses her possession of an unartificial beauty. Of what kind [was that finery]?
Where there is an arrangement and placement of white mustard seeds, cow-horn, and *siddhārtha* grains,
its luster is distinguished by a variegated hue mingled with those sprouts of *dūrvā* grass and blades of young grass.

It is that in which the silken garment covering the hips is no longer present at the navel; for then it is cast off. Or rather, it is that in which the silken garment covering the hips has moved away from the navel—having departed from the navel (*nirnābhi*) and become detached.
With arrows drawn and a shaft held ready; for such indeed is the way of the world. || 7 ||
And the young woman shone, having come into contact with the arrow of the rite of initiation,
like the crescent of the moon being kindled by the ray of the sun at the end of the dark fortnight.

And having attained union with that new bridegroom, who was like an arrow in the rite of marriage-initiation, the bride shone; like what? Like a digit of the moon being kindled and increased by the sun’s ray named Suṣumṇā during the waning fortnight.

They led the lady toward the dais; she had removed the oil from her limbs with a paste of *rodhra* wood, her body was anointed with the drying essence of *kālīya* sandalwood, and she wore garments suitable for the consecration ceremony.
Then, for the purpose of bathing, those widows led her to the four-faced fountain.
Of what sort was she?
She had had the oil removed from her limbs by means of a coarse paste of *rodhra* powder, so that all bodily unguents were cast off.
Likewise, she has kālīya-ointment as her garment and kālīya-ointment as her unguent; kālīya is a fragrant substance resembling saffron, and it is applied to remove any oily smell.
Likewise, she was wearing a garment made of fine cloth, suitable for the consecration and appropriate for bathing; [he entered] the four-pillared chamber of Indra. 9.
Upon that bed, which was inlaid with slabs of lapis lazuli and variegated with patterns of unperforated pearls,
they bathed her while playing musical instruments, having poured water from golden jars.
In that fourfold enclosure, young women, accompanied by musical instruments and cymbals, bathed this bride.
Of what kind was it?
It was one wherein beryl stone slabs were set and joined together for the purpose of demarcating the various sections of the bathing area.

What kind of women were they? They were those by whom water from golden jars—specifically the water from eight-jeweled pitchers—had been poured out with devotion and artistic grace upon a variegated and beautiful mosaic of pearls that had been pierced and strung together. 10.
With her limbs purified by an auspicious bath and wearing beautiful, fresh garments,
she shone like the earth when its sprinkling from the rain-clouds has ceased and the kāśa flowers are in full bloom.
That Gaurī, her limbs purified by the wedding consecration, her body radiant and clad in white, washed garments, shone and gleamed; like what?
Like one upon whom the completed and perfected sprinkling of rain from a cloud—the downpour of water from the clouds—has fallen.
Just as the earth shines in autumn when covered with blooming kāśa flowers, so did he shine,
wearing a pair of pure, washed garments.
And from that place, she was led by women devoted to their husbands to the center of the marriage altar, where a canopy was spread over a prepared seat supported by four jeweled pillars.
From that place, she was led by virtuous women to the center of the marriage altar, onto the lap of the auspicious site.

Of what sort was it? It was provided with a canopy, reddened by vermilion, joined by four pillars of precious gems, and furnished with a seat—a well-arranged *bhadrapīṭha*. (In this verse, the letter *ra* is substituted for *kṛpa* according to the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ*). 12.
Having seated that slender woman there facing the east, the women sat before her for a moment;
though the means of adornment were at hand, their eyes were drawn away by the natural beauty of her form.
There, having seated that slender-limbed woman facing the east,
the young women standing before her remained indifferent for a mere moment, even though ornaments were at hand.

For their eyes were captivated and enticed by her natural splendor, which was the reality of things; for what need is there for ornamentation for a form that is unartificial? "Bhūtārtha" means that which is ultimate or absolute. 13.
A certain woman draped her inner blossoms— which had been made free of moisture by incense and which brought an end to her afflictions—
with the pale luster of madhūka flowers and dūrvā grass tied in a grand knot.
Then, in a mere moment, a certain woman wound and bound his mass of hair with a crest of white madhūka flowers entwined with young grass.
Of what kind was it?
It had been stripped of its moisture and thoroughly dried by the smoke of incense such as aguru and other perfumes.
It has flowers within it, being "flower-filled" (kusumagarbha).
Because of its length, it is noble (udāra), meaning its knot or joint (bandha) is excellent. 14.
They adorned her limbs with streaks of white sandalwood paste and yellow pigment, along with decorative leaf-patterns;
she stood there, surpassing in splendor the sandy banks of the triple-streamed Ganges marked by ruddy geese.
The women prepared her body in this manner. In what way?
It was smeared with white aloe-wood (*śuklāguru*), a specific type of white unguent applied thereon.
Aloe-wood exists in two forms according to the distinction between white and black.

Likewise, her breasts and other parts were adorned with leaf-patterns made of gorocanā pigment; thus, she was "possessed of leaf-designs with gorocanā" (*sarocanāpatravibhaṅga*). Consequently, that Gaurī surpassed the splendor of the triple-pathed river (the Gaṅgā), whose banks are marked by the names of the rathāṅga birds (cakravākas).
For she was white; because of her brightness, she resembled a ruddy goose. 15.
Surpassing the lotus with its bees rendered motionless and the orb of the moon veiled by a streak of clouds, the beauty of her face—
with its well-known tresses— cut short any possibility of comparison.
The splendor of her face, by means of its well-known curls, cut off even the occasion for the speech of comparison— the opportunity to say, "What could its likeness be?"—
and it eclipsed both the lotus with its clinging bees and the lunar orb accompanied by a fragment of cloud.
Having conquered both the lotus and the moon, which are indeed the standard comparisons for her face, the cause of their defeat is simply the act of adorning it.
On her cheek— which was roughened by the astringent dye of *rodhra* applied to the ear and pale as a streak of yellow orpiment—
the sprout of a barley grain, having attained a superior luster, captivated the eyes.
The barley sprout placed upon her ear bound the eyes of the world and turned them away from other objects. Why?
Because of the attainment of an excellence of beauty resulting from the gain of a contrasting hue on her cheek. Of what sort was it?

With the decoction or juice of *rodhra* on a rough or uneven surface, as well as with *gorocanā*, there is a splitting or cracking; likewise on an excessively pale surface. And in this way, on a pale surface, there is the attainment of an excellence of luster from the green [pigment].
And because rice, barley sprouts, and so forth are praiseworthy, they constitute a treasure-store. || 17 ||

And the lower lip of her with well-proportioned limbs—marked with lines and slightly tinted with beeswax—cultivated an indescribable beauty through its quivering movements, bearing as it were the imminent fruit of loveliness. (18)
The lower lip of her, whose limbs were well-proportioned due to the power of youth, fostered—that is, increased—a certain indescribable splendor through its quiverings or tremors.
Of what sort was it? It was divided, or made twofold, by a central line;
likewise, its redness was slightly removed by a small amount of beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*) applied to it.
The intense redness [of the lip], heightened by betel and other substances, is made sweet by being wiped with beeswax.

It is called *adharo* because it is situated below (*adhas-bhava*), resting at the base (*budhnastha*), and its fruit is beauty (*lāvaṇya-phala*) which is brought near through the kissing of the beloved. 18.
"Touch the crescent moon on your husband's head with this," said her friend jokingly;
she, while coloring her feet, was thus blessed and struck her back wordlessly with a garland. 19.

That goddess silently struck her with a garland on her crest as a wordless blow, because her friend, while dyeing her feet, had offered such a blessing in jest. To explain how: "With this foot, touch the crescent moon situated upon the head of your husband Śiva, by virtue of the particular nature of sexual union."
And for this reason, out of anger, there was the striking with a garland. || 19 ||

Beholding her eyes, which were as beautiful as the petals of a well-grown lotus, the female attendants did not apply auspicious black collyrium to them out of a perception of any particular excellence in their luster. (20)

Having observed that her well-formed eyes were as lovely as blue lotus petals, the adorners applied collyrium to them out of a sense of auspiciousness, and not from a desire for superior beauty; for they were already by nature like blossoming blue water-lilies.
How can that wretched collyrium possibly enhance the beauty of those two? || 20 ||
Like a creeper with blossoming flowers, like the night with rising stars,
or like a river with birds alighting upon it, she shone as her ornaments were being put on.
Being adorned with ornaments, that goddess shone and gleamed.
To explain the comparison—since the ornaments possess many colors—he states the similes:
she was like a creeper beautified by blossoming flowers; thus, there is the acquisition of rubies, sapphires, and other gems.
The acquisition of pearls is indicated by the rising stars, as if it were night;
the acquisition of golden ornaments and the like is indicated by the cakravāka birds embracing, as if it were a river.
Beholding her own radiant form in the surface of a mirror, the large-eyed woman became eager for Hara’s arrival; for the purpose of women’s attire is indeed the sight of their beloved.
Then Gaurī, beholding her own self shining in the circle of the mirror with her steady, wide eyes, became eager for the arrival of the Three-eyed Lord;
for the dress, attire, and ornaments of women have as their fruit the sight of a beloved.
For when the beloved is not in sight, what is the use of adornment? || 22 ||
Then his mother, lifting up his face— which was adorned with pure ivory ear-ornaments— took moist, auspicious yellow orpiment and realgar from her two fingers.
Mena somehow managed to make that very same first longing— which had grown ever stronger following the blossoming of Umā’s breasts— the auspicious tilaka mark for her daughter’s marriage initiation.

Then Menā, lifting her daughter’s face and taking yellow orpiment and red arsenic with her index and middle fingers, applied a tilaka for the sake of auspiciousness during the marriage initiation; because her vision was clouded by tears of joy, she performed it with some difficulty. It is imagined: [as if] following the budding of Umā’s breasts.
Along with the emergence of her breasts,

he made that very desire— which had grown toward obtaining a worthy husband— seem as if it had already been attained; this inference arises because [the desire] was then as if it had emerged from her heart.
The word *eva* is used in the sense of *iva* (as if). Of what kind is the face?
It is one upon which a spotless ivory ornament (*dantapatra*)—a leafy vine fashioned from the tusk of an elephant—is fixed or attached to the ears.
The particle *anu* in the phrase "following the budding of the breasts" (*stanodbhedamanu*) is a *karmapravacanīya* used in the sense of the third case. (23–24)
And with her gaze distracted by fear, she fastened the woolen amulet-string— which had been arranged in a particular position—
onto her wrist as it was being pulled away by the fingers of her nurse.
Not only did she apply a tilaka mark upon Gaurī, but she also fastened and then released a woolen auspicious wrist-thread (kautuka-sūtra).

Of what sort was it? Because her eyes were restless with tears, its arrangement was misplaced; and thus, it was being shifted by the hand of the nursemaid and led back to its proper position. || 25 ||
Clad in fresh silk garments, she shone all the more as she held up the mirror, like the shore of the milk-ocean with its mass of foam, or like an autumn night with the full moon.
Clad in a fresh garment of fine silk and bearing a jeweled mirror, that queen shone with exceeding brilliance;
she gleamed like the Milky Ocean adorned with its ring of foam, or like a night of moonlight under a full moon. || 26 ||
Having offered that [gift] to the family deities whom she had worshipped and having performed the ritual for the stability of the lineage, the mother—
who was skilled in what ought to be done— caused the virtuous women to perform the traditional salutation by grasping her feet in due order.
Having caused that goddess to bow down before the household deities who had been worshipped with flowers and other offerings, Menā,
being skillful and proficient in performing necessary duties, subsequently made her pay homage by touching the feet of virtuous women in order of seniority.
Having caused that queen—the foundation of the lineage and the bringer of fame—to bow down, [he said] "iti ayāmantrata"; here, there is the substitution of *ay* for the suffix *ṇi*. || 27 ||
"May you obtain unbroken love from your husband"—thus was Umā addressed by them as she bowed;
yet, because she had already obtained half of his body, even the blessings of her affectionate kinsfolk were rendered secondary by her.

It was said that when she had been saluted by those non-widowed women, the queen, bowing before her husband, would receive from him unbroken and perfect love—an excess of affection. Yet, she subsequently set aside and disregarded even such abundant blessings from her kinsfolk;
why? Because of her attainment of half the body of that husband.
For since even half of her body was given by him, it is not difficult to obtain mere love from him; "half of the body" means *ardhaśarīra*, where the word *ardha* is neuter. 28.
Having performed his duty for her without remainder in a manner consistent with her desires and his own power,
the skillful king remained in the assembly hall while his friends were present, awaiting the arrival of the Bull-bannered God.

Then the Lord of the Nagas, accompanied by his friends and kinsmen, remained in the assembly hall at the wedding ceremony awaiting the arrival of Hara; having performed all the rites for his daughter in a manner consistent with both his desire and his wealth, he brought them to completion.
He is "kṛtī" (accomplished) because he has performed his duty;
he has achieved his purpose by bestowing his daughter upon the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of All.
He is "sabhya" (refined) because he is excellent in the assembly, being preeminent in lineage, character, and other such qualities.
The form "aśeṣayitvā" belongs to the root *śiṣ* of the curādigaṇa, used in the sense of "having left nothing remaining" (having exhausted). || 29 ||
Meanwhile, on Mount Kailāsa, the bridegroom’s adornment— befitting his previous marriage—
was prepared by his devoted mothers and placed before the command of Smara.

Just as Gaurī was being adorned, so too, on Mount Kailāsa—the abode of Kubera—were ornaments suitable for her first marriage placed before the groom, the enemy of Smara (Śiva), by the Mothers and the deities who exerted themselves for his sake. || 30 ||
Out of respect for him, she was touched by the Lord only with the splendor of his auspicious ornaments;
yet it was her own attire that assumed a different state to become the desired form of the bridegroom.

Then, out of respect for his mother, the King merely touched that splendor of festive ornaments; he did not place it upon her body, for it was the very attire of the Lord himself that had assumed another form—the desired and preferred state of the bridegroom. (31)

For instance: ashes alone became his white cosmetic; a skull alone was the splendor of his stainless crest-ornament; and the very elephant hide, marked with yellow pigment at its edges, served as his silken garment. (32)

His very ashes were his white body-unguent and his sandalwood ointment; his skull alone was the splendor of his stainless crest and the beauty of his ear-ornament. Likewise, it was the elephant-hide itself, the very skin of a slain elephant...
The state of being a cotton cloth became that of fine silk; its borders, in the regions of the fringes,
were marked with a sign as if by yellow pigment— meaning it was beautiful with a pair of swans drawn in yellow pigment.
The reading *siṃhājina* (lion-skin) is indeed a corruption, because Bhava is clothed in elephant-hide;
as was stated previously:
"The bride’s silk garment marked with swans, and the elephant-hide raining drops of blood."
Thus [ends verse] 32.
That eye which shines from within the conch-shell, with its pure tawny pupil set deep inside, has become,
by virtue of her proximity, as if fashioned from yellow orpiment for the purpose of a decorative mark.

Between those two temples at the ends of the forehead, that third eye which shines and blazes—that very eye has become, in the sense of being present as a mark made of yellow orpiment (haritāla), produced upon the path of existence.
The meaning is that the eye on the forehead became a tilaka-mark of yellow orpiment. What kind of eye? One in which a pure, tawny pupil is situated within. || 33 ||
Just as the lords of serpents were about to become mere ornaments according to their respective positions,
so too did their bodies undergo transformation, yet they remained adorned with the splendor of the jewels upon their hoods.

As the lords of the nāgas, beginning with Vāsuki, fashioned various ornaments such as armlets and bracelets according to the dimensions of their arms and other limbs, their bodies alone underwent a transformation consisting of jewelry;
however, the splendor of their crest-jewels remained exactly as it was, assuming no other form, for jewels are by their very nature ornaments. (34)

Even by day, the moon—whose rays are emitted with a light that, due to its infancy, has not yet manifested its full characteristics—is constantly fixed upon the crest of Hara, whose crown is ever divided [by it]; so what need is there for him to seize the moon as a crest-jewel? 35.
Regarding the crest-jewel— the matter of the head-ornament— what is the point of grasping it, what is the respect shown?
The meaning is that he did not consider human bone to be anything other than a crest-jewel,
since [Śiva] always has his matted locks distinguished by a crown split by the moon.
Of what kind? Even during the day, its splendor is diffused by its rays;
likewise, because it consists of only a single digit, its characteristics are not manifested, and its stain is unapparent.
For this [moon] becomes fully manifest when it is complete. And therefore—
How could he whose head is adorned with such a moon as this require a crest-jewel? [The word] grahaṇa [here implies] respect. || 35 ||
Thus, the Creator— the sole source of wonders— by his power having established the prescribed rules for attire,
beheld himself reflected in the sword brought forward by the attendant Gaṇas, as if it were his own image fixed within it.
Then Hara beheld himself reflected in the surface of the mirror presented by the attendant standing at his side;
he was thus adorned with a completed arrangement of attire, having perfected the well-known rite of dressing, wondering, "What kind of majesty is this through my power?
For he is the sole source of wonder, the unique treasury of marvels, and the Creator, the fashioner.

Supporting himself on the arm of Nandin, he set out after mounting his bull— whose broad back was covered with a tiger skin and whose massive proportions were diminished by devotion to him— just as if he were ascending Mount Kailāsa.
Then the God, leaning upon the shoulder of Nandin, mounted the bull and departed.
Of what sort was it? Its broad back was covered and concealed by a tiger skin, that is, a leopard skin.

On account of its whiteness, it is imagined as follows: the meaning is that he went, having ascended Mount Kailāsa, which was like a mountain whose great dimensions had been contracted by his devotion to the Blessed One. || 37 ||
The divine Mothers, following after him, their ornaments swaying from the agitation of their own mounts,
made the sky appear like a bed of lotuses with their faces, pale as dust from the circles of radiance.
As the Mothers followed that god, they made the sky appear like a cluster of lotuses with their faces—
since their faces resemble lotuses— and with their halos,
which were white and tawny like pollen; for a lotus must indeed possess pollen.
What are they like? They are those whose ear-ornaments and crests (śekhara) move due to the agitation of their respective mounts, such as buffaloes, owls, and so forth. || 38 ||
And behind those women of golden luster, Kālī, adorned with skull ornaments,
shone forth like a row of dark clouds streaked with cranes, with a flash of lightning cast far ahead.
Among those mothers of golden hue, the mother known as Kālī, adorned with white skulls, shone and blazed forth.
Just as a row of black clouds, from which lightning has been cast far away at the front by a crane, appears beautiful—such was she; this is the meaning.
Because she is black (kāla) by virtue of being dark-colored, her name is Kālī; the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied here according to the rule for feminine gender based on color.
Then, the sound of auspicious musical instruments, raised by the hosts of gods led by the wielder of the trident (Śiva),
and penetrating the peaks of the celestial chariots, announced the time for service to the deities.
Then, the sound of auspicious musical instruments such as the *ḍhakkā*, produced by the attendants (*pramatha*) walking before Hara, announced the occasion for service to the gods.

For, pervading the peaks of the celestial chariots and heard from above, it surely indicated that the Lord had set out for the wedding; thus, [the gods] spoke of the time for service, saying, "Since this sound of musical instruments is heard, let us go before him. (40)
He describes that very service:
The thousand-rayed sun took up the new parasol fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ for him;
with his crown not far from its silken cloth, he shone as if bearing a stream of the Gaṅgā. (41)
Tvaṣṭṛ, the architect of the universe, took up for this god the parasol fashioned at that very moment,
which possessed a thousand rays;
and Hara shone with his head close to that silk cloth of the parasol, his crown near its edge.
Because of its whiteness, it is imagined as carrying a stream like the flow of the Gaṅgā; for he is indeed the bearer of the Gaṅgā. 41.
Then the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, having taken embodied form, waited upon the god with chowries,
appearing like two rivers entering the sea despite their change of form, yet still accompanied by their swans.
If the two rivers, Gaṅgā and Yamunā, were to serve that Lord, holding chowries and fanning him; and he,
because of his lack of desire, is imagined— even though there has been a reversal of form in the ocean-going [rivers]— [as being indifferent].
Even when the watery form has been abandoned, they appear as if accompanied by the flight of swans;
for in the case of rivers, which consist of flowing currents, there must be swans. And at that time, even though the water has become solidified and is no longer liquid, [the appearance remains].
Because of the presence of white chowries, there is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) that they are in contact with swans.
"The rivers flowing to the ocean assumed their form consisting of currents"—this is the aorist (luṅ) in the active voice (kartari). 42.
The first Creator and the Puruṣa himself, marked with the Śrīvatsa, approached him, magnifying his greatness with the word "Victory! as if kindling a fire with an oblation.

The first creator, Brahmā, and the Puruṣa Viṣṇu, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, approached that Lord face-to-face; by uttering the words "Victory! Victory! to this deity, they themselves increased his majesty, just as one increases the fire with an oblation.
For the one of variegated luster increases by means of the oblation; the Śrīvatsa is a particular mark upon the chest of Hari. 43.
One might ask: "Since Brahmā and Viṣṇu are the most excellent of all, how could they have uttered words such as 'victory' to Hara? To this he says:
"That single form was divided into three; their commonality consists only in being first and last."
Viṣṇu is the destroyer of that [Rudra], Hari is the creator of Viṣṇu, and at other times Brahmā is the creator of those two; thus, even those two are worthy of praise by the Creator.
That single form, characterized as Hara, Hari, and Hiraṇyagarbha, divided itself into three modes; having undergone division, it became "this is Hara," "this is Hari," and "this is Brahmā.
As it has been said: "Salutations to you, the one whose form is threefold.
And therefore, the state of being first or last, of being primary or secondary, and of being the worshiper or the object of worship among these three, is common—that is, shared—among them.
For instance, sometimes the Lord is the one to be praised and lauded by Viṣṇu; sometimes Hari [praises] him; sometimes Hari and Hara both praise Brahmā; and sometimes he praises them both. 44.

The world-protectors, headed by Puruhūta, their attire subdued by the manifestation of auspicious marks, signaled Nandin to grant them an audience; directed by him, they bowed with palms joined in reverence.
Śakra and the other lords of the directions bowed down to that god. Of what sort were they?
By the relinquishing—that is, the renouncing—of the auspicious marks such as the parasol and the chowrie, they were modestly attired, their ornaments laid aside.
Likewise, those by whom a sign or agreement had been made with the doorkeeper Nandi for the purpose of obtaining an audience—meaning, "Grant us an opportunity;
show us [the Lord]"—were then shown by that Vīraka. Having been shown, they joined their palms in reverence and paid homage to the Lord, the God. 45.
With a nod of his head he honored Brahmā, the lotus-born; with his speech, Hari; with a smile, the slayer of Vṛtra;
and with a mere glance, he honored all the gods without exception, according to their rank.
Then Dhūrjaṭi won over those gods, beginning with Viriñca, according to their rank and in accordance with their respective powers.
For he honored Brahmā by a nod of his head;
then Hari with a word; and Indra with a slight smile.
And he [subdued] the other gods merely by his glance. || 46 ||
He first bestowed upon him blessings of victory; then, with a smile, he said to the Seven Sages:
"Since this marriage sacrifice is now being performed, you shall be the officiating priests (*adhvaryu*) appointed by me beforehand. (47)

The benedictory invocation "Victory! Victory! was uttered by the sages, Vasiṣṭha and others, in the presence of the deities. Then, he said to them with a smile: "In this extensive and unfolding marriage ceremony, you were already appointed by me to the office of Adhvaryu priests."
Therefore, the sense is: "Go quickly from there. || 47 ||
While his heroic deeds against Tripura were being sung by masters of music led by Viśvāvasu,
the wearer of the crescent moon traversed the path that is difficult to cross due to the transformations of darkness.
Then the god traversed the road and proceeded on his way. Of what sort was he?
He was one whose marvelous deed—the burning of Tripura—was being loudly sung by those who were preeminent, namely the Gandharva king Viśvāvasu, and by other masters skilled in song.
His internal darkness—that is, the mental gloom—and its transformations such as dejection and the like did not [afflict him].
"Laṅghyaḥ" means not to be transgressed;
the meaning is that he is free from egoism even when beholding such greatness.
"Tārādhipakhaṇḍadhārī" means one who bears a digit of the moon. Here, by the word "tripura,"... [the reference is to] Śiva.
Its burning is perceived. 48.
A horse, moving with a playful gait and adorned with jingling golden bells, bore him along;
it repeatedly shook its long, thick mane as if its horns were stuck in mud due to striking the riverbank.
The bull Bāhu carried that Lord through the sky. Of what sort was he?
He moved with a playful gait, walking with grace;
likewise, he was one whose golden bells—small golden tinkling ornaments—were accompanied by sound.

Likewise, as he shook his horn—his tusk—as the clouds were densely woven together, it is imagined that he was shaking it because it had become stuck in mud from the impact against the riverbank during his sporting in the water;
for the shaking of the horn occurs due to its adherence to the mire. 49.
In a moment, he reached the city protected by the Lord of Mountains, which had not yet been subjected to the assault of enemies,
and which seemed to be drawn forward by golden threads— the falling glances of Shiva that clung to its front.
That lord reached the mountain of herbs (Oṣadhiprastha) in a mere moment—a place where no enemy attack had been encountered and which was not surrounded by foes.
It is imagined as if it were being drawn along by golden threads, caused by the glances from the third eye of Śiva fixed upon it ahead;
for otherwise, how could there be such a swift arrival from such a distance? This is the intended meaning.
However, with the instrumental case denoting the agent (*kartṛtṛtīyā*), it would be difficult to establish a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) without a second *iva* word.

In the phrase "as if with golden threads" (*suvarṇasūtrair iva*), this single *iva* has the sense of a simile (*upamā*) regarding the glances; it is not capable of conveying a poetic fancy either. Therefore, the employment of two *iva* words is logical.
Just as—
seizing the mass of darkness with its rays as if with fingers,
the moon seems to kiss the face of night, whose lotus-eyes are closed into buds.
But in the case of the instrumental case expressing causality, there is nothing that is not pleasing to the heart. || 50 ||
Near its edge, the god whose throat is deep blue, watched by the citizens with upturned faces out of curiosity,
descended from the path marked by his own arrow and reached the surface of the ground nearby.

The Blessed One went to the vicinity, that is, the neighborhood, of that mountain, descending from the sky along a path marked by his own arrows. Its status as being "marked by his own arrows" arose because he discharged them from the heavens at the time of the destruction of Tripura. Of what nature was he?
With a throat as dark blue as a dense cloud, his neck was like the color of a rain-cloud;
thus he was gazed upon by the citizens with faces upturned in curiosity.
The sovereign of mountains, delighted by their arrival, went out to meet him with throngs of elephants mounted by his powerful kinsmen,
as if with his own mountain ridges covered in blossoming trees.
The Lord of the Mountain went out to meet that Lord [Śiva] as he emerged before him. With what?
With elephant-herds mounted by his swelling kinsmen, which were like his own flanks with their blossoming trees.
Of what nature was he? Delighted and overjoyed by the arrival of the Blessed One. 52.
Both hosts— the gods and the mountain-dwellers— met at the city gate whose cover had been lifted,
their far-reaching clamor like two torrents of water breaking through a single dam.

Those two hosts of gods and demons met and joined together at the city gate, whose cover was lifted and whose door-panels were swung open. Like what? Like two floods of water meeting when a common embankment between them has been broken and washed away.
The two come together. "A bridge" is the simile for the door.
"With sounds spreading afar" is an epithet applied to both. That by which something is covered or shut is a "covering," namely, a door-panel (kavāṭa). || 53 ||
The mountain became filled with shame after being saluted by Hara, who is worshipped by the three worlds;
for previously, his head had been so deeply bowed by the mountain's own greatness that he was not even aware of it.
Because he had previously been saluted by Hara, who is worshipped by the three worlds, the Lord of the Mountains felt ashamed;
though the Lord of All was the first to bow,
the Mountain did not perceive— that is, did not recognize— that his own head had been bent down so far as to be completely bowed.
Why? Because of his *mahiman*—his preeminent power.

For even though it was performed later, the agent considers how great the salutation is toward one who is most exalted. Alternatively, since the Blessed One stands above all, while the worlds are situated below, it should be understood here, as before, that [the head] of oneself [is directed] downward.
But it is not by mere prostration alone;
for by its very greatness, everything has already been bowed down by the Blessed One.
In this view, the word "by greatness" does not depend upon an act of bowing.
The instrumental case is used here in the sense of the agent; therefore, he did not perceive this.
For had he perceived it, he would not have been ashamed, because he was constantly bowing down. 54.

With the beauty of his face blooming from the joy of the union, he took the lead before his father-in-law and led him into the magnificent palace, where flowers were strewn up to the ankles along the paths of the market stalls.
Out of affection for his son-in-law, Himavat, having granted him the honor of leading the way, led Śrīkaṇṭha into his own palace—

a residence that was prosperous, flourishing, and overflowing with wealth, where flowers were strewn upon the market paths and the thoroughfares of the shops. (In the reading *antare*, it means "in between" or "within.")
Within the city, there are main roads and side streets. || 55 ||
At that moment, in the palace rows of the beautiful women of the city who were longing for the sight of the Lord, there occurred such activities as these, having abandoned all other duties. 56.

Then, at that very moment, upon the arrival of the great king, the various activities and gestures of the city women—who, longing for a glimpse of the bridegroom, had abandoned all other tasks—were as follows on the rooftops of the rows of palaces: 56.
To the question "How so?", he says:

By one woman who was suddenly rushing toward the path of light, her mass of hair—its garlands already disgorged by the untying—was not even noticed as a kinsman; though held back by her hand, it was not secured. (57)
Suddenly, upon perceiving the path of light, a certain city-dwelling woman who had gone to the window did not even think of,
nor was she even prompted to, bind her mass of hair; let that be— she did not even [do so] with her hand.

"Obstructed" means not being held back. Therefore, the meaning is that where there is a state of non-momentariness due solely to the haste of the obstruction itself, any discussion of "binding" is utterly out of place.
Because of the unwinding [of the hair], the garland has been cast off as its binding has been released; this is because it was situated within [the hair].

A "garland" (*mālya*) is a collection of garlands (*mālā*). By the rule *pāśādibhyo yaḥ*, the suffix *ya* is applied. The words *hasta*, *pakṣa*, and *pāśa* denote excellence when referring to hair. (57)
A certain woman, having cast aside her foot— still wet with red lac— as it was being held by her maid,
abandoned her graceful gait and left a trail marked by red dye from the window as she went.

A certain woman, having flung down at the window the tip of her foot—upon which a liquid dye held by a *sairandhrī* (maid) had been applied and which was still wet with lac—abandoned her graceful gait and left a trail marked by the juice of the *yāvaka* dye.
As for the term "agra-pāda" (the tip of the foot), it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇa-samāsa*) based on the non-difference between the quality and the possessor of the quality;
however, according to the alternative view that they are distinct, it would be a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) of "pāda-agra" and so forth.
Or it is a locative compound (saptamīsamāsa), meaning "the foot at the front" (*agre pādaḥ*), thus *agrapādaḥ*. || 58 ||
Having adorned her right eye with collyrium, another woman, whose left eye was thus deprived of it,
approached the window in that very same manner, still carrying the applicator.
Another woman, having applied collyrium to her right eye but not applying it to the left, approached the window while holding a brush in her hand and maintaining that same playful gait.
A *vātāyana* (window) is so called because the wind (*vāta*) passes through it. 59.
Another woman, her gaze directed through the lattice window, did not fasten her waist-knot which had loosened during her departure;
she stood there holding up her garment with a hand whose brilliance was enhanced by the ornament resting upon her navel.
Another woman, out of haste as she was departing, did not fasten her loosened girdle because her eyes were fixed through the opening of the window;
she simply stood there, holding her garment in her hand. Consequently, the luster of her waistband appeared to have entered into her navel.
At that moment, as a certain woman rose quickly with her waistband only half-fastened, it slipped at every step;
the girdle remained as nothing more than a thread fastened to the base of her big toe.
And as another woman rose up in haste at that moment, her girdle became nothing more than a single thread remaining at the base of her big toe;
for it had been half-filled and woven,
and thus, slipping away step by step, she was divested of her ornaments.
A bad omen is a deposit or a treasure that has been poorly placed; it is a "badly deposited" (durnimita) thing that is wasting away.
For this very reason, there remains only a mere thread [of existence]. 61.

With their faces filled with the fragrance of wine, the windows— whose interiors were pervaded by those women of intense curiosity and whose flickering eyes were like bees— became as if adorned with thousand-petaled lotuses.

Then, the windows, filled with the faces of those women who were full of intense curiosity, became as if adorned with lotuses—because their faces resembled lotuses. He expresses that very similarity: "by those whose interior or essence was the fragrance of wine (*āsava*), that is, the scent of liquor."
By those whose very eyes, flickering like bees, were the bees themselves.
Drinking him in with their eyes as his sole object of vision, the women were unaware of other sensory objects;
for at that time, the functioning of their remaining senses had entered, as it were, entirely into their eyes.
(63) Thus, the city-dwellers, drinking him in with their glances because of his extreme beauty, were unaware of—and did not even perceive—other sensory objects such as sound and the like.
For, because their minds are directed toward him, they see nothing else, hear nothing, smell nothing, nor experience touch.
