Therefore, it is inferred: surely at that time, the function—the activity such as hearing—of their remaining senses, including the ears and so forth, has entered entirely and completely into the eyes alone, just as if they were the eyes themselves.
The sense is that it is logical for the rest of the physical substratum to become as if empty.
The word *jajñuḥ* is the perfect (liṭ) form of the root *jñā* (to know). And that which is singular and visible is "the single visible" (*ekadṛśya*). || 63 ||
It is fitting that this difficult penance was performed for his sake even by the delicate Aparṇā;
for what woman would not consider herself successful if she were to obtain even servitude from him, let alone a bed upon his lap? (64)
If the Creator had not joined this pair, whose forms were mutually desirable to one another,
then his effort in fashioning their beauty would have been in vain.
Surely his body was not consumed by the god of the flower-bow out of rising wrath;
rather, I think that Kāma himself abandoned his own form upon beholding this god with shame.
Having fortunately obtained this alliance with the Lord as requested by his heart's desire,
the King of Mountains will, O friend, exalt his head— already lofty from supporting the earth— to an even greater height.
Thus, listening to the ear-pleasing stories of the women sporting on the mountain of herbs,
the three-eyed god reached the abode of Himālaya, where handfuls of parched grain were ground into powder by their armlets.
A group of verses (kulakam).

Hearing such words from the ladies who were the mistresses of the city on the lord of mountains—words that brought delight to their ears—the Blessed One reached his father-in-law’s residence. At the time of entry, women scatter parched grain as an auspicious offering; these grains, crushed and ground by the mutual clashing of armlets and bracelets upon his arms, formed a fine powder upon his webbed hands.
"What kind of talk is this? he asks, and says "In this place," and so forth.
That asceticism which was performed by Aparṇā—though she is Umā and exceedingly delicate—is appropriate in this place;
for even a woman who has attained the status of a servant to this god would have her purpose fulfilled.
How much more so their dwelling upon one another's laps? Regarding the phrase "mutually" and so forth:

if the Creator had not joined this pair together, then his labor in fashioning the excellence of beauty in this couple would have been in vain and fruitless, due to their being brought together with one another who are not suited to each other. Of what nature is this pair?

Their mutual splendor was desirable to one another, and their exceeding loveliness was such that he desired her, thinking, "She is delightful," and she too desired him, thinking, "This bridegroom is excellent.

Since there is no occurrence of a past action contrary to expectation (kriyātipatti), the use of the conditional (lṛṅ) here is difficult to justify. [The verse continues with] "na nūnam" and so forth.

It is certain that this [Lord Śiva], though enraged and possessed by rising fury, did not reduce the body of Smara to ashes; rather, upon beholding this Lord endowed with such preeminent beauty, Kāma himself, out of shame, abandoned his own body, thinking, "Alas! I have been defeated by this excellence of form.
The word *vrīḍā* (shame) applies to both men and women. As for the word *anena* (by him): [it refers to the Lord].

Another friend says to her: "O dear friend, having obtained this alliance with this divine lord—which was the object of her heart's desire—the Lord of Mountains will now hold his head even higher, though it is already elevated by the protection of the earth.
For being the son-in-law of the Lord of All is indeed a cause for supreme exaltation.
The indeclinable *diṣṭyā* is used here in the sense of joy.
Listening to such stories, the Three-eyed Lord reached his abode on Himālaya;
[the absence of the nasalization (ṇatva) in *trinetratrinayana* etc. is due to the rule *kṣumnādi*.]
Meanwhile, the moon-crested Lord reached the royal highway, which was crowded with banners and adorned with lofty arches;
he made the pinnacles of the palaces appear with a doubled luster, as if bathed in moonlight even during the day.

While the women of the city were speaking thus, the moon-crested Lord reached the royal highway, making even the palace rooftops whiter still by bathing them in moonlight. Of what sort was the royal road? It was crowded with banners and thick with victory flags.
That place where the archways were raised high is called "Uttoraṇa. || 69 ||
Then, having descended with the hand of Acyuta supporting him— like the sun from an autumn cloud—
he entered the inner courtyards of the mountain king, which had previously been traversed by the lotus-seated Brahmā.
Then Śiva, taking hold of Hari’s hand, entered the seven enclosures of Himavat previously traversed by Brahmā. Having done what?
Having descended from the bull (ukṣan). From what, like whom? He says: just as the sun (dīdhitimat), possessing rays, descends from a white autumnal cloud.
Then the gods, headed by Indra, and the supreme ṛṣis led by the Seven Sages,
along with their hosts, approached the mountain-dweller, just as those who seek the highest goal approach a praiseworthy undertaking.
Following behind the Blessed One, the gods, sages, and attendants went toward and entered the abode of Himālaya;
for those who seek the highest goal pursue excellent things as the very means to their renown. Indeed, an illustrious deed undertaken by auspicious persons is certain to succeed.
The word *anvak* means "afterwards. || 71 ||
There, the Lord, being worthy of a seat, accepted as was fitting a jewel, an offering of water (arghya), and honeyed products of the cow;
and he accepted all these, which were not devoid of mantras, upon two new silk cloths brought by the mountain-dweller.

There, seated upon his throne in the father-in-law’s house, the Blessed One accepted and took all of this— without it being devoid of mantras— the water for the *arghya* offering accompanied by jewels given by the Lord of Mountains (*adrinātha*), as well as the *madhuparka* consisting of cow's products and honey from bees; and a pair of brand-new silk garments (*dugūla*).

*Argha* means worship; water for that purpose is *arghya*. [The suffix] *-ya* is applied according to the rule "after *pāda* and *argha*. *Mantravandhya* means void or empty of mantra; thus, it is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*).
*Yathāvat* has the sense of "according to rule" (*vidhivat*) and serves as an adjective qualifying the initiation (*upanayana*).
"But [the phrase] 'not barren of counsel' refers to the act of receiving. || 72 ||
Clad in a linen garment, he was led by humble guards of the inner apartments to the presence of his bride,
just as the ocean, with its rows of white foam, is led by the new rays of the moon to the edge of the shore.
Clad in a fine woolen garment and white silk raiment, that bridegroom was led with humility by the chamberlains and guards of the inner apartments into the presence of Umā;
he was led there just as the ocean, its surface displaying rows of fresh foam, is led to the shore by the rising rays of the moon,
owing to the joy they evoke.

The ocean was the comparison for Hara; the moonbeams were the comparison for Gaurī’s inner apartments; and the mass of foam was the comparison for the silken garments of the lords of those quarters—thus [the comparisons] function as the objects of the action. 73.
With the radiance of that maiden’s moon-like face, Śiva’s lotus-eyes blossomed and the waters of his heart became serene; being united with her, he became like the world at the arrival of autumn.
United with her, who possessed the luster of the full moon’s face, Maheśvara became one whose lotus-eyes blossomed and whose waters of consciousness grew serene.
The meaning is that there was an expansion in both his eyes and his mind.
Just as the world, when joined with the beauty of a river possessing the brilliance of the waxing moon, becomes clear-watered and filled with blooming night-lotuses.
For then the water becomes clear, the night-lotuses bloom, and the moon becomes radiant. || 74 ||
In their meditative absorptions,
their eyes— timid, slightly fixed and withdrawn, yet longing for one another— suddenly experienced the restraint of shame.

At that moment, at the time of their union, the eyes of those two deities, longing for one another, experienced a constraint of shame—that is, they became overwhelmed with bashfulness. Of what sort? During the consummations—the mutual attainments—they were timid, unsteady, and impossible to behold. Then, having been somewhat composed, cast toward the corners of the eyes, they were immediately withdrawn and turned back by shame. And it was this very [shame] that they attained as a charming "constraint" (hrīyantraṇā); such is an alternative reading.
They attained; they reached. || 75 ||
The Eight-formed Lord (Śiva) took her hand, which was brought forward with the weight of a mountain and possessed copper-colored fingers;
it was like the first sprout of Smara, whose body was hidden in the form of Umā, taken while he was still apprehensive.
The bridegroom took the hand of that bride, whose fingers were joined with those of Himavat;
because of its coppery hue,
it was imagined to be like the first sprout of Madana, whose body was concealed in the form of Umā— that is, in the form of Gaurī.
For it must arise from desire;
and prior to its arising, there occurs the emergence of a copper-colored sprout.
A thrill of horripilation appeared on Umā, and the bull-bannered god’s fingers became moist with sweat;
by the joining of their hands, the activity of the God of Love was, as it were, equally divided between them.

By the power of the touch of her hand, Gaurī’s hair stood on end, while the bull-bannered god (Śiva) became one whose hand-branches were frozen with cold. Therefore, it is figuratively imagined: through the contact of their hands, the activity of the Mind-born (Kāma) has been, as it were, equally divided between the two.
Sweating, horripilation, and so forth are functions of desire, because they arise under its influence. || 77 ||

When another bride and groom, having already performed the ceremony of joining hands, attain supreme beauty through the presence of these two at that time—tell me, what can be said of the glory of that couple? 78.
Furthermore, at the time of marriage, even another woman or maiden flourishes—that is, attains—excellent splendor due to the presence of this couple, Gaurī and Śiva.
How can poets describe the beauty of that pair?
For when the wedding splendor of another arises through their entry [into the scene], the natural radiance of those two must necessarily be preeminent.
The entire class of *dvandva* compounds ending in "bride and groom" (*vadhūvara*) may optionally be treated as a singular. || 78 ||
Having led the couple three times around the fire, the priest, while their eyes were closed by the touch of the tips of each other's hands,
caused the bride to cast the parched grain into that flame of kindled fuel.

That priest, Brahmā, having led the bride and groom—the couple—three times around the fire, circumambulated them; thereafter, he had Gaurī alone cast the parched grain (*lāja*) into the fire whose flames were flickering.
The couple, their eyes closed out of modesty due to the experience of pleasure from the touch of the tips of his hands, had their eyes contracted. "The couple" is the object of the action.
*Pariṇaya* means circumambulation; here, the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is to be understood.
Otherwise, because the agents would be different, the suffix -ktvā would be difficult to obtain. || 79 ||
Following her teacher’s instruction, she brought the fragrant smoke of the parched grain from her joined palms to her face;
its crest, gliding over her cheek, for a moment attained the state of an ear-lotus.
By the command of Viriñca, that bride took the handful of parched grain and smoke toward her face,
for it was there that the fragrance, possessing a desirable scent, was to be smelled.
And that smoke, because its crest spread across her cheeks, momentarily assumed the likeness of blue lotuses upon her ears.
Because it resembles the petal of a blue water-lily. || 80 ||

From the inhalation of the ritual smoke, the bride’s face became such that the lines of her cheeks were slightly moist and reddened, the black collyrium on her eyes was smudged by her sighs, and the barley-ear ornaments grew dull.
Her face became thus from the mere inhalation of the smoke of the ritual:
of what sort? Where the cheeks were slightly moist and reddened;
and where the application of collyrium to the eyes was becoming loose and spreading.
Likewise, where the barley sprout is withered;
the practice of perceiving smoke [as a sign] arises from the performance of worldly custom. || 81 ||
The twice-born spoke to the bride: "O child, for you alone is the fire the witness from the outset regarding this marriage;
you must practice dharma together with your husband Śiva, free from all hesitation. (82)
Then the twice-born Brahmā said to Gaurī: "What [is your intention]? He said: "Together with your husband, the Lord, you must practice dharma without hesitation, having abandoned all deliberation;
for the performance of dharma together is the vow of a virtuous woman. And in this marriage—"
This Agni is your first witness; therefore, it is not fitting for you to deviate from this word—this is the sense.
*Caraṇa* means conduct (*caryā*). [The suffix] *yat* is applied according to the rule *gada-mada-cara-yamaśca*.
Having turned her ear toward him, Bhavānī drank in those words of the Guru until their conclusion,
just as the earth first drinks the rain from Indra when parched by the intense heat of the summer season.
Gaurī drank that word of Brahmā, stretching her ears to the very edges of her eyes;
she heard it and accepted it, just as the earth drinks the first rain from the clouds during the summer season when the sun’s rays are scorching.
The narration of great joy. 83.
Urged by her husband Dhruva to look at Dhruva, she—having raised her face, though her throat was choked with shame—somehow said, "He is seen. (84)

Then, urged by her eternal husband Dhruva to inquire about the appearance of the star Dhruvatārā, she raised her face and, with her throat choked by bashfulness, said with difficulty, "He has been seen.
For such indeed is the custom of the world. 84.
Thus, having performed the rites of marriage according to the prescribed rules by the officiating priest,
the two parents of all creatures bowed down to the Grandfather seated upon his lotus throne.

Then those two lords, having been instructed in the procedure for marriage by the family priest—a Brāhmaṇa who was conversant with the customs of the wedding season—according to the aforementioned rite, immediately thereafter paid homage to Brahmā, whose seat is the lotus.

Both the mother and the father are "the parents"; the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*) is established because the root *nam* (to bow) is included among the roots that govern the dative case, though the accusative is more appropriate here. 85.
"The bride was congratulated by the Creator with the words, 'O auspicious one, may you give birth to heroes.
Though he was the Lord of Speech, he remained silent regarding this blessing before the Eight-formed One (Śiva), as his thoughts were absorbed in contemplation. (86)
Then Gaurī was greeted and blessed by the prostrating Creator.
He said: "O blessed lady, may you give birth to a hero; may you have a valiant son.
For even Vāgīśvara himself, though he be such, is to be desired and wished for in Maheśvara."
He became motionless in thought: "What can I hope for? The sense is that, because of his perfection, there was nothing left to be hoped for. || 86 ||

Having first reached the sacrificial altar with its four sides prepared for the ritual service, the husband and wife, seated upon golden thrones, then experienced the worldly rite of scattering moist grains of parched rice.
Then the bride and groom,
having approached the square altar-platform strewn with heaps of flowers, performed the rite of placing moist unhusked rice grains and partook of the offering of raw barley;
for that which is desired in the world must be performed according to worldly custom.

For it is the custom of the world that when a wedding has been successfully completed, food should be offered by the Brahmins, kinsmen, and widows with moist hands; you, however, are here concerned with the pressing matter of the marriage ceremony itself.
That which is desired must be sought; it is an indispensable duty. || 87 ||
Above them, Lakṣmī held a lotus-umbrella with a long stalk, its beauty enhanced by clusters of water-drops hanging from the edges of its petals like a net of pearls.

Upon the heads of Gauri and Ishvara, Kamalāsana himself held and bore a lotus as a parasol; what kind of parasol? One whose beauty of pearl-strings was surpassed by the clusters of water-drops clinging to its petals.
Likewise, the staff must belong to the same category as the umbrella;
for the umbrella should indeed be accompanied by a staff made of pearls. 88.

And Sarasvatī extolled that couple with two kinds of speech: she praised the bridegroom, the most excellent of men, with language purified by grammatical refinement, and the bride with language whose composition was easy to grasp. (89)
Sarasvatī also praised that couple—that pair—with a twofold literary composition (*vāṅmaya*).
Regarding this very division, he says: she praised the bridegroom with refined Sanskrit purified by grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*), but the bride with ease, without difficulty.

"By him"—meaning by one whose grasp, understanding, connection, and composition are [ordinary], that is, by a common person; for that is easily understood, being appropriate for the praise of a young woman.
"Vareṇya" means excellent or superior. "Vāṅmaya" is a derivative of speech (vāc), meaning prose and verse. || 89 ||

For a moment, they beheld the first performance of the Apsarases, in which the distinctions of the emotional modes were manifested through the transitions, the passion was fixed upon various sentiments, and the graceful movements of the limbs were displayed.
The couple beheld— that is, they gazed upon— the performance, the enactment, the drama, which was the primordial, preeminent, and ancient one, employed by the celestial nymphs;
it was characterized by the junctures known as the opening (mukha), the development (pratimukha), the middle (garbha), the pause (vimarśa), and the conclusion (nirvahaṇa).
In which the distinction among the dramatic styles (vṛtti)—namely the Sāttvikī, Ārabhaṭī, Kaiśikī, and Bhāratī—is manifested or made manifest;

for it is through the division of junctures (sandhi) that the styles find their place therein. Likewise, regarding the various sentiments (rasa), such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and others, within those specific aesthetic flavors.
Where passion remains fixed and bound, meaning that even when shifting to another sentiment (*rasa*), a state of detachment has not arisen;
where there is graceful and delicate movement of the limbs, that is dance (*nṛtta*).

Indeed, dance is of two kinds, distinguished as *komala* (tender) and *uddhata* (vigorous). There are nine aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*) born of emotional states (*bhāvas*): the erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, the furious, the comic, the terrifying, the pathetic, the marvelous, and the tranquil.
At the end of that [period], the gods, bowing with their joined palms pressed against their crowns before the consort of Hara’s head,
requested the service of the five-arrowed god, whose body had been restored at the conclusion of his curse.

Then, at the conclusion of that dance, at the end of the performance, all the gods prostrated themselves on the ground and requested service from Bhava, whose arrows are peerless, now that he had completed his marriage. They entreated him, their palms joined in reverence with their fingers resting upon their crowns.
Of what kind was Kama? He who had been regained at the end of the curse.
Of him who was thus characterized by having a physical form—that is, a body—as it has been said:
"When he shall marry Pārvatī," and so forth;
the Blessed One, free from anger, permitted his activity even with respect to his own self through arrows.
Indeed, a request made at the proper time by those who know the right timing attains success with their masters. || 92 ||
Then the God, having been entreated by the gods and being free from all opposition, consented—that is, he accepted—the falling of arrows even upon his own body for the sake of Kāma;
for a petition made at the proper time succeeds with lords, and that very moment was the right occasion because [the God] had already performed his marriage. 92.

Thereafter, having bowed down according to the prescribed rites, the Lord of the Mountain King offered separate honors with jewels to the lords of the three worlds, each according to their preeminence, as presented by Menā.

Thereafter, the Lord of the Mountains, Himālaya, performed for each of the gods, beginning with Śakra, according to their rank—that is, according to who was most preeminent—a separate worship consisting of offerings of jewels and precious objects brought by Menā; he did so according to rule, meaning after first bowing down, that is, after performing a prostration. This is to say, "having propitiated them. 93.
Then, having dismissed those hosts of gods, the moon-crested Lord took the daughter of the mountain king by the hand,
which was graced by the beauty of the devotion shown in protecting the golden pitcher.
Having prepared a bed upon the bare ground, he went to the chamber of auspicious rites. || 94 ||

Then Śaśiśekhara, having sent those hosts of celestial beings to his own abode and supporting the daughter of the Mountain King with his hand, went to and entered the chamber of curiosities, the auspicious dwelling place.
Of what sort was it?

It was endowed with splendors and radiance produced by golden jars—vessels of gold—and by artistic arrangements made of gems and medicinal herbs, as well as by the decorative patterns formed from flowers, conch shells, and colored powders;
likewise, it possessed a bed prepared upon the ground rather than on a couch or similar furniture, because he had been sleeping on the floor for three or seven nights. 94.
There, the Lord somehow managed to make Gaurī— who was adorned with the ornament of the shame of her recent marriage—
lower her face, even though she had been granted permission by her bed-friends to speak. He did so by raising it up himself.
He caused a secret laughter by means of the distortions of his face as he sportively crushed [them]. || 95 ||
There, in that bedchamber, the Three-eyed Lord made his beloved laugh with deep and manifest mirth through the facial contortions of his attendants, the Pramathas;
for he somehow managed to speak even to those female friends who were lying on the bed, though they were full of confidence,
and thus, even when addressed, she remained overcome with bashfulness.

The meaning is that the Lord did not mix his speech with the hosts who had deformed appearances; rather, having exhorted them, saying, "Make contortions of the face for the sake of manifesting a smile," he laughed with them.
Of what sort was she? She was one who was turning her face away from that Hara—shifting it elsewhere—as its upward-lifting or raising had been performed by him;
for that very shame or modesty which arises from a new marriage...
"She whose ornament it is"—referring to her who possesses that [ornament]. Here, the *mālinī* meter is employed in both verses.
Thus ends the seventh canto in the commentary on the *Kumārasambhava* composed by Vallabhadeva, the son of Ānandadeva.

The eighth canto. Immediately following the rite of joining hands, the daughter of the King of Mountains experienced a charming pleasure of longing for love toward Hara, arising from her being seized by both emotion and timidity.
Then, after Pārvatī had taken Śiva’s hand in marriage, her body experienced a state of blissful languor due to the longing of desire—that is, the yearning of the god of love.
Why was this so?
Because of the simultaneous presence, or rather the coexistence, of both emotion and trepidation—namely, joy and fear.
And in that regard, there is a natural simile: [her] timidity arises from being newly married. In this canto, the Rathoddhatā metre is employed. || 1 ||
Though addressed, she gave no reply; she desired to depart while clutching her garment;
she attended the couch with her face turned away—yet even so, she was for the pleasure of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
For the sake of engaging in conversation, Gaurī, though she was in such a state, did not offer a reply even when addressed; with her garment clinging to her, she desired— that is,
longed— to go to the bed.
Though she served him with her face turned away, he served her in return;

nevertheless, even while acting thus, she became a source of delight for Soma, the wielder of the Pināka bow, Śiva—for such behavior is indeed the cause of passion on the bed for young brides. || 2 ||
While she lay there in feigned sleep, Pārvatī turned her face toward him out of curiosity;
as her eye opened with a smile at her beloved, it closed again, struck as if by lightning.
While he lay there under a pretext— that is, while he was asleep— that Pārvatī Kātyāyanī,
out of curiosity, thinking "I shall look at him," cast her eye toward his face; and having done so, she smiled with a gentle laugh.
Like a flash of lightning, she struck down, struck, and utterly dispelled that which had been darkened, covering it over—when?
When her beloved opened his eyes with a smile; the meaning is that she did so while he was wide-eyed and awake. || 3 ||
The hand of Śaṅkara, placed upon her navel, was obstructed by her trembling body;
meanwhile, her hips themselves became far removed from the fastening of her garment due to its being loosened.

By that Gaurī, Śiva’s hand was placed upon her navel and pressed against the expanse of her hips; thus it was held fast. Then, from the touch of her beloved’s hand, her hips—the region of her waist—themselves became so exceedingly distended that the knot of her lower garment loosened and the binding of her skirt slackened of its own accord.

"Thus, O Ālī, Śaṅkara should be enjoyed in secret once your timidity has been overcome"—this was the advice given by her friends, but she, being distraught, did not remember it while her beloved stood before her. 5.
"O friend Āli, having restrained your timidity— that is, casting aside fear— you must thus win over your beloved in private upon the bed. "Thus"—
that method which was instructed by them must also be understood by her in the presence of her beloved.
It was not remembered. || 5 ||
Although the subject was non-existent, the Command of Ananga (Kāma), intent on initiating a conversation, addressed her with a question;
Pārvatī, accepting it with a glance, gave an answer consisting of a nod of her head.
Seeing her beloved asking [a question], Pārvatī gave him an answer by grasping his head with her gaze and by nodding, but not with words, out of modesty—
even though he was addicted to questioning even regarding matters that were unreal or useless.
For the purpose of initiating conversation, she asked him, "Let my discourse proceed with her";
but she (the other woman) answered him by means of a gesture. || 6 ||
Having covered his two eyes with her two palms and having her garment snatched away,
she stood there in secret, distressed by her futile efforts, while he gazed at her with the eye on his forehead.

Although she covered the pair of eyes of her beloved Hara with both hands because he had stripped her of her garments in secret, she became distressed by her futile efforts and agitated by her fruitless exertion;
for while he was looking at his third eye, she could not [see it]. Indeed, she could not.
That is ceased. || 7 ||
In their kisses, they omitted the drinking of the lower lip; in their embraces, their hands were restrained by intoxication;
though their passion was somewhat subdued, the beloved’s pleasure remained difficult for the lord to repay.

That beloved husband’s pleasure with his bride—the act of sexual union with his newly wedded wife—was performed even though it frustrated the god of love (Kāma) due to its lack of reciprocity; yet it was not unknown [to her], for she was adorned solely by her modesty.

He describes that very act as one where a reciprocal response was difficult to obtain: "In kisses, devoid of the offering of the lower lip; in merciless embraces, with hands withdrawn and arms indifferent. For when drinking from the beloved's lip, one should perform a throat-embrace, and in an embrace, one should offer a counter-kiss and so forth; however, because she was a newly wedded bride, she did not do so.

Pārvatī could endure only those things done by her beloved with tenderness—the seizing of her face that left her lower lip uninjured, the nail-marks that bore no scars, and the love-making that was compassionate; she could not endure anything else.

Gaurī endured that passionate embrace performed by her beloved which involved drinking from her mouth with unbiting lips, scratching with fingernails without leaving wounds, and other acts of lovemaking that were compassionate and free from blows such as striking with the fists;
she did not endure the other kind, which was the opposite—harsh. 9.

At the time of dawn, she did not allow her circle of friends, who were eager to question her about the events of the night, to be free from curiosity; out of modesty, she refrained from speaking, yet she was inwardly anxious to tell them.

At the time of dawn, that Gaurī did not cause the people who were reclining to cease their nighttime activities—desiring to ask about them—and she made them free from curiosity and devoid of eagerness; yet, in her heart, she hastened to tell those things, she made haste, meaning she desired to speak. For such indeed is the nature of a newlywed bride.
And beholding her reflection in the mirror while her lover sat behind her watching her enjoyment, what things did she not do out of shame? 11.

That queen, having begun to look into the mirror at the marks of her lover’s enjoyment, such as the bite on her lip, saw the reflection of her own face—cast into the nearby mirror—of her beloved who was seated secretly behind her; and out of modesty, what indescribable things did she not do?
For the reflection is near to the original form.
The word "ca" (and) serves as a conjunction in relation to what precedes it, and so it is used elsewhere as well. 11.
Seeing her whose youth had been enjoyed by Nīlakaṇṭha, the mother took heart;
for, through their devotion to their husband, women of the harem dispel their mother's mental grief.
Then Menā, beholding her daughter whose youth had been enjoyed by Hara, was comforted and rejoiced;
for well-dressed women, by being pleasing to the hearts of their mothers, remove their sorrow.
The word "samāśvasat" (was comforted) is in the imperfect tense.
After some days, by a certain means, her beloved was made to stand still by Śiva;
and she, gradually becoming aware of the essence of love, slowly abandoned her habitual aversion to the pain of sexual union.
For several days, Gaurī was somehow with great difficulty made to take her place—that is, she was made to remain—by Sthāṇu, who is Bhava;
she was made to feel confidence.
Immediately thereafter, because she experienced the essence of love, she gradually abandoned her disposition toward pain and her painful nature in the matter of sexual union.
The meaning is that he experienced sexual pleasure by virtue of the enjoyment of sensual desires.
"Padam" refers to stability in one's position. "Akāryatā" is derived from the causative form (ṇyanta) in the sense of the object (karman). || 13 ||
He describes her reluctance to abandon her habitual modesty:

She embraced her beloved, pressing him close to her breast; she did not lift up his face when he requested it, and she loosely held back his hand as it reached out to loosen the knot of her girdle. (14)
Having pressed him firmly against her as if he were a beloved fruit squeezed in her arms, she embraced him tightly;
and when he took hold of her face for a kiss, she did not turn it away.
When he reached for her girdle, entreated her for her waist-band, and sought to strip the garment from her hips, she checked the movement of her lover’s hand with her own.
Previously, however, it was exactly the opposite; at that time, it had become like this.

In just a few days, their love— which was indicated by gestures, which had never witnessed any unpleasantness, which was full of endearments, and which was anxious at the thought of even momentary separation— became firmly rooted and mutually dependent.
Then, after only a few days had passed, such love as this became firmly rooted between that couple, and an exceedingly intense passion arose.
Of what kind was it?
It was a *hāva*, which is a particular gesture indicative of the intentions of the heart. || 15 ||
The bride delighted in that groom who was her equal, and the groom likewise in her;
for the Jahnavi never departs from the ocean, and he too finds his sole satisfaction in the taste of her waters.
In whatever manner she loved that excellent husband who was worthy of herself, in that very same way he also loved her as his wife; this describes their mutual affection.
He confirms this very point with an illustration:
"For the Jāhnavī never departs from the ocean."
The Gaṅgā does not enter [the ocean] except for the sea;
that ocean, moreover, has its sole satisfaction and exhilaration from the flow of the water from her mouth— the Jāhnavī—
for no other river than the Gaṅgā is capable of filling it.
For a couple who are in love, the giving of mutual pleasure is their bliss;
otherwise, the state of being separated from one another would be appropriate.
The form *anvarajyata* is used in the active sense (the agent). 16.
Having sought refuge in secret with Śaṅkara, who was instructing her in the arts of love,
that young woman offered as her teacher’s fee precisely that proficiency she had learned from him.

The skill in women—that proficiency in the arts of love which was learned and practiced by her after becoming a disciple of Hara, the instructor in the acts of dalliance—was itself offered as the preceptor’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā) to Hara; for she employed that very skill against him. It is a rule that a pupil must give a fee to the teacher.
With her sprout-like hands trembling from the pain,
Ambikā momentarily cooled her bitten lower lip with the cool fragment of the moon upon the head of the Wielder of the Trident.

This describes the conduct of a mature woman (prauḍhā): Gaurī first bit her lower lip with her beloved's [teeth], then, when it was wounded, she released it and cooled it with the cool crescent moon on Śiva’s head; thus she comforted it as it regained its breath.
The phrase "with hands like tender sprouts shaken" (vidhūtahastapallavā) is an epithet for Ambikā, meaning one whose sprout-like hands were trembling due to the pain caused by that biting of the lip.
Even Śaṅkara gave his forehead-eye, defiled by the powder from Gaurī’s hair during their kiss,
to the breath from Pārvatī’s mouth, which possessed the fragrance of a blooming lotus.

Not only did Śiva cool Gaurī’s lip with the moon, but he also offered his third eye— tormented by the powder from her hair and the grind of sandalwood and other unguents due to the force of the kiss— to the breeze from Pārvatī’s face.
Because by blowing upon it with the mouth, the eyes would become free of dust;
[he is] for him whose fragrance—his sweet scent—is like that of a blooming lotus as it breathes forth.
And because of the comparison...
Thus, there is the substitution of *it*.
Thus, having indulged in the path of sensual pleasure and being favored by the god of love,
the bull-bannered Lord dwelt for one month with Umā in the palace of the King of Mountains.
In this manner, the Lord remained with his beloved in his father-in-law’s house for the duration of a month, according to his desire.
Of what sort?
He by whom the God of Love (Manmatha) was favored through the service of that path or way which brings pleasure to the senses, such as young women and the like.
Having thus consoled Himavat— who was afflicted by the pain of separation from his daughter— the Self-born One wandered here and there,
traveling on his bull of immeasurable speed.

Then Bhava, having consoled, obtained permission from, and comforted his father-in-law who was grieving over the separation from his daughter, traveled on his swift-moving bull and sported in those celestial gardens which are about to be described.
The meaning is: having obtained permission after having made him agree.
He describes those very places of recreation:

Having reached Meru, the skillful Indra, whose vehicle is drawn by horses, attended by Pārvatī’s breasts, spent the night devoted to amorous dalliance upon a bed formed by the arrangement of golden sprouts. 22.
Then the God, having gone to Mount Meru and being solely intent on dalliance, enjoyed the night upon a bed of golden shoots— a couch with a coverlet of gold leaf—
while his bull, swift as the wind,
carried him and was preceded by the breasts of Pārvatī.
Because of her subsequent remaining there, it is called *yāna* (a vehicle/bed).
And thus, the fortunate man becomes a partaker of merit through the touch of his beloved’s breasts.
That which is spread out is a *saṃstara*, meaning a bed (*talpa*).
On the rocky surfaces marked by the footprints of Padmanābha, he tasted fresh drops of nectar;
and on the ridges of Mount Mandara, he dwelt as a bee upon the lotus-face of Pārvatī.
At times, that bee hovering over the lotus-face of his beloved remained upon the slopes of Mount Mandara.
Of what kind?
Having obtained fresh drops of nectar,
due to its being a mountain of churning.
For this very reason, on stones marked with the two feet of Viṣṇu— that is, on stones bearing his footprints—
the state of being marked by bracelets [is explained] because they have been fashioned into clusters upon her pair of arms.
Frightened by the roar of Rāvaṇa, she— her firm arms wound around his neck—
accompanied the Teacher of the World as he entered the bright moonlight on Mount Ekapiṅgala.
At one time, that Teacher of the World entered and took his meal upon Mount Ekapiṅgala.
Of what sort was he?
He whose thick arm-encirclement—a noose of arms—was clung to his neck by Gaurī, who was terrified by the speech of the ten-faced one.
For previously, Kailāsa had been shaken by Rāvaṇa out of a desire to uproot it.
Even at that time, there is possibility.

The southern breeze, bearing sandalwood creepers and lavanga and kesara flowers, drank away the fatigue of his beloved— she who delighted in the slopes of the Malaya mountain— just as a flatterer drinks up the weariness of his patron.
The wind from Mount Dardura, for him who took pleasure in the ridges of the Malaya mountains, consumed her exhaustion like a servant.
For the Malaya and Dardura mountains are interconnected.
What kind of wind is it?
It is that by which the sandalwood creepers have been shaken and made to tremble.
Likewise, "salavaṅgakesaram" means "together with cloves and saffron," which is an expression of fragrance.
It must be considered whether this exhaustion belongs to the Goddess or to the Lord.
[She whose] beloved was struck by a golden lotus had her eyes closed by the water from his hand. 25.

Gaurī plunged into the river in the sky for the sake of water-sports; she agitated the *taraṅgiṇī*, the celestial river in the firmament. Of what sort was she? Her girdle was made redundant by the rows of fish [in the river]. 26. Her girdle was made redundant by the rows of fish. 26. Gaurī plunged into the river in the sky for the sake of water-sports; she agitated the *taraṅgiṇī*, the celestial river in the firmament. Gaurī plunged into the river in the sky for the sake of water-sports; she agitated the *taraṅgiṇī*, the celestial river in the firmament. Of what sort
She whose beloved was struck and distressed by red lotuses and golden water-lilies now has her eyes closed by the waters from his hands—
the water poured from his palms—
while she possesses a second girdle that is merely a row of fish, serving as a repetition of her [existing] one.
Because he stood with his body turned toward her hips,
the three-eyed god, while adorning her with pārijāta flowers fit for the curls of Puloma’s daughter,
was gazed upon with longing by the celestial damsels in the Nandana grove for a long time.

As the three-eyed Lord adorned that beloved woman with pārijāta flowers worthy of Śacī’s own mass of hair, he was watched longingly by the celestial women, Indrāṇī and the others, who thought: "Blessed indeed is she, for even the Lord of All speaks such endearing words to her. Now, wishing to describe the setting of the sun and so forth, he says:

Having thus experienced celestial, terrestrial, and human happiness in the company of his beloved, Śaṅkara once returned to the Gandhamādana mountain when the sunlight was turning crimson at sunset. Thus, having enjoyed celestial, terrestrial, and human pleasures born of the world of men along with the Goddess, the Lord once turned back toward his own dwelling on Mount Gandhamādana and returned there, as the sun’s heat grew reddish due to the power of its setting.
The non-red becomes red; it turns crimson, and there is also a return, a cessation.
Just as when she has gone abroad, food, progeny, dharma, fame, and happiness depart.
When she has returned, oh, the noblewoman, who is a kinsman, turns back.
There, resting upon a surface of golden rock and beholding the sun within the range of his vision,
he addressed his partner in dharma, who was leaning against his left arm.

There, in the grove of Kailāsa, having taken his seat upon the back of a slab of the golden mountain and gazing at the beautiful sun visible to the eye, Hara spoke to his wife standing at his left side.
He says:

"O Lord of Creatures, as if transferring the lotus-like luster from the three parts of the dawn's redness onto your two eyes, this lord of day withdraws the day at its end, just as you withdraw the world. (30)
This lord of the day, the master of the day, withdraws the day and causes it to perish,
just as Rudra at the end of an aeon [withdraws] the three worlds;
as if having transferred the splendor of the lotus to your two eyes with their red outer corners.
This inference arises from the lack of luster in the lotuses and the presence of passion in her eyes.
"Aharpati" means the lord of the day;
[this is] from the word *ahan*.
The letter *r* [is substituted] when followed by a consonant other than *s*.
As the sun declines, casting its rays far away from the spray of water droplets,
these waterfalls of your father reach a state devoid of the encircling rainbow.

These waterfalls of your father Himavat— meaning the falling waters— reach a state of emptiness or separation from the "encircling" (pariveśa), which is the pervasive presence of Indra’s bow (the rainbow).
Why?
Because when the sun has set and Vivasvat is hanging low, he causes the contact with water droplets—the mingling of spray—to be removed by his rays.
[This is expressed] by deriving a verbal sense from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
Thus ends the section on the causative suffix *ṇic*.

Of the two cakravāka birds in the lake, who have abandoned the filaments of the lotus they had bitten, who are crying out with their necks turned back, and who are helpless—their small separation has become vast.
Even the slight interval or separation between the pair of cakravāka birds in the lake has become no longer small; it has become great and far-reaching.
Because it is impossible to effect their union,
since they are helpless and not under their own control; by the power of fate, there is a separation between them at night.
And thus, out of the power of grief, having abandoned the filaments of the lotus— which was spotted and torn—
the two birds, with their wings drooping and crying out,
had their throats turned and rendered discordant.
For in separation, those two have hoarse throats;
"virahadīnakaṇṭhayoḥ" is an alternative reading.
The word *nighna* is used here like *śatrughna* and other such terms.
In the case of the two cakravāka birds, the male is mentioned first [along with] the female.
Having left their daytime resting place, which was scented with the broken-off branches of *sallakī* trees,
these elephants take water for their morning ablutions— the water in which bees cling to the lotuses.
These elephants, having abandoned their midday station, take up water and resort to its center.
For the sake of that meal which is taken at night until the end of the night when it has dawned, they wander about the water at night.
What kind of place is it?
It is perfumed—that is, made fragrant—by the breaking off of the branches, the fragments of shoots, of the *sallakī* trees, which are a species of water-born creepers.
What kind of water is it?
It is that in which bees are trapped within the lotuses due to their closing.
"Behold, O you of measured speech, the golden bridge-like embankment created by the sun as it hangs over the western horizon, fashioned by its long reflection upon the waters of the lake.

O you of measured speech, O you who speak little, look! By the sun situated in the region of Varuṇa, a golden bridge-like embankment has been fashioned as if out of the lake's water by means of its long reflection—that is, by its elongated image; it has been constructed like a golden causeway.
Because of the pervasion of the near and far shores by the image.
Having waded through and scattered the pond of thick mud after enduring the heat of the sun,
the leaders of the forest boar herds emerge, like fanged creatures with their curved tusks having bitten through lotus shoots—
having dispersed the dense mire of the pool and cast it aside, they ascend the dry land, free from distress.
Because the heat has passed;
for, out of fear of the scorching heat, boars, buffaloes, and other such animals spend the day in the midst of the mud.
Those who possess tusks are called *daṃṣṭriṇaḥ*.
Therefore, it is suggested (utprekṣyate): they are like those whose curved lotus-sprouts are bitten and stuck [in their mouths].
The tusks possess a white curvature similar to that of lotus-sprouts.
Although this is an invariable fact, the qualification "tusked ones" (daṃṣṭriṇaḥ) is used for the sake of poetic suggestion (utprekṣā).
Perched upon the tip of this tree, its circle of plumage as bright as the essence of gold,
this peacock, O lady of full thighs, seems to drink up the waning heat of the day at its close.
(36) O you of great thighs, this peacock, seated on the edge of the tree, seems to drink— that is, to swallow— the fading, diminishing heat of the day's end.
Of what kind?
Its circular expanse is as white as molten gold, like liquid gold, and its rim is copper-colored.
Some, however, say that this is an adjective qualifying the peacock feather.
And this is irrelevant, because he lacks whiteness.
The sky, appearing as if its mud has been laid bare on one side by the onset of the darkness of the eastern quarter,
shines like a lake from which the water of sunlight has been carried away by the sun, leaving only a small remnant.
The sky appears and manifests as if something remains, like a pond with a little water left;
for in its eastern part, due to the emergence of darkness from the direction of Indra (the east), it is imagined to have become, on one side, as if its mud were exposed.
This very sky has its "water" consisting solely of the heat that has been withdrawn by the sun.
For when the heat has been drunk up by the sun, there occurs the manifestation of a small amount of remaining mud;
that which remains of it is "that which has a remainder" (śeṣavat).
The word "iva" (as if) is displaced [in the compound].
With deer dwelling in the courtyards of their leaf-huts, with young trees succulent from the watering of their roots,
and with the sacrificial cows for the fire entering [the enclosures], these hermitages, in which the fires have been kindled, possess a manifest splendor.
These hermitages bear beauty.
By whom?
By the deer and antelopes occupying the courtyard of the hut— the open space of the leaf-hut—
and by the young trees and saplings, which were nourished and made to flourish by being watered at their basins.

The compound *agnidhenūḥ* is a genitive-tatpuruṣa (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), where the word *agni-* is understood through the dative case (*caturthī-arthapratipādya*) as being equivalent to "food for a horse" (*aśvaghāsa*).
Even when its bud is closed, the lotus remains for a moment with its opening slightly ajar,
as if desiring to grant an entrance to the bee out of affection.
This lotus, though its bud is bound and yet possesses a slight opening— meaning it is still closed— [remains thus].
The western quarter, its immeasurable rays submerged deep within, shines with the sun turned crimson;
it gleams like a maiden adorned with a tilaka of bandhujīva flowers upon her forehead,
which is covered in hair.

The sun is qualified as having rays that are "sunk" (dūramatyarthaṃ bruḍitāḥ) very deeply, and for that reason "measurable" (parimeyāḥ)—that is, few—even by [the comparison of] a *tilaka* flower possessing filaments (*kesara*) and anthers (*sakiñjalka*).
Accompanied by thousands of Sāman-chanters whose voices were as heart-pleasing as those of the horses of a chariot... (8.41ab)
Those who subsist on the warmth of his rays praise Bhānu, whose splendor is scattered by fire.
These thousand Vālakhilyas, his companions, chant the Sāman hymns to the Sun;
they are called "companions" because they travel together with the chariot of the Sun.

Due to their great number, they are said to be "in the thousands. Of what kind were these *sāman* chants? They were those whose sound was heart-pleasing—that is, captivating—to the horses of the chariots (*syandanāśva*).
Of what sort was the sun?
It was one whose splendor was scattered into fire—that is, whose brilliance had been cast or deposited into the fire.
For it is a well-known tradition that at night the sun sets after casting its brilliance into the fire.
Of what nature are the Vālakhilyas? They are so called because they drink the heat—the warmth—of the rays.
With horses whose necks are bent low, eyes flickering at the touch of the chowries against their ears,
and manes disheveled by the yoke, he sets toward the great ocean as the day comes to an end;
when the sun has departed, the sky is as if fast asleep— such is the course of great splendor.
Indeed, as much as he has risen, he is lost by his very closing.
(8.43cd) The station of the sun, followed even by twilight, is worthy of worship as it is delivered to the crest of the setting mountain;
how could she, who was formerly honored by him at his rising, not follow him in his time of distress? (8.44ab–cd)
O lady with curly hair, these millions of clouds, crimson, yellow, and brownish-red, appear like well-arranged streaks of paint beautifully applied by the twilight hour;
they rest upon the manes of lions on the mountains and upon trees laden with sprouts. (8.45–8.46ab)
Behold the twilight glow upon the mountain peaks, as if divided among themselves.

These ascetics, who have released their feet from the earth and perform water-offerings with pure waters from the lakes, being knowers of the ritual rules, reverently recite the hidden Veda at the time of twilight for the sake of purification. (8.46cd–8.47)
"Therefore, you ought to grant me a moment for the observance I have begun.
Your circle of friends, skilled in diversion, will amuse you, O sweet-spoken one.
Then, pouting her lower lip, she became intent on disregarding her husband’s words.
Vijayā spoke senseless words to the daughter of the mountain king who was standing nearby.
The Lord, too, having performed the ritual appropriate for the end of the day preceded by mantras,
approached Pārvatī— who remained silent out of resentment— and spoke to her again with a smile.
"Abandon your anger, O you who are prone to causeless wrath; I have been saluted by the twilight.
Do I not know my own wife, whose conduct is like that of the cakravāka bird?
O fair-limbed one, she is the body which was formerly cast off by the Self-Existent One when he created the ancestors."
Thus, O proud lady, she both sets and rises; for that reason, I hold her in high esteem.
Behold her, oppressed by the increase of darkness, with shadows clinging to the ground, like a river flowing down a slope, its banks lined on one side with rows of *tāla* trees.
The western quarter bears the remaining glow of twilight, a streak of red light,
like a blood-stained sword-blade cast aside askance upon the battlefield.
While the radiance born of the junction between night and day is obstructed by Mount Sumeru...
This unrestrained, blinding darkness spreads in all directions before the eyes of the steadfast;
8.55cd Neither upward can the gaze go, nor downward, neither to the sides, nor in front, nor behind;
8.56ab Enveloped by this gloom like a fetus in the womb, the world remains thus at night. 8.56cd

Whether pure or turbid, stable or moving, crooked or endowed with the quality of straightness—everything is made uniform by darkness. Fie upon the greatness of the wicked, for which there is no distinction!
Surely the Lord of Sacrifice is rising to dispel the darkness of night. (8.57–8.58ab)
O lotus-faced one, the face of the quarter seems struck by the pollen of ketaka flowers;
the night, its form veiled by Mount Mandara, is perceived through the moon along with the stars.
You, having met with your dear friend, seem as if you will hear words from behind me.
The lunar orb, urged by night, vomits forth this secret of the quarters— its former smiles of bodily luster seen until the end of day were now blocked from emerging (8.60ab)—
as it appears with the glow of the *pākava* fruit, its reflection marking the sky like a lotus pond (8.61ab).
The pair of cakravāka birds is mocked by the moon, whose object is far removed [from them].

(8.61cd) It is possible for you to fashion an ear-ornament from the new sprouts of the Lord of Herbs (the moon), which are as tender as young grass-blades, using your fingertips with untrimmed nails. (8.62ab–8.62cd)
As if gathering the mass of darkness with its rays like a tangle of hair with fingers,
the moon seems to kiss the face of the night, whose eyes are the lotuses now closed in buds.
Behold, O Pārvatī, the vault of the sky, where the dense darkness has been pierced by the beams of the new moon.
The Mānasa lake, defiled by the bodies of elephants, appears as if it has become completely clear.
(8.64cd) Having abandoned its state of redness, this moon has arisen with a perfectly pure orb.
(8.65ab) Indeed, a transformation born of the fault of time does not persist among those whose nature is stainless. (8.65cd)
The moonlight rests upon the heights, while the night’s darkness takes refuge in the depths;
surely the Creator has fashioned here the course of virtues and faults according to their own nature.
Upon the mountain, droplets of water from the moonstones flow forth, impelled by the rays of the moon.

The peacocks are awakening these [birds] who were sleeping on the trees that serve as their girdles at an untimely hour. Now, O lady of faultless beauty, the moon approaches with eagerness, as if to count the strands of necklaces with its rays shimmering upon the tops of the wish-fulfilling trees.
Due to its undulating ridges and hollows, this moonlight on the mountain, mingled with darkness,
shines like the decorative patterns applied in various ways to an elephant in rut.
This mountain, as if unable to endure the weight of the moon’s radiance that it has inhaled and now exhaled, [shines forth].
The night-lotus, its sound silenced by the departure of the bees, is being severed from its stalk.
Behold, O passionate one, as the wind blows, the garment hanging from the wish-fulfilling tree— its true form obscured by the pure moonlight—
is revealed only as it flutters about.

It is possible, O lady with lovely face, that these clusters of fallen flowers from the trees— delicate as they are, tossed upward by fingers and resembling the massed radiance of the moon frayed by leaves— may serve to bind back your disheveled tresses.
And this moon, with its shimmering orb, is now joined by the constellation Tārakā.

Like a bride newly initiated, trembling with nervous apprehension, she approaches her groom. O you whose eyes are marked by the reflection of the moon’s orb, the moonlight seems to grow upon the two streaks of your cheeks, which are as fair as the stalks of ripened reeds and radiant with their shimmering reflections.
Bearing for herself the honey of the Kalpa-tree placed in a vessel of red coral,
this presiding deity of the Gandhamādana forest has come before you in person.
Your face is naturally fragrant with moist filaments and possesses eyes that are intoxicated with passion.
"O playful one, what further quality will intoxication add to you who have already attained sovereignty here?
Or rather, let your circle of friends, who honor you with devotion, partake of this which kindles the god of love.
Having spoken thus nobly, Śaṅkara made Ambikā drink the beverage.

Pārvatī, though experiencing a transformation born of that enjoyment, became like a mango tree turning into a *sahakāra* tree— a change wrought by the inconceivable power of destiny— even as her charming friend [Manoharā] remained unaware.
At that moment, their modesty was overturned and their passion kindled, yet they did not proceed to the bed.
That fair-faced woman became subject to the will of both her beloveds and to intoxication.
With her face—her eyes rolling, her speech faltering, with beads of sweat and a smile born of intoxication—the Lord did not yet drink in Umā’s face for long; rather, he drank it in with his eyes.
Carrying that heavy burden of hips adorned with a girdle of dangling gold,

Hara entered the crystal stone chamber, which was the domain of the splendor accumulated through meditation. There he saw a couch with a coverlet as white as a swan, as beautiful to behold as the sandy banks of the Ganges.

Accompanied by his beloved, he reclined upon the couch like the lord of Rohiṇī amidst an autumnal cloud. (8.82cd) That lovemaking with Pārvatī—wherein the hair was disheveled, the sandal-paste on the chest was completely rubbed away by fingernails, and the waist-bands were torn asunder—did not lead to satiety, even though it was performed with passion. (8.83)
When the rows of stars had bowed down out of compassion for his beloved alone,
he, whose chest was embraced by her, indulged in the curiosity of closing his eyes.
That wise man, worthy of such praise, awoke together with the golden lotus-pools.
At dawn, the auspicious songs of the *kiṃnara*s, accompanied by melodies in the *keśika* scale, were sung for them.
For a moment, the couple relaxed their embrace as the breezes from the forests of Gandhamādana— announcing the blooming of lotuses and stirring the waves of their hearts— waited upon them.
At that moment, Hara’s eyes were captivated by the rows of nail-marks at the base of her thighs;
he stopped his beloved as she was tightening her loose garment.
He [beheld her] with eyes reddened by sleeplessness and a lower lip deeply bitten by his teeth.

Beholding her face with its hair disheveled and its painted markings washed away, he did not attain satisfaction. At the end of the night, even though the bed was spotless, he could not leave it— its coverlet torn and uneven, its girdle knotted together in the middle, and stained by the red dye from her feet.
Desiring to enjoy day and night the nectar of his beloved’s face, which increases his thirst,
he became invisible to those who sought him by sight, due to his departure for the sake of announcing his victory.
There, at the junction of day and night, he remained with his companion Śambhu.
A hundred seasons passed for her like a single night;
yet he did not become one whose thirst was severed from the pleasures of love, remaining like a fire within the ocean, [craving] its waters.
Thus ends the eighth canto in the Kumārasambhava; the work of the illustrious Kālidāsa—may it be auspicious!
